Foundations · Chapter 1

Set up your machine and refresh Python

Install Python 3.13 with uv, get one LLM key into .env, and know which of the course's refresher files covers what, so the later chapters never stall on tooling.

FoundationsClasses 01 to 0310 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Most "my agent does not work" problems in the first week are setup problems: the wrong Python, a key in the wrong place, a notebook run from the wrong folder. Doing this once, properly, saves the whole course.

One-time setup (from PREREQUISITES.md)

Step What the repo says
Python 3.10 or newer; individual projects pin an exact version in .python-version (the course pins 3.13)
uv The package and project manager used all course long; each code folder ships pyproject.toml and uv.lock, so uv sync rebuilds the exact environment
Windows Use Git Bash or Windows Terminal, never plain CMD or PowerShell
Editor VS Code, because the course leans on .py scripts, a real terminal and proper debugging, not only notebooks
LLM key At least one provider key. Free: Groq and OpenRouter (its openrouter/free model name auto-routes to a free model so it never goes stale). Paid: OpenAI, Anthropic
.env Copy .env.example to .env, paste a real key (for example GROQ_API_KEY=...), then uv run main.py. .env is git-ignored at the repo root, so a real key cannot be committed by accident

The free model in the LangChain notebook is created with init_chat_model("openrouter/free", model_provider="openrouter") (the notebook also names one specific free model, nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free).

Common trapA real key is hard-coded in a notebook

Langchain (1).ipynb (Weekend 04, Models) sets an OpenRouter key directly in a cell, and the shared 12 July Colab sets a Groq key in a cell. I am not reproducing either. Treat any key that has been committed or shared as compromised: revoke it and use .env or Colab Secrets. (Chapter 18 notes a similar case.)

From the class 1 and 2 write-ups

Read in full: 01 - 27 June - Python Setup & API Basics.md and 02 - 28 June - Python Refresher.md.

Class 1: environment and first API call.

  • Ground rules. Class starts at 8:00 AM IST, with a short grace only in class 1 and a five-minute wait after. Confirm video, audio and screen. Take notes and watch live rather than coding along, then practise from the recording: for every hour of class, about two hours of your own practice.
  • Shell. Avoid CMD and PowerShell for this course: many Linux-style commands fail there, nearly every cloud machine you will SSH into is Linux, and the aim is to be platform-agnostic. On Windows use Git Bash or Windows Terminal. WSL works but was described as heavy.
  • uv replaces the juggling of pip, venv and conda or poetry with one tool. The "room" analogy: uv venv builds a room, activating it walks you in, and what you install stays inside. uv init creates a project with a pyproject.toml (Python version and dependencies), like a recipe with exact quantities; it is the same idea as package.json or Maven. uv reads only pyproject.toml, so avoid mixing pip install and uv add in one project, and you can run through uv run without activating.
  • Why VS Code, not notebooks. This is an agentic AI course, not classic data science: it leans on .py scripts, a built-in terminal (you will SSH into remote machines) and easier debugging.
  • Python highlights. No type declarations, f-strings, and docstrings that matter more here because agent tooling reads them later. if __name__ == "__main__": was left as homework.
  • First API call. The demo used requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10) against a live currency-rate API (the timeout is "hanging up if no one answers in 10 seconds") and checked the USD to INR rate against a web search. If your code needs outside data, it needs an API, which is how LLMs are called too.
  • Framework philosophy. "Agent is a concept; never learn a concept through a framework first." Plain Python before LangChain.

Class 2: Python refresher.

  • Windows fix-up. Use Git Bash inside VS Code's terminal, not PowerShell. When an activation command differs by OS, ask an assistant to translate it instead of memorising variants.
  • Refresher. Types, f-strings, if/else, lists, and indexing: positive from 0 and negative from -1 (in ["Tokyo", "Delhi", "London"], index -1 is London).
  • Classes. A BankAccount with __init__, deposit, withdraw and a history list. Refusing a withdrawal larger than the balance is a first guardrail check.
  • @dataclass. Removes boilerplate by generating __init__ from the fields; use field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults. It does not validate types.
  • Decorators. A decorator wraps a function without changing it, like gift-wrap. @decorator is shorthand for func = decorator(func). Use functools.wraps so the original name survives. The same pattern underlies the @tool decorator later.
  • Why Pydantic. Python allows create_user(25, "Mayank") with the arguments swapped, and manual isinstance checks do not scale. A BaseModel converts "25" to 25 and raises ValidationError for a list. The book on Pydantic follows this one.
  • Q&A worth keeping. The instructor said he personally avoids agent frameworks in his own production work when he can, preferring simple API orchestration to control token cost and execution; frameworks are like WhatsApp compared with SMS, convenient but worth understanding underneath. Agents for DevOps are framed as "mini interns". Vibe coding can get an app 80 to 90 percent of the way, but have a developer review security and data handling before publishing.

(The class 1 write-up also contains job-referral details, which are not study material and are left out.)

Repo noteA cross-OS path audit in the course repo

.github/workflows/path-audit.yml runs scripts/check_repo_paths.py on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS for every push and pull request. The checkout itself is the real test, and the script then checks tracked paths for illegal Windows characters, reserved device names, leading or trailing spaces and dots, non-ASCII names, case-only and Unicode collisions, symlinks, submodules, paths over 200 characters (a warning at 180, because Windows allows 260 for the whole path including the student's clone folder), files over 50 MB, committed junk such as .DS_Store or .venv, and nested .git folders (which make git add skip a folder). It is a small, good example of a CI check that protects students, and a useful idea for your own repo.

Repo notePlaceholder files in the repo

The Weekend 03 .env.example lists five provider keys (OpenAI, Groq, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter) with empty values, and its main.py is only the uv init placeholder that prints a greeting. The Weekend 13 README is an empty file. The Weekend 00 README says no code ships for the induction weekend and points to the prerequisites; the Weekend 08 README is a short index for class 14 (shell tools and custom middleware), noting the class code was not shared and linking the class Colab.

Foundations · Chapter 1A

APIs, JSON and HTTP in plain words

Every AI call is an API call. This chapter explains requests, JSON, endpoints, the five HTTP verbs, headers, authentication and status codes with a restaurant analogy, using real Tavily, Apify and Claude requests as examples.

FoundationsClass 01 and the instructor's guide "APIs, Properly Explained"15 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Class 01 of the course is "Python setup and API basics" for a reason: an LLM, a search tool and a connector are all reached the same way. If you can read a request and a status code, most integration failures stop being mysterious.

Core ideas

An API is a waiter

You do not cook in the restaurant kitchen. You tell a waiter what you want, the waiter takes it to the kitchen, and food comes back. Ask, do the work, hand back the result: that round trip is every API, including the ones behind ChatGPT and Claude. Your app sends a message to Claude's API, Claude's servers do the thinking, and text comes back; your app never touches a GPU.

Claude's connectors are the same trip. When you ask what is on your calendar, Claude sends a real request to the Calendar API using a token you approved, gets JSON back, and turns it into a sentence. It never sees your Google password.

JSON is a labeled box

Almost every request and response is JSON: curly braces, labels, values. Text goes in quotes; numbers and true/false do not.

{ "dish": "Pizza", "size": "Large", "extraCheese": true }

When your code sends role: "user", content: "Hi!" to Claude, that one labeled box is the whole message.

Endpoints and query parameters

An endpoint is a fixed URL that always means the same thing (Tavily search is always api.tavily.com/search). Parameters customise a call without a new endpoint: after a ? in a URL, or in a request body (max_results, search_depth). Same endpoint, same shape; only the parameters move.

The five HTTP verbs

Verb Meaning Restaurant version
GET Read Check on your order
POST Create Place a new order
PUT Replace the whole thing Swap the whole order
PATCH Change one detail Tweak one detail
DELETE Remove Cancel it

With Apify you POST to start a scraper run, GET its status, and DELETE a schedule you no longer need.

Body versus headers

The body is the order itself (the JSON). Headers ride alongside: the format you send (Content-Type: application/json), who you are (Authorization: Bearer ...). A GET has no body. Calls to Claude carry a content-type header and an x-api-key; leave one out and the call fails before Claude sees your message.

Pro tipHeader habits

Never put a key in the URL (URLs get logged and pasted). Always set Content-Type when sending a body. Keep keys in environment variables, and use a separate key per project so one leak does not mean rotating everything.

Authentication ladder

From weaker to stronger: no auth, an API key, a bearer token, OAuth 2.0. API keys and bearer tokens are what modern AI tools use. OAuth is the "sign in once, get a token" flow behind connectors. Others you may meet: Basic and Digest auth, OAuth 1.0, custom or query-string auth (avoid the last).

Testing a call

Postman is a visual form for building a request, a friendly first stop before putting a call into n8n or code, and it can show the equivalent cURL command. cURL makes the same request from a terminal, like phoning the kitchen directly. The three real shapes in the guide (Tavily, Apify, Claude) all follow the same pattern: bearer token, content-type header, JSON body, JSON response.

Status codes

Only the first digit matters at first: 2xx good news, 4xx you slipped up, 5xx they did.

Code Meaning
200 / 201 / 204 OK / created / done, nothing to return
400 Bad request (malformed)
401 Unauthorized (missing or wrong key)
403 Forbidden (known, but not allowed)
404 Not found
405 Method not allowed
429 Too many requests (slow down)
500 / 502 / 503 / 504 Server error / bad gateway / unavailable / gateway timeout

Whose fault it is tells you what to do: fix your request (4xx) or wait and retry (5xx). A 401 from Tavily means a wrong or expired key; a 429 means add a delay.

When it gets real

Rate limiting (a cap on how fast you may ask), pagination (big answers one page at a time), webhooks (the kitchen calls you), and error handling. The guide names these without detail. Docs and versioning: read the provider's docs first, and pin a version; Claude requires an anthropic-version header so integrations keep working as new features arrive.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Key in the URL Key in logs and chat Put it in a header
Forgetting Content-Type Valid JSON read as garbage Set application/json
Hammering an API 429 Add a delay or backoff
Treating every error alike Retrying a 401 forever 4xx: fix the request; 5xx: retry later

Interview corner

What is the difference between a header and the body?

The body is the data you are sending (the order). Headers are metadata about it: the format, who you are, how to handle it.

What do 401, 403 and 429 mean?

401: not authenticated (missing or wrong key). 403: authenticated but not allowed. 429: you are sending requests faster than the limit.

How does a Claude connector work?

Claude makes a normal API request to the service (for example Gmail) with a token you approved via OAuth, receives JSON, and summarises it. It never sees your password.

Foundations · Chapter 2

LLM basics in plain words

What an LLM actually is, what tokens, context windows and embeddings mean, and why a model remembers nothing, explained with the instructor's analogies before any agent code appears.

FoundationsClasses 03 to 0515 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Every later topic (cost, memory, RAG, guardrails) is a consequence of a few basic facts about how models work. If these are clear, the rest reads as common sense instead of jargon.

Core ideas

LLM calls are stateless

Key ideaThe model remembers nothing

Each API call takes an input and returns an output. A chat app only looks like it remembers because it resends the whole conversation on every message. Memory is something you build around the model.

Five terms to know before building an agent (from the class-03 write-up): an LLM predicts the next token, not the next word; tokens are the billing currency and output costs more than input; embeddings put similar meaning close together; the context window is a whiteboard of fixed size; parameters are billions of weights fixed at training time, not the same thing as tokens.

  • Three message roles. The system message ("You are a helpful assistant...") is optional but good practice, and it is resent on every call because the model is stateless. Sending a single "hi" still transmits system plus user plus the assistant reply so far, which you can see in a raw request payload.
  • Knowledge cutoff. Every model card lists a cutoff date; a raw model cannot browse, so asked about yesterday's match it admits it cannot know. A web app can browse only because it layers search on top. This is exactly why agents need tools.
  • Web app versus API. A web subscription is an all-you-can-eat buffet (flat price, usage not shown per token); the API is à la carte (pay per token, full transparency). OpenRouter gives one key for models from every major provider, with the exact input and output token counts visible in its dashboard.

AI terms in plain words (21 terms)

The instructor's glossary site groups 21 terms in six groups and gives each one an analogy.

Group Term One line and the analogy
Foundation Large language model A next-word predictor wearing the costume of understanding: a friend who read everything but was never told what any of it means
Foundation Tokens Lego bricks, not whole words. Prices are counted in tokens, so unusual long words cost more
Foundation Vectors (embeddings) A GPS coordinate for meaning: similar meanings sit close together, so distance between ideas can be measured
Foundation Context window A whiteboard of fixed size: once full, the oldest writing is erased whether or not it mattered
Foundation Parameters Billions of tiny mixing-console sliders, none meaningful alone. Size is only a rough proxy for capability
Reads you Attention Each word decides which neighbours matter ("bank" plus "deposited" means money), for every word at once
Reads you Transformer The engine; the LLM is the car. GPT, Claude, Gemini and Llama all run a version of it
Learns Training Millions of fill-in-the-blank quizzes where the real text is its own answer key
Learns Fine-tuning A focused residency after a general degree; it also teaches what not to say
Learns RLHF Puppy training at scale: humans pick the better answer, nudging behaviour. Raters can reward a confident tone over honesty
Talking to it Prompting Zero-shot is a one-line instruction; few-shot adds worked examples and makes output far more consistent
Talking to it Temperature A dial between the safe answer and the adventurous one. Low for facts and code, higher for brainstorming
Talking to it Hallucination A confident guess wearing the costume of a fact; the matching tone is what makes it dangerous
Getting smarter RAG An open-book exam: fetch relevant documents first, then answer. Only as good as what is retrieved
Getting smarter Context engineering Deciding what is already on the table before the model speaks: history summary, documents, preferences
Getting smarter MCP One universal port (USB-C) instead of a drawer of custom cables
Beyond chat AI agents Hands, not just a mouth: a goal, steps, tools, observe, loop until done
Beyond chat Multimodal More than one sense: images, audio and video as well as text
Beyond chat Reasoning models Trained to think step by step before the final answer
Beyond chat Small language models A tutor for a few subjects, often distilled from a large model: faster and cheaper
Beyond chat AGI vs ASI AGI matches a skilled human at any task; ASI exceeds human ability broadly. Neither exists today

See tokens

Interactive demo (needs JavaScript): type a sentence and see it split into token-like pieces.

Play with the context window

Interactive demo: a conversation that forgets its oldest messages when the window is full.

Interactive demo: save a fact, flood the window, and see a hallucinated answer appear.

What the instructor's simulator teaches (site read in full)

NoteSource

context-with-mayank.netlify.app: all four tabs and the page's own script, read on 31 Oct 2026.

The site is one small page with four tabs. Each is a toy model, and the script shows exactly what it simulates.

  • Context Window. It starts with the line "Hi! My name is Rahul and I love football." and a reply. Every message costs tokens, counted as words times 1.3, rounded up (a rough guess, not a real tokenizer). A slider sets the window from 40 to 300 tokens (default 120). The page counts tokens from the newest message backwards; messages that fit are "Still Remembered", older ones become "Forgotten". A bar shows the window filling, one block per 5 tokens.
  • Memory Types. Short-term memory is the current conversation: limited, fast, forgotten when the window is full. Long-term memory is stored preferences or an external memory system that can persist across chats and be retrieved later. In the demo, a short-term item turns grey once its message is pushed out of the window, while long-term items stay green. The long-term list is simply kept outside the chat, which is the point.
  • Hallucinations. Save a fact ("Example: My favorite city is Tokyo"), flood the window with large text, then ask "What was my favorite city?". If the fact is still in the window the AI answers correctly; if not, it gives a made-up answer such as Paris or London. The lesson on the page: hallucinations often happen when important context is forgotten or unavailable.
  • Temperature. A slider from 0 to 2 (default 0.7). Below 0.4: very factual and deterministic. 0.4 to below 1: balanced creativity and accuracy. 1 and above: highly creative with a higher hallucination risk. The page lists low temperature as better for coding and maths, and high temperature as more random and diverse.

Where it simplifies. The made-up answers are a random pick from four fixed cities, not a model; the token counter is a word-count estimate; and the temperature tab only changes a sentence, it does not change any output. A real model forgets by truncation or by the app dropping old messages, and real long-term memory needs retrieval (see the RAG book).

What the AI terms site adds beyond the table

From a full read of all 21 pages of the instructor's AI terms site. The table above has the one-liners; these are the extra points each page makes.

  • LLM: asked "the capital of France is", the model is not looking up a table; it is computing that "Paris" is overwhelmingly the most likely next word.
  • Tokens: every price you see is counted in tokens, so a long unusual word quietly costs more than it looks. "Unbelievable" splits into three pieces.
  • Embeddings: once meaning is a location, the distance between two ideas is measured the way a map measures distance between cities ("dog" and "puppy" near, "dog" and "spreadsheet" far).
  • Context window: "why did it forget what I said three messages ago" is the whiteboard filling up, not carelessness.
  • Parameters: a "70-billion-parameter model" is a slider count, a rough proxy for capacity, never a guarantee of a good answer.
  • Attention: the same word means different things depending on neighbours ("bank" with "deposited" locks onto money), computed for every word against every other, all at once.
  • Transformer: LLM and Transformer are not the same thing; the Transformer is the architecture (stacked attention layers) that makes next-word prediction possible. Early layers catch obvious relations; deeper ones catch tone and implication.
  • Training: hidden text with the real text as its own answer key, so no human labels are needed, which is what makes training at scale affordable.
  • Fine-tuning: a focused residency after a general degree. It teaches what not to say too, including training out confident guessing.
  • RLHF: humans pick the better of two answers and that nudges future behaviour. Caveat from the site: raters may reward a confident, pleasant tone over an honest "I'm not sure".
  • Prompting: zero-shot has no examples; few-shot shows two or three worked examples and makes output much more consistent.
  • Temperature: low for facts, data extraction, code and numbers; higher for brainstorming and creative writing.
  • Hallucination: the model has nothing inside that separates "I know this" from "this sounds plausible", and the matching tone is the danger. Double-check anything that matters.
  • RAG: only as good as what is retrieved. Pulling the wrong document, common when the query is worded differently from the source, makes the model confidently build on the wrong foundation.
  • Context engineering: sits above prompting and RAG. It is why an assistant seems to remember you across sessions even though each message starts from a blank page.
  • MCP: the USB-C idea, one standard port for every tool.
  • Agents: the difference is not intelligence, it is whether the AI has hands or just a mouth.
  • Multimodal, reasoning models, small models, AGI vs ASI: more senses; a trained step-by-step thinking stage before the answer (the "thinking..." pause is real reasoning, not an animation); a distilled specialist that is faster and cheaper; and two theoretical levels (matching, then exceeding humans) that do not exist today.

What AI costs: subscription versus API

From the instructor's guide "AI Web vs. API Economics" (read in full). Its figures are reported 2026 industry numbers, quoted as the guide gives them; check current prices before budgeting.

Buffet versus à la carte. A chat subscription (Claude Pro, ChatGPT Plus) is a buffet ticket: one flat price, one human, one seat, fair-use limits. The API is à la carte: you pay for exactly what you order, and software can order, not just people. Three reasons a $20 login cannot power your app: the licence is for a human in a browser, flat pricing assumes humans pause while software does not, and the providers' terms separate the chat app from programmatic access.

Design it versus run it. You can ask Claude in a normal chat to design an n8n workflow or write code. The moment it must run unattended (on a schedule, on a webhook), it needs its own API key.

The ladder. Asking a question fits the subscription. A chat widget on your site, an automated support agent, or a full agentic system needs the API.

Why bills surprise people: the multiplication, not the price.

  • The API is stateless, so every turn resends the whole conversation, plus the system prompt and tool definitions, plus raw tool results, plus any retry. A demo with one message is the cheapest possible use.
  • The guide reports: an agent handling a request costing about $1.20 in 2026 versus about $0.04 for a 2023 chatbot reply; agentic tasks using on the order of 1,000 times the tokens of a simple reply; and 73 percent of enterprises exceeding their AI budget while per-token prices fell. Falling price per token and rising total spend are not a contradiction.
  • Its case study: Uber reportedly spent its 2026 AI budget in about four months after rolling out token-billed coding tools to roughly 5,000 engineers, then capped spending per employee per tool.

Model pricing. Prices are per million tokens, billed separately for input and output. The guide's July 2026 table spans about 71 times on input price between the cheapest open-weight model and the most expensive premium one, in four tiers: premium (frontier reasoning), mid-tier, budget (classification, extraction, routing: the workhorse for high volume) and open-weight.

Open and self-hosted. Cheaper open-weight models can be called through a low-cost API or run on your own hardware. Self-hosting trades a metered bill for GPUs, engineers and uptime; the guide puts the crossover in the tens of millions of tokens a month for budget models, lower for premium ones. Data that legally cannot leave the building is another reason.

Three questions to choose. Does a person click send every time? Could it run thousands of times a day? Tens of millions of calls a month? Real projects mix all three: a subscription for team chat, an API for the customer bot, an open model for the highest-volume low-stakes task.

Common trapDo not confuse the two products

A subscription login is not an API key. Using a consumer login to drive your own app is outside what it is licensed for.

Open-source and open-weight models

From the instructor's guide "Open Source AI" (read in full). Benchmark figures are the guide's 2026 snapshot and shift with every release.

Two separate questions. Free versus paid is about money. Open versus closed is about whether the trained model itself is published for anyone to download. They are independent: Claude Pro is paid and closed, a free chatbot tier is free and closed, and an open model can be run by you for free or by someone else for a fee.

What "open" means. Open-weight means the trained parameters are released. Licences differ: some (Apache 2.0, MIT) have no real restrictions on use or selling products; others (the guide puts Llama 4 here) add rules; check the licence before shipping commercially.

Where models live. Hugging Face is the shared public library for models, with model cards describing what each does. Ollama's library and LM Studio's search are friendlier windows into it.

Closing the gap. The guide reports the best open models trail the closed frontier by months, not years, on many benchmarks, and that closed models still hold an edge on the hardest reasoning, multimodal and safety-critical work.

Running one yourself. Ollama (command line; ollama pull then ollama run) and LM Studio (a graphical app) both run models on your computer through the same engine, llama.cpp, and expose a local server (the guide gives localhost:11434 for Ollama), so a local model answers like any other API.

Model size and memory. Size is in billions of parameters (7B, 32B, 70B); bigger needs more memory. A graphics card speeds things up a lot, and a plain laptop can run smaller models slowly.

Quantization. Rounding a model's numbers to be less precise shrinks the file a lot for a small quality loss. Most local models are quantized; the tools pick a sensible default.

Why companies do it. Security (nothing leaves your machine; works air-gapped), cost at volume, and speed (no network round trip). Honest trade-offs: you own maintenance and updates, hardware costs money up front, the closed frontier still leads at the very top, and you build the guardrails and polish yourself. Many real systems route routine high-volume work to an open model and keep a frontier model for the hard questions.

Three questions to choose a path. Is the data sensitive or regulated? Is the volume high? Does the task need the single best reasoning available?

Interview corner

Why can a $20 subscription not power my app?

It is licensed for one human in a browser, flat pricing assumes humans pause, and providers' terms separate the chat app from programmatic access. Apps use the metered API instead, where cost grows with the tokens you send, including the whole conversation resent each turn.

Why do LLMs need memory added to them?

Each API call is stateless. The app stores the messages and sends the full history on every call, so the model can use earlier turns.

Follow-up to expect: "What is the cost of that?" Tokens grow with every turn, which is why later chapters cover trimming and summarising history.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Assuming the model remembers earlier calls It "forgets" what you said Resend the history yourself on every call
Treating tokens as words Surprise bills on long or unusual text Count tokens; output costs more than input
Trusting a fluent answer A confident wrong fact Treat fluency as no evidence of truth; retrieve or verify

Foundations · Chapter 3

What an agent is

An agent is an LLM that decides which tool to call, inside a loop, with its memory kept as a growing list of messages. Every later chapter is a better-engineered version of this loop.

FoundationsClasses 04 and 0515 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Frameworks change every year, but this loop does not. Interviewers who ask about LangChain, LangGraph or MCP are usually checking whether you understand what sits underneath. If you can write the loop on a whiteboard, every framework question becomes easier.

Core ideas

1. Model, chatbot, agent

Model Chatbot Agent
Has history No Yes Yes
Has tools No No Yes
Decides what to do next No No Yes

An agent has three parts: a brain (the LLM), memory (the message list) and tools (functions it may call).

2. The model never runs a tool

Common trap"The model calls the function"

It does not. The model only returns a request: a tool name and its arguments. Your code runs the function and sends the result back as a new message. This is why you can validate, log, approve or block any call before it runs.

3. The model sees a description, not your function

You give the model a schema for each tool: a name, a description and the parameters. The description is what it reads to decide when to use the tool, so write it like an instruction.

get_weather_schema = {
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "description": "Get the current weather for a city. Use this whenever "
                       "the user asks about weather in a specific place.",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"city": {"type": "string", "description": "e.g. 'Tokyo'"}},
            "required": ["city"],
        },
    },
}

One question can trigger several tool calls in a single reply. In class, a single question about capitals produced three calls at once.

4. Brain, memory, tools

An agent is just an orchestrator of three things: a brain (an LLM), memory (chat history, in a database or in memory) and tools. The intern analogy: a great brain with no tools cannot act in the world, and a weak brain with a laptop and every tool still fails on complex tasks. The brain's capability is a hard ceiling, and the agent code is plumbing; only the model makes decisions. The mentor's line: once you understand this without a framework, LangChain, LangGraph and CrewAI all become easy because "they are all doing exactly this".

The agentic loop

def run_agent(messages, max_turns=4):
    for _ in range(max_turns):
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=model, messages=messages, tools=TOOL_SCHEMAS)
        message = response.choices[0].message

        if not message.tool_calls:               # plain text = final answer
            messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": message.content})
            return message.content

        messages.append(message)                 # keep the model's tool request
        for call in message.tool_calls:          # may be several in one reply
            args = json.loads(call.function.arguments)
            result = TOOLS_BY_NAME[call.function.name](**args)
            messages.append({"role": "tool",
                             "tool_call_id": call.id,
                             "content": str(result)})
    return "Reached max_turns without a final answer."
Key ideaWhy the loop calls the model again

The model cannot see a tool's output until you append it as a message. So after every tool run, you call the model again. The loop ends when the model replies with plain text instead of a tool request.

Watch the loop

Interactive demo: perceive, reason, act, observe, repeat.

Under the hood

  • Memory is a Python list. In the terminal chat, conversation_memory is one growing list. In Streamlit it lives in st.session_state, because plain variables reset on every rerun.
  • max_turns is a safety cap. Without it, a confused model can loop forever and run up cost.
  • No tool means no tool call. Asked for a currency conversion with no currency tool defined, the model answered in plain text instead of inventing a call.
  • Providers share one shape. OpenAI, Groq and OpenRouter use the same chat format. Anthropic's SDK differs: client.messages.create() and response.content[0].text.
  • Structured output. To get reliable data, ask for JSON only, strip any code fences, then validate with Pydantic before trusting a field.
  • Safe eval. The calculator tool allowed only digits, operators and parentheses before running eval().

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Not appending the tool result Model asks for the same tool again Append a tool message with the matching tool_call_id
No turn cap Endless loop, surprise bill Always set max_turns
Vague tool description Wrong tool chosen, or none Write the description as an instruction

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

An agent is an LLM in a loop. It reads the conversation, decides whether to answer or call a tool, my code runs the tool and returns the result as a message, and the loop repeats until the model answers in plain text. Memory is just the message list I keep resending.

Who actually executes a tool call?

My code does. The model only emits the tool name and arguments. That separation lets me validate arguments, log calls, require approval or block a call before anything runs.

How is an agent different from a chatbot?

A chatbot has history. An agent also has tools and a loop in which the model decides what to do next, including whether to stop.

The model returned an empty answer with a tool call. Is that a bug?

No. When the model wants a tool, content is empty and the useful data is in tool_calls. Your loop should check for tool_calls first.

Foundations · Chapter 4

Agents in plain Python

Build the whole agent with no framework, in sixteen small ideas and seven files, so a framework later is just the same loop with less typing.

FoundationsWeekend 02 and the instructor's site20 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Once you have written the loop yourself, LangChain, LangGraph and CrewAI stop being magic. The mentor's line in class: they are all doing exactly this.

Agents, with just Python: the concept path

The instructor's site builds an agent in 16 small ideas, always with the "windowless room" analogy (a brilliant reader with no phone). This is the same loop as above.

Step Idea in one line
AI model, chatbot, agent A model guesses the next words; a chatbot is the same model handed the whole transcript each turn; an agent is the same model handed a phone and deciding itself when to use it
Calling a real model One plain function call: text in, text out; everything else is a layer around it
Paid vs free providers The shape of the call barely changes between providers (one difference in how the reply is unpacked)
Failing loudly With no working provider, raise a clear error; a confidently fake answer is far worse
Structured output Ask for a fixed JSON shape so code can read the reply
Validation Check the shape the moment the reply arrives and reject anything that does not match
What is a tool An ordinary function with no awareness of AI
Manual tool calling We still decide and call it; the model decides nothing yet
The tool schema A menu, not the kitchen: the model only sees the description, so the wording carries the weight
The model chooses Given a question and the schema, it states which tool and arguments it wants, before any code runs: this is the moment it becomes an agent
The agent loop Decide, act, observe, repeat; the number and order of steps are decided fresh each time
Memory A growing list of messages and tool results re-sent on every call; no hidden memory system
The complete agent and why no framework first Every piece in plain code; a framework later is the same loop with less repetition

Project 0: the agent built in seven files

Weekend 02's Project 0/ folder builds a complete agent with no framework, one idea per file. This is the same loop as in What an agent is, written out in code.

File Idea
_01_ai_model_vs_chatbot_vs_agent.py A model alone, a chatbot (history re-sent), an agent
_02_calling_the_ai_paid_and_free.py The same call against Groq, OpenRouter or OpenAI
_03_structuring_with_pydantic.py Ask for a fixed shape, validate it
_04_giving_it_a_tool.py A plain function that knows nothing about AI
_05_teaching_it_to_choose.py The tool schema, so the model chooses
_06_project_zero_agent.py The assembled loop with max_turns as a safety limit
_07_streamlit_app.py A chat UI with three tools (sample weather, a guarded calculator, currency conversion)

Three patterns worth stealing from them:

  • A provider picker. Groq, OpenRouter and OpenAI all speak the OpenAI-compatible API, so one client works for all three by changing base_url and the model name (llama-3.3-70b-versatile on Groq, openrouter/free on OpenRouter, gpt-4o-mini on OpenAI), and it raises a clear error if no key is set. Anthropic's tool-calling response has a different shape and is covered later in the course.
  • max_turns. The loop gives up after a fixed number of turns and returns "Reached max_turns without a final answer", so a confused model cannot loop forever (the same idea as ModelCallLimitMiddleware in Chapter 7).
  • A guarded calculator. Only digits, operators and parentheses are allowed through before eval() runs, so arbitrary code cannot be smuggled in through the expression.

In _07, memory is st.session_state.messages, a plain list. The Python refresher's last files (_10 to _14) build the same agent as a class: a tool that calls the model, an agent that only talks, an agent with one tool, with three tools (currency, weather, calculator), and finally with memory, whose docstring says memory "is just a Python list" that has been there since _11 as self.messages.

Repo note`_06_project_zero_agent.py` does not run as committed

It parses, but it will fail on the first tool call. It defines get_currency twice (the second definition is just pass, so it returns None and replaces the first), lists only get_weather in TOOL_SCHEMAS, and has leftover live-coding scratch inside run_agent: a line that builds a tool_calls list using an undefined name function (a NameError when reached), plus l1 = [1,2,3,4,5] and some empty nested loops after the function. Use _07_streamlit_app.py for a version that is meant to run.

Key ideaWhere Pydantic fits

Step 3 of Project 0 and the structured-output idea in the table above rely on Pydantic. The Pydantic book covers it in full, and Agentic AI with LangChain chapter 4 uses it for structured output.

The "Agents, with just Python" site, page by page

From a full read of all 22 pages. The whole site uses one picture: a brilliant reader in a windowless room.

  1. AI model: predicts the next words; for anything that needs the current state of the world (today's weather) it can only guess confidently, because guessing is its only tool.
  2. Chatbot: the same model handed the whole transcript each turn. That fixes forgetting but not checking anything real: remembering the conversation and knowing today's weather are different problems.
  3. Agent: the same model handed a phone. The key word is decides: a chatbot with a weather function bolted on is not an agent if a human decides when to call it. The decision has to belong to the model.
  4. Calling a real model: underneath every chat interface is one plain call (text in, text out); memory, tools and judgement are layers wrapped around it.
  5. Paid vs free providers: the call has nearly the same shape across providers, with one difference in how the reply is unpacked.
  6. Failing loudly: with no working provider, fail immediately and name what is missing. A fake plausible answer is a trap, because nobody notices it needs fixing.
  7. Structured output: ask for a fixed shape (a small JSON object) so code can read the reply instead of a human retyping it.
  8. Validation: check the shape the instant a reply arrives and reject mismatches with a precise reason, turning "probably correct" into "nothing proceeds unless provably correct".
  9. What is a tool: an ordinary function with no awareness of AI. What matters is who decides to call it.
  10. Manual tool calling: we read the reply and call the function ourselves. Fine as a first step, but the model still decides nothing.
  11. The tool schema: a menu, not the kitchen. The model never sees the code, only the description, so the wording carries all the weight.
  12. The model chooses: given the question and the schema together, it states which tool and arguments it wants before any code runs. This is the moment a system becomes an agent.
  13. The agent loop: reason, act, observe, repeat. This one idea separates an agent from a fixed hand-coded sequence, because the number and order of steps are decided fresh each time.
  14. Memory: a running list of messages and tool results, re-sent on every call. No hidden memory system, just a growing notepad, and it is what lets the loop work at all.
  15. The complete agent: every piece from plain code; a framework later is the same loop with less repetition.
  16. Why no framework first: you can build something that works while understanding almost none of why; building the loop once means a framework reads as a shortcut, not a black box.

Interview corner

What stops an agent looping forever?

A turn cap such as max_turns, plus timeouts and clear tool descriptions. Production systems also add budgets and monitoring.

Why build the agent in plain Python before using a framework?

The framework hides the same loop: call the model, run the requested tool, append the result, repeat. Knowing it lets you debug a framework, and explain what it does when an interviewer asks.

Interview question bank

Chapter 1A: APIs, JSON and HTTP in plain words

What is the difference between a header and the body?

The body is the data you are sending (the order). Headers are metadata about it: the format, who you are, how to handle it.

What do 401, 403 and 429 mean?

401: not authenticated (missing or wrong key). 403: authenticated but not allowed. 429: you are sending requests faster than the limit.

How does a Claude connector work?

Claude makes a normal API request to the service (for example Gmail) with a token you approved via OAuth, receives JSON, and summarises it. It never sees your password.

Chapter 2: LLM basics in plain words

Why can a $20 subscription not power my app?

It is licensed for one human in a browser, flat pricing assumes humans pause, and providers' terms separate the chat app from programmatic access. Apps use the metered API instead, where cost grows with the tokens you send, including the whole conversation resent each turn.

Why do LLMs need memory added to them?

Each API call is stateless. The app stores the messages and sends the full history on every call, so the model can use earlier turns.

Follow-up to expect: "What is the cost of that?" Tokens grow with every turn, which is why later chapters cover trimming and summarising history.

Chapter 3: What an agent is

Who actually executes a tool call?

My code does. The model only emits the tool name and arguments. That separation lets me validate arguments, log calls, require approval or block a call before anything runs.

How is an agent different from a chatbot?

A chatbot has history. An agent also has tools and a loop in which the model decides what to do next, including whether to stop.

The model returned an empty answer with a tool call. Is that a bug?

No. When the model wants a tool, content is empty and the useful data is in tool_calls. Your loop should check for tool_calls first.

Chapter 4: Agents in plain Python

What stops an agent looping forever?

A turn cap such as max_turns, plus timeouts and clear tool descriptions. Production systems also add budgets and monitoring.

Why build the agent in plain Python before using a framework?

The framework hides the same loop: call the model, run the requested tool, append the result, repeat. Knowing it lets you debug a framework, and explain what it does when an interviewer asks.

Cheat sheet

The key ideas and the agent loop on one page, for revision before moving to the Pydantic and LangChain books. Every item links back to its chapter.

Quick referenceCode is condensed. See the chapters for the full versions
Jump to a section

Setup in five lines (Ch 1)

uv sync                      # rebuild the exact environment from pyproject.toml + uv.lock
cp .env.example .env         # then paste ONE provider key (Groq or OpenRouter are free)
uv run main.py               # .env is git-ignored, so the key cannot be committed

Use Git Bash or Windows Terminal on Windows; use VS Code, not only notebooks. Any key that was ever committed or shared is compromised: revoke it.

An API call in your head (Ch 1A)

Part Remember
Endpoint A fixed URL; options go after ? or in the body
Verbs GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH change a bit, DELETE remove
Headers Content-Type: application/json, Authorization: Bearer ...; never put a key in the URL
Status 2xx fine, 4xx fix your request (401 key, 429 slow down), 5xx wait and retry
Auth ladder none, API key, bearer token, OAuth 2.0

LLM facts that explain most bugs (Ch 2)

  • Stateless: every call starts blank; memory is the message list you resend.
  • Tokens: the unit of cost and of limits; output usually costs more than input.
  • Context window: a fixed whiteboard; when full, the oldest text goes first, and then the model may guess (hallucinate).
  • Temperature: low for facts and code, higher for brainstorming.
  • Embedding: numbers for meaning. Numbers from two different models cannot be compared.
  • Subscription vs API: an app plan is flat-rate; code calls are paid per token.

What an agent is (Ch 3)

Model Chatbot Agent
History no yes yes
Tools no no yes
Decides next step no no yes

Agent = brain (LLM) + memory (message list) + tools. The model only requests a tool; your code runs it and appends the result.

The loop (Ch 3, Ch 4)

def run_agent(messages, max_turns=4):
    for _ in range(max_turns):
        message = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=model, messages=messages, tools=TOOL_SCHEMAS).choices[0].message
        if not message.tool_calls:                    # plain text = final answer
            return message.content
        messages.append(message)                      # keep the model's tool request
        for call in message.tool_calls:               # may be several in one reply
            result = TOOLS_BY_NAME[call.function.name](**json.loads(call.function.arguments))
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id, "content": str(result)})
    return "Reached max_turns without a final answer."

Run in a test with a stub client (key-free): a tool request, then a final answer, gives two model calls; a model that always asks for a tool stops at max_turns.

A tool schema

{"type": "function", "function": {
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get the current weather for a city. Use this whenever the user asks about weather.",
    "parameters": {"type": "object",
                   "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"]}}}

The description is what the model reads to decide when to call it; write it like an instruction.

Common traps

  • "The model calls the function": it does not; it returns a request.
  • No tool in the list means no tool call.
  • Forgetting max_turns means a runaway cost.
  • Keys in a notebook or Colab cell: treat as compromised.
  • Next: Pydantic, then Agentic AI with LangChain.

Pydantic · Chapter 1

Why validation exists, and type hints

Python will happily run with garbage data. Type hints say what you expect, but only a library like Pydantic enforces it at the door.

PydanticClass 03, the notebook, the instructor's site10 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Data from outside your code (an API, a form, a file, an LLM) can be anything. If nothing checks it when it arrives, the crash happens deep inside, far from the real cause. Pydantic's own docs describe it as the most widely used validation library for Python, and the class note lists the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs among the places it is used.

Core ideas

Why Python is "loose"

The class explained it like this: in Java or C++ a variable reserves a block of memory of a declared type. In Python a variable is a pointer to a value, so the same name can point at an int, then a string, then a list, with no complaint. That is great for learning and dangerous in production, where real users, or people trying to break the system, send you data.

AnalogyThe courier with no intake desk

A courier that loads any parcel finds the problem three stops into the route. Pydantic is the intake desk that refuses a bad parcel at the door. (From the instructor's site.)

The notebook shows it with register_user: it computes 2026 - age. age=28 works. age="unknown" crashes inside the subtraction, and age=10000 quietly gives a birth year of -7974, because the types are fine and the value is nonsense. That is the difference between type validation (what kind of data) and data validation (does the value make sense).

Pro tipThe class's point on AI-written code

If AI writes your code, you still need to understand Pydantic to debug or trust it. (Class 03, paraphrased.)

Type hints are documentation, not enforcement

age: int = "not a number" runs. Hints are read by humans, IDEs and Pydantic, and nothing else at runtime.

tags: list[str] = ["python", "pydantic"]     # lowercase built-ins since Python 3.9
word_counts: dict[str, int] = {"error": 12}

def format_price(amount: float, currency: str = "USD") -> str:
    return f"{currency} {amount:.2f}"

Optional and Literal

str | None (or Optional[str]) allows a missing value. The class adds a Python reminder: the missing value is None, with a capital N; there is no null. Literal["low", "medium", "high"] limits a value to a fixed set. Alone they are only documentation; with Pydantic they are enforced, and Literal is how you stop a model returning "kinda urgent i guess".

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Believing a hint is a check Wrong types flow through silently Validate at the boundary with a BaseModel
Checking only the type age=10000 passes Add value constraints (chapter 3)

Interview corner

Does Python enforce type hints?

No. At runtime they are ignored. They help readers, IDEs and libraries such as Pydantic, which reads them and enforces them.

What is the difference between type validation and data validation?

Type validation checks the kind of data (an int). Data validation checks the value makes sense (an age of 10000 is an int but not valid). Pydantic does both: types from hints, values from Field constraints and validators.

Pydantic · Chapter 2

Your first model

A BaseModel validates on creation, converts safe values, collects every error, and has a small set of methods you should know by name.

PydanticDocs "Models", class 03, the notebook15 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

A plain class and a dataclass look like a model but check nothing. Only BaseModel refuses bad data before the object exists.

Core ideas

Three ways to define a data shape

Option Accepts arguments Validates
Plain class (you write __init__) Yes No
@dataclass (auto __init__) Yes No: age="banana" is accepted
BaseModel Yes Yes

The class demo showed a plain class and a dataclass silently accepting garbage, and only BaseModel raising at once.

AnalogyThe customs form

A plain class is a form nobody hands out, a dataclass is a form nobody reads, and a BaseModel is a form with an officer behind it. (Instructor's site.)

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

class SignupForm(BaseModel):
    username: str
    age: int
    newsletter_opt_in: bool = False     # a default makes it optional

SignupForm(username="a", age="28", newsletter_opt_in="True")   # age -> 28, flag -> True
try:
    SignupForm(username="Mayank")        # missing age
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)                             # lists every problem field

A default value is what makes a field optional; without one the field is required. If you do not know the right default, use None.

Coercion ("lax mode")

Pydantic converts reasonable input: the string "28" becomes 28. It refuses what it cannot convert safely: "28eight" fails, and so does 28.5 for an int field (class demo). The docs add that conversion can lose information in some cases (a float like 3.0 becomes 3) and that strict mode turns conversion off (chapter 7).

Common trapCoercion is not symmetric

"25" becomes 25 for an int field, but 12345 is not turned into "12345" for a str field. It is rejected. (Instructor's site.)

The methods to know

Method Use
Model(**data) / Model.model_validate(data) Validate a dict (the second takes options such as strict=True)
Model.model_validate_json(text) Validate a JSON string or bytes directly; generally faster than parsing the JSON yourself
model_dump() / model_dump_json() Back to a dict or JSON string (chapter 5)
model_json_schema() The JSON Schema for the model (chapter 7)
model_copy(update=...) Copy; the updates are not validated, and the copy is shallow unless deep=True
model_construct() Build without validation, for data you already trust; nested dicts stay dicts and the result can be invalid
model_fields_set Which fields were explicitly provided

The docs use "validate" for everything except JSON, where they say "parse". The model's guarantee is about the output: after validation the object matches its declared types and constraints.

Extra data

By default unknown keys are silently ignored. extra="forbid" raises an error, and extra="allow" keeps them. Add extra="forbid" to any model you hand to an LLM provider as a schema, so the model cannot add surprise keys.

Other behaviours worth knowing

  • Models are mutable by default; frozen=True blocks assignment (a "faux" immutability, since nested dicts can still change).
  • Fields are validated in declaration order, and errors, serialization and schema follow that order.
  • Names starting with an underscore are private attributes, not fields.
  • from_attributes=True lets a model read attributes from any object, which is how ORM objects are validated.
  • Inheritance works: a model can extend another and inherit its fields and validators (class Q&A).
  • A custom __init__ is discouraged; use an after-validator or model_post_init instead.
Repo noteIn the notebook

The notebook's years_experience and age demos are the same ideas as above, with "True" coerced to True and age=28.5 rejected.

Configuration in depth (from the official Configuration page)

NoteSource

Pydantic docs, Configuration, read in full on 31 Oct 2026.

Behaviour is controlled by ConfigDict values. Where you can set them:

  • Models: model_config = ConfigDict(...) (a plain dict also works) or class arguments such as class Model(BaseModel, frozen=True). Type checkers understand class arguments, so frozen=True makes mutation a type error. The old V1 Config class still works but is deprecated.
  • Pydantic dataclasses: @dataclass(config=ConfigDict(...)).
  • TypeAdapter: TypeAdapter(list[str], config=ConfigDict(coerce_numbers_to_str=True)). Passing config when the adapter wraps a type that already has its own config is a usage error.
  • Stdlib dataclasses and TypedDict: a __pydantic_config__ attribute, or the @with_config decorator (which avoids type-checking errors on TypedDict).
  • @validate_call also accepts config.
  • Inheritance. Subclass config is merged with the parent's, so one custom parent class can change behaviour globally. With several base classes Pydantic does not currently follow the method resolution order (the docs link an open issue).
  • plugin_settings passes options to plugins, keyed by plugin name; the main one is Logfire, for example {'logfire': {'record': 'failure'}} to record only failures.
  • Propagation, the surprise. Pydantic models and Pydantic dataclasses are each a configuration boundary: a parent's str_to_lower=True does not reach a nested User model. Stdlib dataclasses and TypedDict do inherit the parent's config unless they set their own.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Using a dataclass for external data Bad types pass silently Use BaseModel
Trusting model_construct() output Invalid data inside a "model" Use it only for already-validated data
Assuming unknown keys raise They are dropped silently Set extra="forbid"

Interview corner

BaseModel versus dataclass?

Both give a clean constructor from hints. Only BaseModel validates and coerces, raising one ValidationError before the object is created.

What does the default extra setting do?

It ignores unknown keys. forbid raises; allow stores them.

model_validate versus model_construct?

model_validate checks the data. model_construct skips all checks, so use it only for data you already trust.

Pydantic · Chapter 3

Fields and constraints

Types are not enough. Field() adds ranges, lengths, patterns, defaults, aliases and more, and Pydantic ships ready-made types for emails, URLs and secrets.

PydanticDocs "Fields", class 03, the notebook15 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

age: int accepts -50 and 10000. Real rules (minimum length, a range, a format) belong in the model, so the data is checked in one place.

Core ideas

Constraints

Kind Options
Numbers gt, ge, lt, le, multiple_of
Strings and sequences min_length, max_length, pattern (a regex)
Decimals max_digits, decimal_places 
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class JobApplication(BaseModel):
    full_name: str = Field(min_length=2, max_length=100)
    years_experience: int = Field(ge=0, le=50)

On an optional field (X | None) the constraint applies to the non-None part.

Field() versus Annotated

Two equivalent styles:

from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class A(BaseModel):
    years: int = Field(ge=0, le=50)                    # direct

class B(BaseModel):
    years: Annotated[int, Field(ge=0, le=50)]          # Annotated

The docs recommend Annotated because required fields stay visibly required, you can stack several pieces of metadata, types become reusable, and constraints can target inner items (list[Annotated[int, Field(gt=0)]]). The class note says Mayank prefers plain Field() for readability but warns that AI-generated code often uses Annotated, so you must recognise both. default, default_factory and alias still use normal assignment.

Defaults

  • A plain value, or Field(default=...).
  • default_factory takes a callable, for example one that makes a new id. Since Pydantic 2.10 it may take one argument, the already-validated data, so fields it reads must be declared earlier.
  • Mutable defaults such as a list are copied per instance, so instances do not share state.
  • Defaults are not validated unless you set validate_default=True.

Aliases

alias renames a field for both input and output. validation_alias affects only input, serialization_alias only output. Output uses aliases only when you call model_dump(by_alias=True).

Other options

strict=True (no coercion for this field), frozen=True (cannot be reassigned), exclude=True (omitted from model_dump), repr=False, discriminator (choose a union member by a field's value), deprecated, and schema-only options title, description, examples.

Special types

Type What it does
EmailStr Validates email format (needs pip install "pydantic[email]")
HttpUrl Validates URLs
SecretStr Masks the value in output and logs; read it on purpose with .get_secret_value()
PositiveInt, NonNegativeInt Shortcuts for gt=0, ge=0

The class singled out SecretStr as underused but important in this course, since API keys are handled constantly. In the notebook, account.model_dump(mode="json") is what gets written to a JSON file.

Beyond the classCollection helpers

OnErrorOmit drops invalid items from a collection instead of rejecting the whole thing, and FailFast stops at the first bad item. (Docs "Types".)

Aliases in depth (from the official Alias page)

NoteSource

Pydantic docs, Alias, read in full on 31 Oct 2026.

An alias is an alternative name for a field. There are four ways to set one: alias, validation_alias (a str, AliasPath or AliasChoices), serialization_alias, and alias_generator in the config.

  • AliasPath reads a value from inside nested data: AliasPath('names', 0) takes names[0], and AliasPath('contact', 'address') takes contact['address'].
  • AliasChoices accepts several input names; earlier choices win. If both first_name and fname are sent, first_name is used. Choices can mix plain names and AliasPath.
  • Alias generators name every field at once. Three are built in: to_pascal, to_camel, to_snake. A plain callable works (lambda name: name.upper()), and AliasGenerator lets validation and serialization use different generators.
  • Precedence. An explicit alias on a Field beats the generator by default. alias_priority=2 means the generator never overrides it; alias_priority=1 means the generator does.
  • Config switches. validate_by_alias is True and validate_by_name is False by default; setting both to False is an error. serialize_by_alias is off by default, and the docs say they expect to change that in V3. The same switches exist per call: by_alias and by_name on model_validate, model_validate_json, model_validate_strings and TypeAdapter, and by_alias on model_dump, model_dump_json (default False).
  • Not captured: the other tabs of the config and runtime examples; only one example per group was readable.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Expecting a default to be validated Invalid default slips through validate_default=True
Using Field(...) inside a union on the wrong side Constraint has no effect Put the metadata around the whole union
A plain str for an API key Key appears in logs SecretStr

Interview corner

Field() or Annotated?

Both work the same. Annotated keeps required fields visibly required and is reusable, which is why the docs prefer it. The class prefers plain Field() for readability but wants you to recognise both.

alias versus validation_alias versus serialization_alias?

alias applies to input and output, the other two to only one direction. Output uses aliases only with by_alias=True.

Pydantic · Chapter 4

Validators

Write your own rules: field validators for one field, model validators for rules across fields, in four modes, with a fixed order of execution.

PydanticDocs "Validators", class 03, the notebook20 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Built-in constraints cover most cases. Business rules ("a disposable email is not allowed", "password must equal confirm_password") need code.

Core ideas

field_validator: one field

It sees one field's value and nothing else. Return the value (cleaned or not) to accept, or raise ValueError to reject. Raise ValueError or AssertionError, not ValidationError: Pydantic turns those into entries in its single error. (AssertionError checks vanish if Python runs with -O; PydanticCustomError gives the most control over the message.)

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, field_validator

class JobApplication(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr

    @field_validator("email")
    @classmethod
    def no_disposable(cls, value: str) -> str:
        if value.split("@")[-1].lower() in {"yopmail.com", "mailinator.com"}:
            raise ValueError("disposable email domains are not accepted")
        return value.lower()

Four modes of field validator

Mode Runs Notes
after (default) After Pydantic's own validation The value already has the right type
before On the raw input, before parsing Use Any as the hint; good for cleaning "5 years" to 5
plain Replaces Pydantic's validation Later validators and the type check are skipped, so bad input can pass
wrap Around Pydantic's validation, with a handler Can run code before and after, catch errors, retry with other input, or skip the handler
Common trapThe notebook's "strip years" validator

In the notebook, strip_years_suffix says it runs "BEFORE the int type-check" to turn "5 years" into 5, but it is declared without mode="before". The default is after, so by then Pydantic has already rejected "5 years" as not an int and the validator never sees it. Add mode="before" for the behaviour its docstring describes.

model_validator: rules across fields

The class posed the problem: an applicant with an @infosys.com email needs at least 5 years of experience. A field validator cannot do it, because it sees one field at a time (the class called it "Schrödinger's field"). A model validator sees the whole model.

from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator

class SignupForm(BaseModel):
    password: str
    confirm_password: str

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def passwords_match(self):
        if self.password != self.confirm_password:
            raise ValueError("passwords do not match")
        return self

Model validators also have before (a classmethod receiving raw input, which may not be a dict) and wrap modes. An after-validator is an instance method and must return self.

Key ideaFixed order

Every field validator runs first, for every field. Then the model validator runs on the fully validated object. (Class 03.) Within one field, before and wrap validators run right to left, then after validators run left to right.

Validators that need more context

A validator can take an optional ValidationInfo argument. It carries data (fields already validated, so only earlier fields), a user-supplied context, the mode, and the field_name. Pass context with Model.model_validate(data, context=...); plain Model(...) cannot take it.

Reusable validators

With the Annotated pattern, AfterValidator(fn) and friends attach to a type, so you can define something like an "even number" type once. With the decorator, one function can target several fields, or all of them with '*'.

Repo noteDuplicate method names in the notebook

In the notebook's SignupForm, two field_validator methods are both named reject_disposable_domains. In Python the second definition replaces the first, so only one validator survives. The bodies also raise ValidationError, which is not how you reject a value; they should raise ValueError(...). And they lower-case the password, which would silently change the user's password. Treat that cell as a sketch.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Forgetting to return the value The field becomes None Always return the (cleaned) value
Reusing a method name One validator silently disappears Give each a unique name
Cross-field rule in field_validator Cannot see the other field Use model_validator
Raising ValidationError yourself Wrong error type Raise ValueError
Cleaning raw text in an after validator Never reached Use mode="before"

Interview corner

field_validator versus model_validator?

The first checks one field with no view of the others. The second sees the whole model after every field check has passed, so it handles cross-field rules.

What does mode="before" do, and when do you need it?

It runs on the raw input before type coercion, so you can clean messy input before Pydantic tries to read it. Without it, the validator only sees an already-valid value.

What is the difference between a plain and a wrap validator?

A plain validator replaces Pydantic's check entirely, so invalid input can slip through. A wrap validator calls Pydantic's check through a handler and can catch errors or retry.

Pydantic · Chapter 5

Computed fields and serialization

Derive values instead of storing stale ones, then control exactly what leaves a model: dict or JSON, which fields, which names, and in what shape.

PydanticDocs "Serialization" and "Fields", the notebook15 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Some values should always be calculated from others, and almost every real API must hide or trim fields. Both are small settings once you know them.

Core ideas

@computed_field

Stack @computed_field on a @property. The value is read-only, appears in model_dump() and in the serialization JSON schema (marked read-only), and is recomputed on every access. Pydantic adds no validation or caching to the property.

from pydantic import BaseModel, computed_field

class JobApplication(BaseModel):
    full_name: str
    years_experience: int

    @computed_field
    @property
    def experience_tier(self) -> str:
        return "junior" if self.years_experience < 2 else "mid" if self.years_experience < 7 else "senior"

The notebook builds exactly this tier example.

AnalogyThe receipt total

A receipt total is added up at checkout rather than typed in, so a changed price shows on the next receipt. (Instructor's site.)

Pro tipDo the arithmetic in code, not in the LLM

Models are unreliable at consistent arithmetic. Let the model classify (for example a priority), then derive numbers such as an SLA with a computed_field.

dict, JSON and modes

Call Result
model_dump() A Python dict; nested models converted recursively. Values keep Python types (a tuple stays a tuple)
model_dump(mode="json") Only JSON-compatible types (a tuple becomes a list). The notebook uses this to write account.json
model_dump_json() A JSON string, with support for datetimes, UUIDs and sets

Choosing fields

Option Effect
include, exclude Sets, or nested dicts to reach into lists ('__all__' for every item)
Field(exclude=True) Always omit this field; wins over include
exclude_none=True Drop fields currently None
exclude_defaults=True Drop fields equal to their default
exclude_unset=True Keep only fields the caller explicitly set; the one for PATCH-style partial updates. Assigning a field later adds it to the set
by_alias=True Use serialization_alias names

Custom serializers

@field_serializer changes how one field is written (for example a datetime to an epoch number), and @model_serializer shapes the whole output. Plain mode replaces Pydantic's logic; wrap mode calls a handler and edits the result. Only one serializer applies per field or model.

Subclasses and secrets

When a field is annotated with a model type, only that type's declared fields are serialized, even if the value is a subclass. This is deliberate: it stops a subclass's extra field (such as a password) leaking by accident. Opt in to the runtime subclass with polymorphic_serialization or serialize_as_any.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Storing a derived value It drifts out of sync computed_field
PATCH that dumps defaults Overwrites stored data with defaults exclude_unset=True
Writing model_dump() straight to a JSON file A non-JSON type raises Use mode="json" or model_dump_json()

Interview corner

Why exclude_unset for PATCH?

It serialises only what the caller explicitly provided, so unset defaults do not overwrite stored values.

model_dump versus model_dump(mode="json")?

The first keeps Python types; the second converts to JSON-compatible ones (tuples to lists, and so on).

Pydantic · Chapter 6

Nested models

Use one model as another's field type and validation cascades through every layer, with errors that name the exact path.

PydanticDocs "Models", class 03, the notebook10 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Real data, including JSON from an API or an LLM, is nested: an applicant has an address, an order has a list of items. The class pointed out that nested models mirror nested JSON, which is the shape of most API payloads and LLM structured outputs.

Core ideas

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Address(BaseModel):
    city: str
    state: str
    pin_code: str

class Applicant(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: str
    address: Address
    history: list[str] = []

a = Applicant.model_validate(
    {"name": "R", "email": "r@x.com",
     "address": {"city": "Pune", "state": "MH", "pin_code": "411001"}})
a.address.city          # dot-chain access, fully typed
  • Validating the outer model builds the inner models from the inner dicts. model_dump() converts everything back, recursively.
  • A bad inner value gives an error whose location is the full path, such as address.pin_code.
  • A whole nested object can be optional with Address | None = None. Lists of models work the same way. There is no practical depth limit.
  • The notebook's version of this puts a Field(gt=1000, lt=43125315) constraint on pin_code, to show that nested models carry their own rules.
AnalogyThe org chart

A company contains departments, which contain employees. Validate the company and every layer beneath is validated for you. (Instructor's site.)

Inheritance is also allowed

From the class Q&A: a model can extend another (class Applicant(Address) inherits its fields and validators) with ordinary Python inheritance. Prefer composition (a field of type Address) when the data really is "has an", and inheritance only when it is "is a".

Self-referencing data and forward references

Data that refers to itself (a parent that points back to a child) is detected and reported as a ValidationError instead of recursing forever. A model that mentions a class defined later uses a string annotation, and you call model_rebuild() once the names exist.

Unions (from the official Unions page)

NoteSource

Pydantic docs, Unions, read in full on 31 Oct 2026.

A union is different from every other type: only one member has to validate. Three approaches exist.

  • Left to right (Field(union_mode='left_to_right')): members are tried in order, the first success wins. Order matters: with id: int | str, the string '456' becomes the integer 456, because lax mode lets it pass int first. If all members fail, you get one error per member.
  • Smart mode (the default in V2). It tries all members and picks the best match using two scores: the number of valid fields set (for models, dataclasses and TypedDict, added in v2.8.0; nested fields count too) and then exactness (exact type match, then success in strict mode, then success in lax mode). The algorithm may change in minor releases, so use left to right or a discriminator if you rely on exact behaviour.
  • Discriminated (tagged) unions: only one member is tried, chosen by a tag, so validation is faster and errors are shorter. Use Field(discriminator='pet_type') on a union of models that each have a Literal field, or the Discriminator class with Tag for a callable discriminator (it must handle both dicts and model instances, and returning None gives a union_tag_not_found error). Only one discriminator per field is allowed, so nest Annotated unions for two levels. The generated JSON Schema carries the OpenAPI discriminator.
  • Errors. Plain unions give verbose errors, especially for recursive models. Discriminator accepts custom_error_type, custom_error_message and custom_error_context, and Tag names make error locations readable.
  • Not captured: the "all other types" tab of the smart-mode steps, so only the model steps are confirmed.

Dataclasses and TypeAdapter (from two official pages)

NoteSources

Pydantic docs, Dataclasses and Type Adapter, both read in full on 31 Oct 2026.

Pydantic dataclasses. @pydantic.dataclasses.dataclass adds validation to a standard dataclass, so User(id='42', signup_ts='2032-06-21T12:00') converts the values. The docs say they are not a replacement for models.

  • Same as models: configuration (but no model_config attribute), nested classes, and Field() or dataclasses.field().
  • Different: no model_validate, model_dump or JSON Schema methods (wrap the class in TypeAdapter); extra data is dropped from serialization; generics are supported but a parameterised class like Foo[int] is treated as Foo[Any], so wrap it in TypeAdapter.
  • Config: the config= argument or a __pydantic_config__ attribute. rebuild_dataclass() rebuilds the schema.
  • Stdlib dataclasses can be inherited, and used as fields in a model; for Pydantic to revalidate an existing instance the model needs revalidate_instances='always'. Arbitrary types need arbitrary_types_allowed. is_pydantic_dataclass() tells the two kinds apart.
  • Validators work. __post_init__ runs between the before and after model validators, and in a before validator the input is an ArgsKwargs object, not a dict.

TypeAdapter validates, serializes and builds JSON Schema for any type without a model. TypeAdapter(list[User]) validates a list of TypedDicts, and validate_python, dump_python, dump_json and json_schema are the main methods.

  • dump_json returns bytes, while model_dump_json returns a str (a V1 compatibility leftover).
  • Do not use TypeAdapter as a field type.
  • Building it has noticeable cost, so create it once and reuse it.
  • defer_build=True (v2.10) postpones the build; rebuild() builds it later, which helps with forward references.
  • Not captured: the Python 3.12 tab of the generic dataclass example.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Expecting int to str coercion in a nested field A nested 12345 is rejected for a str field Convert it yourself
Calling dict() and expecting nested dicts Inner models stay as models Use model_dump()

Interview corner

How does validation work for nested data?

Pydantic builds the inner model from the inner dict and validates it with its own rules; errors report the full path, such as address.pin_code.
