Pydantic · Chapter 7

Strict mode and JSON Schema

Turn coercion off when silent conversion would hide bugs, and turn a model into a JSON Schema, the document that tells an API or an LLM what shape to expect.

PydanticDocs "Strict mode" and "JSON Schema"12 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Lax mode is friendly, but it can hide mistakes. The schema is how a model becomes machine-readable, and chapter 11 uses it to ask an LLM for a specific shape.

Core ideas

Strict mode

Strict mode refuses to convert: "123" is no longer an int. Four ways to turn it on:

Where How
One call Model.model_validate(data, strict=True)
One field Field(strict=True) or Annotated[int, Field(strict=True)]
A type StrictInt, StrictStr, StrictBool, or Annotated[UUID, Strict()]
The whole model model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True); a field can opt out with Field(strict=False)

Python mode and JSON mode differ: with strict on, a date string is rejected from Python input but accepted from JSON, since JSON has no date type. When adding strict mode to a running app, watch for callers who relied on coercion.

JSON Schema

Model.model_json_schema() returns a dict (not a string) describing the model, using JSON Schema 2020-12 and OpenAPI 3.1. TypeAdapter(list[int]).json_schema() does it for any type.

from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Ticket(BaseModel):
    priority: Literal["low", "medium", "high"]
    summary: str = Field(max_length=200, description="One-line summary")

Ticket.model_json_schema()
  • Constraints map to standard keywords: max_length becomes maxLength, gt becomes exclusiveMinimum, PositiveInt becomes exclusiveMinimum: 0, EmailStr becomes format: email, and SecretStr adds writeOnly.
  • title, description, examples and json_schema_extra on a field show up in the schema. The description is what a model reads, so write it as an instruction.
  • Nested models go under $defs and are referenced with $ref.
  • mode="validation" (default) describes accepted input; mode="serialization" describes output. A Decimal accepts a number or string as input but is emitted as a string.
  • An Enum becomes an enum list. (The docs say little about Literal; check the output of your own models.)
Key ideaWhy chapter 11 cares

The dict from model_json_schema() is exactly what you hand a provider as a tool's input schema. Add extra="forbid" so the schema forbids unknown keys.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Turning on strict mode without checking callers Clients that sent "5" now fail Roll out gradually and watch failures
Treating the schema as a string Type errors It is a dict; json.dumps it when needed

Interview corner

How do you turn off coercion?

Strict mode: per call (strict=True), per field, with a Strict* type, or for the whole model through ConfigDict(strict=True).

What does model_json_schema give you?

A dict describing the model's fields, types and constraints in JSON Schema, which APIs use for documentation and LLM providers use to constrain output.

Pydantic · Chapter 8

Settings and secrets

Replace string-only os.getenv() with a typed settings class that reads the environment and .env files, masks secrets and validates defaults.

PydanticDocs "Settings", class 03, the instructor's site12 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

os.getenv() always returns a string or None. DEBUG="false" is a non-empty string, so if debug: is true. Every project ends up rewriting the same parsing code.

Beyond the classRead most of the settings page

The settings docs page is long. I read the first 100,000 of its roughly 103,900 characters; the last part (the end of the secrets section) was not read, and SecretStr is not covered on that page.

Core ideas

BaseSettings (from the separate pydantic-settings package) extends BaseModel. Fields not passed as keyword arguments are filled from the environment, and keyword arguments are handy for overrides in tests.

from pydantic import Field, SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class AppSettings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", extra="ignore")
    api_key: SecretStr
    max_connections: int = Field(default=100, ge=1, le=1000)
    debug: bool = False
Feature How it works
Name mapping The variable name matches the field name, case-insensitive (api_key reads API_KEY). alias, validation_alias, AliasChoices or env_prefix change it
.env files env_file, or a tuple of files where later ones win. Real environment variables beat the file
Unknown entries With the default extra='forbid', unknown .env entries raise an error; extra="ignore" skips them
Nested values With env_nested_delimiter="__", DB__HOST fills db.host. Lists and dicts are read as JSON
Secrets directory secrets_dir: each file's name is the key, its contents the value. Lower priority than the environment and .env
Priority Environment over .env over secrets directory; settings_customise_sources reorders
Defaults Validated, unlike in BaseModel (set validate_default=False to skip)
Command line cli_parse_args=True parses sys.argv into fields

settings.max_connections is a real int, debug a real bool, and api_key prints masked; read it on purpose with .get_secret_value().

AnalogySensor wires versus a dashboard

os.getenv() gives raw unlabeled wires. BaseSettings is the dashboard that shows typed gauges. (Instructor's site.)

Pro tipSame file as Foundations chapter 1

The .env file the Foundations book sets up is exactly what this class reads. The Meridian project uses the same pattern in config/settings.py.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
if os.getenv("DEBUG") "false" is truthy A bool field in BaseSettings
Keys as plain str Secret printed in logs SecretStr
Unknown entry in .env ValidationError on start extra="ignore"

Interview corner

Why BaseSettings over os.getenv?

It gives typed, validated configuration with defaults and constraints, reads .env, and masks secrets, instead of hand-written string parsing.

Which wins: an environment variable or the .env file?

The real environment variable. A tuple of .env files loads in order, with later files overriding earlier ones.

Pydantic · Chapter 9

Reading validation errors

A ValidationError collects every problem in one pass, and each entry says where, what and why in a form code can read, which is what makes automatic retries possible.

PydanticDocs "Error handling"8 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

The error is not just a message for a human. Its structure lets you show clear feedback to an API caller, or hand the failure back to an LLM so it can correct itself.

Core ideas

One ValidationError bundles all errors from a validation pass, not the first one. Ways to read it:

Call Gives
str(e) A readable block per error
e.errors() A list of dicts
e.error_count() How many
e.json() The list as JSON

Each entry in errors():

Key Meaning
type Machine-readable id such as missing, greater_than, int_parsing, value_error
loc A tuple: field name first, then nested names or list indexes, for example ('items', 1, 'value')
msg Human-readable message
input The value that failed
ctx Optional values used to build the message, such as the gt bound, or the original exception
url A link to the docs for that error type 
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

class User(BaseModel):
    id: int
    tastes: dict[str, int]
    signup_ts: str            # required, so a missing value is a second error

try:
    User(**{"id": "not an int", "tastes": {}})
except ValidationError as e:
    for err in e.errors():
        print(err["loc"], err["type"], err["msg"])

For the get-started example in the docs this reports two problems at once: id could not be parsed as an integer, and the required signup_ts is missing.

Your own validators raise ValueError (or AssertionError) and Pydantic turns them into value_error entries whose message starts with "Value error,".

Customising messages

Because every entry has a type and ctx, you can map types to your own templates (for translation or friendlier wording) and rewrite loc into a dotted path like items[1].value. The docs show both as small helper functions over e.errors().

Key ideaWhy this matters for LLMs

The same structured list, passed back to a model as text, is the trigger for the retry pattern in chapter 11.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Showing str(e) to API users Noisy, internal wording Map type to your own message
Catching a generic exception around validation Real bugs get swallowed Catch ValidationError specifically

Interview corner

What is in a Pydantic error entry?

type, loc, msg, input, and optionally ctx and url. loc is a tuple that includes nested names and list indexes.

Sources and further reading

Pydantic · Chapter 10

Pydantic with FastAPI

FastAPI uses your model as the request validator, the response filter and the source of the API docs, all from one class.

PydanticInstructor's site8 min read
Jump to a section
Beyond the classSource for this chapter

The core of this chapter comes from the instructor's Pydantic site, plus the model_json_schema() behaviour from the JSON Schema docs (chapter 7). The section "From the FastAPI documentation" below comes from five FastAPI tutorial pages read in full; other FastAPI pages were not read.

Why it matters

This is where Pydantic is "everywhere": an endpoint that takes a model is validated before your function body runs.

Core ideas

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field

app = FastAPI()

class Applicant(BaseModel):
    full_name: str = Field(min_length=2, max_length=100)
    email: EmailStr

class Receipt(BaseModel):
    full_name: str

@app.post("/apply", response_model=Receipt)
def apply(a: Applicant) -> Receipt:
    return Receipt(full_name=a.full_name)
  • Request validation. Malformed bodies are rejected with a detailed error before the function runs; no manual if checks.
  • response_model= filters what you return down to that shape, a safety net against leaking extra fields.
  • Docs. The model's JSON Schema feeds the /docs page, so every Field() constraint becomes a documented API constraint.
AnalogyOne scanner at the terminal entrance

Instead of each gate building its own detector, the terminal has one scanner everyone passes. Your model is that scanner. (Instructor's site.)

From the FastAPI documentation

NoteSources

FastAPI tutorial pages: Request Body, Response Model, Extra Models, Body - Updates and Query Parameter Models, all read in full on 31 Oct 2026. Other FastAPI pages were not read.

  • Request body. Declare a parameter whose type is a Pydantic model and FastAPI reads the JSON body, converts, validates (a bad body gives a clear error naming the place), gives you a model instance and adds the schema to the docs. Resolution rule: a name in the path is a path parameter, a simple type is a query parameter, a Pydantic model is the body. A field is optional because of its default, not because of | None. Bodies on GET are discouraged.
  • Response model. A return annotation (-> Item) or response_model= validates the output (invalid output is a server error, because your code is wrong), adds a JSON Schema, serializes with Pydantic, and filters the output to the declared fields. If both are given, response_model wins; response_model=None turns it off.
  • Two models, one for input and one for output keeps secrets out: UserIn has password, UserOut does not. A parent/child pair (BaseUser returned, UserIn actually returned) keeps editor support and still filters.
  • Encoding switches: response_model_exclude_unset, _exclude_defaults, _exclude_none, _include, _exclude. Fields explicitly set to a default value are still kept by exclude_unset.
  • Extra models: share fields through a base class (UserBase, UserIn, UserOut, UserInDB). Never store plaintext passwords. A union response (anyOf in OpenAPI) should list the most specific type first. The page also has a note about writing the union as a value on Python 3.10, which I could not confirm from the text I got, so check it before relying on it.
  • Updates. PUT replaces, so omitted fields fall back to defaults and overwrite stored values. For PATCH, use model_dump(exclude_unset=True) and model_copy(update=...).
  • Query parameter models (FastAPI 0.115.0 and later): group query parameters in a model with Query(); extra='forbid' rejects unknown parameters with an extra_forbidden error; several models can be combined, and Model | None = None makes a group optional.

See it at project scale

The Meridian capstone (Agentic AI with LangChain, last chapter, "Module 6") shows this pattern in a real service: four small request and reply classes in schemas.py, seven thin routes, error handlers that turn your own exceptions into 503 and 422 replies, and the /docs page generated from the same code.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Returning an internal model directly Password or internal ids leak Declare response_model

Interview corner

What does response_model do?

It validates and filters the returned object to the declared shape, so extra fields cannot leak, and it documents the response in /docs.

  • Instructor's site: Mastering Pydantic
  • Meridian uses this pattern: see the capstone chapter in the LangChain book

Pydantic · Chapter 11

Validating what an LLM gives you back

LLM text output is unreliable. Ask the provider to guarantee a Pydantic schema, constrain values with Literal, and retry with the validation error when it still fails.

PydanticPydantic's LLM article and docs, the instructor's site15 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

An LLM asked for JSON may add a code fence, a friendly preamble, or return a number as a string. Cleaning that up with string tricks is fragile. Pydantic's own article makes the same argument: model output is untrusted, and a model gives it a defined shape.

Core ideas

Three approaches, from simple to robust

The Pydantic article on LLMs walks through them:

  1. Prompt for JSON, then validate. Ask for a JSON object with given fields and parse the reply with model_validate_json. Simple, but replies can arrive wrapped in a markdown fence or surrounded by prose, which breaks parsing.
  2. Tool calling with a generated schema. Pass Model.model_json_schema() as a function's parameters and require the model to call that function. The prompt holds only the data request; the schema defines the structure, including nesting. Note the article's caveat: tool calling was designed to call external APIs, so using it to format output is a repurposing.
  3. A wrapper library. Instructor wraps the client so you pass a response_model and get a validated object back.

Provider SDKs have since added direct support. The instructor's site shows:

Provider Call Result
OpenAI client.responses.parse(model=..., input=..., text_format=Model) response.output_parsed
Anthropic client.messages.parse(model=..., max_tokens=..., messages=..., output_format=Model) response.parsed_output

The same model works for both; only the SDK call changes. Add extra="forbid" so the generated schema rejects surprise keys. (I did not run these calls; check each provider's current SDK docs.)

AnalogyShouting an order versus a printed slip

A shouted order gets misheard. A printed checkbox slip is a response guaranteed to match a schema you defined. (Instructor's site.)

Literal and the retry loop

Literal physically limits a classification to allowed values. When validation still fails, the ValidationError text (chapter 9) is the trigger for a retry: feed it into the next prompt and ask again, up to a limit.

def classify_with_retry(text, max_retries=3):
    last_error = None
    for _ in range(max_retries):
        raw = ask_llm(text, previous_error=last_error)    # your LLM call
        try:
            return TicketClassification.model_validate_json(raw)
        except ValidationError as e:
            last_error = str(e)
    raise RuntimeError("Failed after max retries")

Pydantic AI, built by the Pydantic team, automates this: when validation of an output or a tool's arguments fails, it sends the errors back to the model and asks it to retry. Its docs also show a validation context: values your validators read from info.context (for example a list of allowed countries) that the model never sees.

Context-aware validators

A validator can check against data supplied at call time through model_validate(..., context=...) (chapter 4), which is how an app can enforce "country must be one of these" without telling the model the list.

Key ideaShape, not correctness

Structured output guarantees the shape. A well-formed answer can still be confidently wrong. Pydantic's article says the same: structurally valid output does not guarantee correct content, and validation catches type and shape problems, not semantic ones.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Cleaning fences with string code Breaks when the format shifts Provider structured output, or a schema-forcing tool call
Treating a valid object as true Wrong facts accepted Verify facts separately
No retry limit Endless loop and cost Cap the retries

Interview corner

How do you get reliable JSON from an LLM?

Pass a Pydantic model to the provider's structured-output call (or its JSON Schema as a forced tool), constrain values with Literal, validate the result, and retry with the error fed back if it fails.

Does validation make an answer correct?

No. It confirms the shape and constraints only. A confidently wrong value in the right shape still passes.

Pydantic · Chapter 12

Where Pydantic goes next, and the final project

An honest map of the ecosystem above core Pydantic, then a small support-ticket triage service that uses every idea in the book.

PydanticInstructor's site and the docs12 min read
Jump to a section

The ecosystem map

This book covers core Pydantic: models, fields, validators, computed fields, serialization, strict mode, JSON Schema, settings, errors, and structured output with provider SDKs. The docs list much more, which this book does not teach: unions and discriminators in depth, TypeAdapter, dataclasses, generics, RootModel, performance, the architecture notes, and extra-types packages.

  • One layer up: Instructor patches an LLM client to validate and retry automatically, which is the retry loop from chapter 11 wrapped up.
  • Two layers up: agent frameworks use Pydantic for tool schemas and structured outputs and add orchestration. Pydantic AI is made by the Pydantic team; LangChain and CrewAI also build on Pydantic. Orchestration (when to call a tool, state across turns) is not Pydantic's job; validating data against a schema is.
  • The docs say around 8,000 PyPI packages use Pydantic, with FastAPI, SQLModel and LangChain among them.
Beyond the classOut of scope here

LangChain is taught in the next book. This book does not teach Instructor, Pydantic AI or CrewAI.

Performance tips (from the official Performance page)

NoteSource

Pydantic docs, Performance, read in full on 31 Oct 2026.

The page opens with a warning: in most cases Pydantic won't be your bottleneck, so only apply these when you are sure it is needed.

  1. Use model_validate_json() instead of model_validate(json.loads(...)) (exception: with a before or wrap validator the two-step way may be faster).
  2. Create a TypeAdapter once, not inside a function that runs repeatedly.
  3. Use list, tuple or dict rather than Sequence or Mapping when you know the input type.
  4. Use Any for values you do not need to validate.
  5. Avoid primitive subclasses that add extra information.
  6. Prefer tagged (discriminated) unions to plain unions.
  7. Prefer TypedDict to nested models: about 2.5 times faster in the docs' own benchmark.
  8. Avoid wrap validators; they force data into Python during validation.
  9. FailFast on a sequence stops at the first bad item (v2.8+), trading error visibility for speed.

Not captured: the "good" tabs for tips 2 and 5.

Final project: support-ticket triage

POST /triage takes a messy support message and returns a validated result: category, priority, sentiment, a computed SLA and redacted customer info.

Piece Concept used
IncomingTicket A mode="before" field_validator redacts email addresses before storing (chapter 4), and it is the FastAPI request body (chapter 10)
TriagedTicket Literal for category, priority and sentiment (chapter 11); a nested CustomerInfo (chapter 6); extra="forbid" (chapter 2)
sla_hours A computed_field from priority: high 4, medium 24, low 72 (chapter 5), so the LLM never does arithmetic
Safety net A model_validator rejects high priority with general_question (chapter 4)
AppSettings Picks Anthropic, then OpenAI, then a free OpenRouter model, whichever key exists (chapter 8)

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Letting the LLM compute derived values Inconsistent numbers Derive them with computed_field
Assuming a framework replaces understanding Cannot debug failures Know the validate-and-retry loop first

Interview corner

How would you design a reliable LLM-backed API endpoint?

Validate and clean the request with a model, ask the provider for a structured response in a Literal-constrained schema, derive computed values in code, add a model validator for impossible combinations, and cap retries.

Interview question bank

Every interview question from every chapter in one place, in chapter order. Tap a question to reveal the answer.

22 questionsRebuilt automatically from the chapters
Jump to a section

Chapter 1: Why validation exists, and type hints

Does Python enforce type hints?

No. At runtime they are ignored. They help readers, IDEs and libraries such as Pydantic, which reads them and enforces them.

What is the difference between type validation and data validation?

Type validation checks the kind of data (an int). Data validation checks the value makes sense (an age of 10000 is an int but not valid). Pydantic does both: types from hints, values from Field constraints and validators.

Chapter 2: Your first model

BaseModel versus dataclass?

Both give a clean constructor from hints. Only BaseModel validates and coerces, raising one ValidationError before the object is created.

What does the default extra setting do?

It ignores unknown keys. forbid raises; allow stores them.

model_validate versus model_construct?

model_validate checks the data. model_construct skips all checks, so use it only for data you already trust.

Chapter 3: Fields and constraints

Field() or Annotated?

Both work the same. Annotated keeps required fields visibly required and is reusable, which is why the docs prefer it. The class prefers plain Field() for readability but wants you to recognise both.

alias versus validation_alias versus serialization_alias?

alias applies to input and output, the other two to only one direction. Output uses aliases only with by_alias=True.

Chapter 4: Validators

field_validator versus model_validator?

The first checks one field with no view of the others. The second sees the whole model after every field check has passed, so it handles cross-field rules.

What does mode="before" do, and when do you need it?

It runs on the raw input before type coercion, so you can clean messy input before Pydantic tries to read it. Without it, the validator only sees an already-valid value.

What is the difference between a plain and a wrap validator?

A plain validator replaces Pydantic's check entirely, so invalid input can slip through. A wrap validator calls Pydantic's check through a handler and can catch errors or retry.

Chapter 5: Computed fields and serialization

Why exclude_unset for PATCH?

It serialises only what the caller explicitly provided, so unset defaults do not overwrite stored values.

model_dump versus model_dump(mode="json")?

The first keeps Python types; the second converts to JSON-compatible ones (tuples to lists, and so on).

Chapter 6: Nested models

How does validation work for nested data?

Pydantic builds the inner model from the inner dict and validates it with its own rules; errors report the full path, such as address.pin_code.

Chapter 7: Strict mode and JSON Schema

How do you turn off coercion?

Strict mode: per call (strict=True), per field, with a Strict* type, or for the whole model through ConfigDict(strict=True).

What does model_json_schema give you?

A dict describing the model's fields, types and constraints in JSON Schema, which APIs use for documentation and LLM providers use to constrain output.

Chapter 8: Settings and secrets

Why BaseSettings over os.getenv?

It gives typed, validated configuration with defaults and constraints, reads .env, and masks secrets, instead of hand-written string parsing.

Which wins: an environment variable or the .env file?

The real environment variable. A tuple of .env files loads in order, with later files overriding earlier ones.

Chapter 9: Reading validation errors

What is in a Pydantic error entry?

type, loc, msg, input, and optionally ctx and url. loc is a tuple that includes nested names and list indexes.

Chapter 10: Pydantic with FastAPI

What does response_model do?

It validates and filters the returned object to the declared shape, so extra fields cannot leak, and it documents the response in /docs.

Chapter 11: Validating what an LLM gives you back

How do you get reliable JSON from an LLM?

Pass a Pydantic model to the provider's structured-output call (or its JSON Schema as a forced tool), constrain values with Literal, validate the result, and retry with the error fed back if it fails.

Does validation make an answer correct?

No. It confirms the shape and constraints only. A confidently wrong value in the right shape still passes.

Chapter 12: Where Pydantic goes next, and the final project

How would you design a reliable LLM-backed API endpoint?

Validate and clean the request with a model, ask the provider for a structured response in a Literal-constrained schema, derive computed values in code, add a model validator for impossible combinations, and cap retries.

Back matter

Cheat sheet

The Pydantic patterns on one page. Every item links back to the chapter that explains it, and every line of behaviour here was checked against real Pydantic (see the home page).

Quick referenceCode is condensed. See the chapters for the full versions
Jump to a section

A model in one picture (Ch 2, Ch 3)

from typing import Annotated, Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, SecretStr, computed_field, field_validator, model_validator

class Applicant(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")            # reject unknown keys
    name: str = Field(min_length=2, max_length=100)
    years: Annotated[int, Field(ge=0, le=50)]
    level: Literal["junior", "senior"] = "junior"       # a default makes it optional
    api_key: SecretStr | None = None

    @field_validator("name")
    @classmethod
    def tidy(cls, v: str) -> str:                       # one field; return the value
        return v.strip()

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def rules(self):                                    # across fields; return self
        return self

    @computed_field
    @property
    def tier(self) -> str:                              # read-only, appears in dumps
        return "mid" if self.years >= 2 else "junior"

Calls to remember (Ch 2, Ch 5)

Need Call
Validate a dict / JSON Model.model_validate(d) / Model.model_validate_json(s)
Back to dict / JSON m.model_dump() / m.model_dump_json()
JSON-safe dict m.model_dump(mode="json")
Only what the caller sent m.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
Hide / show fields exclude=, include=, Field(exclude=True), exclude_none=True
Output with aliases m.model_dump(by_alias=True)
Copy with changes m.model_copy(update={...}) (not validated)
No validation (trusted data) Model.model_construct(...)
Schema Model.model_json_schema() (a dict)
Any type TypeAdapter(list[int]).validate_python(x); create once, reuse

Rules that catch people out

  • Unknown keys are ignored by default; use extra="forbid" for LLM schemas.
  • "25" becomes 25 for an int, but 12345 is not turned into "12345" for a str.
  • Defaults are not validated unless validate_default=True (in BaseSettings they are).
  • A validator must return the value; forgetting makes the field None.
  • Raise ValueError, never ValidationError, inside a validator.
  • Cleaning raw text needs mode="before"; the default (after) never sees it.
  • Two methods with the same name: only the last one survives.
  • A cross-field rule needs model_validator, not field_validator.
  • A model validator is skipped if a field already failed.
  • Config does not pass into nested models; it does pass into stdlib dataclasses.
  • dump_json on TypeAdapter returns bytes; model_dump_json returns a str.

Validators (Ch 4)

Mode Runs Use
after (default) after Pydantic's check value has the right type
before on raw input clean "5 years" to 5
plain instead of Pydantic's check bad input can pass
wrap around it, with a handler catch errors, retry

Order on one field: before and wrap run right to left, then after runs left to right. All field validators run before the model validator.

Unions (Ch 6)

Smart mode is the default. Use Field(discriminator="kind") with a Literal tag for speed and short errors; Discriminator plus Tag for a callable.

Errors (Ch 9)

try:
    Model(**data)
except ValidationError as e:
    for err in e.errors():            # type, loc, msg, input, ctx, url
        print(err["loc"], err["type"], err["msg"])

Settings (Ch 8)

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", extra="ignore")
    api_key: SecretStr
    debug: bool = False

Environment beats .env beats the secrets directory. os.getenv("DEBUG") of "false" is truthy; a bool field is not.

FastAPI and LLMs (Ch 10, Ch 11)

  • A Pydantic parameter is the body; a simple type is a query parameter; a name in the path is a path parameter.
  • response_model=Out filters the output (keeps password out); invalid output is a 500, bad input a 422.
  • PATCH: item.model_dump(exclude_unset=True) then stored.model_copy(update=...).
  • LLM output: schema from model_json_schema() with extra="forbid", validate the reply, on ValidationError send str(e) back and retry with a cap. Valid shape does not mean true facts.

The course roadmap, from the induction session

From classes_transcription_summary/00 - 21 June - Course Induction & Roadmap.md (the batch induction with the founder and the lead mentor).

Agentic 2.0 Agentic 3.0
Focus Understanding agents Using and deploying agents

Tools Basic Claude Code and other coding agents

2.0 comes free with 3.0 enrolment but is not a prerequisite. Azure AI Foundry, Bedrock and Vertex AI each get dedicated sessions.

The curriculum flow: foundations (LLMs and providers), core frameworks and protocols (LangChain, LangGraph, MCP, A2A, RAG, context engineering), mini-projects, interim projects deployed on cloud and a VPS, the coding-agent ecosystem, extended frameworks (ADK, Claude Agent SDK), and about nine production capstone projects. Format: Saturdays and Sundays 8 to 11 AM IST for five to six months, recordings within 24 hours, two years of access, and about two hours a week of self-practice.

Two featured demos: a document-intelligence RAG agent for a US client (Dockerised, with a chunking pipeline that divides data by update relevance) and a multi-agent procurement and finance system on Google Cloud Run with a risk agent, a tax agent, a control agent and a supervisor. The second is the Meridian project in Chapter 20.

The four post-production KPIs (the mentor's "golden rules", and a good interview answer to "how do you judge an agent in production"): cost (including tokens), failure rate (should trend to zero), latency, and quality (is the output actually useful?). His engineering philosophy: simple is scalable; minimise external, API and LLM calls because every hop costs time and money; prefer the simplest system that solves the problem instead of over-engineering for scale that never comes; use multiple LLMs only when the problem demands it (for example failover), because calling models in parallel by default just doubles cost.

Practice projects

Eight small projects, each placed beside the chapter it exercises. Build one at a time.

NoteAbout the domain

Examples lean towards clinical education and research, because a project in a field you know is easier to judge. Never use real patient data with any model or tool; use synthetic or de-identified examples, and keep a human in the loop for anything clinical.

Part A LangChain core · Chapter 1

Introduction to LangChain

LangChain packages the hand-written agent loop from the Foundations book into one call, create_agent(), so you spend your time on tools and behaviour instead of plumbing.

Class 0612 July25 min readCode: Weekend 03
Jump to a section

Why it matters

The raw-Python agent works, but it does not scale. For every project you would rewrite tool schemas, message formats, the loop, memory and provider switching. A framework gives you a tested harness: everything around the model that makes it useful.

Key ideaThe one equation to remember

Agent = Model + Harness

The model is the brain. The harness is the system prompt, tools, memory, loop and middleware around it. A smarter harness cannot fix a weak model, and a strong model is not much use without a harness.

AnalogyA car and its engine

The model is a powerful engine. On its own it cannot go anywhere. Add steering, wheels, fuel lines and brakes (the harness) and you have a car you can drive. Claude and ChatGPT's apps are the same idea: a model wrapped in memory, tools and web search.

Raw Python vs LangChain

You built the first column in the Foundations book (What an agent is and Agents in plain Python). The second column is what create_agent() replaces it with.

Concern Raw Python (Foundations) LangChain
Tool schema Hand-written JSON Inferred from the function signature and docstring
The loop You write run_agent agent.invoke() runs it
Message format Dicts you manage HumanMessage, AIMessage, ToolMessage objects
Switch provider Different SDK per provider Change the model string
Memory A list you maintain A checkpointer you plug in
Visibility Total Less, because LangChain infers a lot
Speed Fastest Slightly slower (extra IDs and bookkeeping) 
# Raw: ~25 lines of loop plus a hand-written JSON schema per tool.

# LangChain: the same weather agent
from langchain.agents import create_agent

def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Get weather for a given city."""
    return f"It's always sunny in {city}!"

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-4o-mini",      # provider:model, use any model you have access to
    tools=[get_weather],             # a plain function is enough
    system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant",
)

result = agent.invoke(
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in San Francisco?"}]}
)
print(result["messages"][-1].content)
Pro tipSay this in an interview

"I built the loop by hand first, so I know what create_agent is doing for me. I use the framework for speed and standard behaviour, and I drop lower when I need control." Interviewers like hearing fundamentals before frameworks.

Three levels of control

LangChain sits in the middle of a family of tools. Pick the level that matches how much control you need.

Tool Analogy What you get Use it when
Deep Agents Food delivery Context compression, a virtual file system and sub-agents out of the box You want a capable agent fast and can accept less control
LangChain Home-cooked meal create_agent, tools, middleware, memory You are building real software and want control over behaviour
LangGraph Raw vegetables Low-level graph of steps, mixing deterministic and agentic logic You need to wire every step yourself
LangSmith Flight recorder Tracing and monitoring of what an agent did You need to observe and debug (it does not build agents)
Beyond the classFrom Class 07

LangGraph is the foundation and LangChain is built on top of it, not the other way round. Class 06 only named the tiers; Class 07 explained how they relate. Also, LangFuse is not part of the LangChain family. It is an independent observability tool.

NoteVersion warning

Everything before LangChain v1 is now called LangChain Classic. Most blog posts and videos still teach Classic. This course teaches v1 and later, so old snippets may not match.

Setting up a project

uv init langchain_course
cd langchain_course
uv add langchain langchain-openai langchain-anthropic
uv sync

Installing three packages pulled in about 45 dependencies. That is normal, because each provider integration brings its own.

Keep secrets out of Git with three files:

File Purpose Commit it?
.env Your real API keys Never
.gitignore Lists .env and .venv so Git skips them Yes
.env.example Same keys with placeholder values, as a template Yes 
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()          # reads .env into the environment
Common trapA real key pushed to GitHub

It happened live in class and the key had to be deleted. Anyone who sees a key in your history can use it. If it happens: revoke the key first, then clean up the repo.

Beyond the classFrom Class 07

LangChain looks for the provider's standard variable name, for example OPENAI_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. If you rename it, or switch provider without setting the matching variable, you get an authentication error. The instructor showed this live in the next class.

How create_agent() works

The inputs you used

Argument What it does
model A "provider:model" string, or a model object from init_chat_model
tools A list of functions or @tool-decorated functions
system_prompt Instructions that shape behaviour
checkpointer Where conversation state is saved (memory)

Later chapters add more: structured output in Chapter 4, middleware in Chapters 6 and 7.

What invoke() returns

agent.invoke() runs the whole loop and returns a dictionary. The part you care about is result["messages"], the full conversation in order. A simplified view of the weather example:

[
  HumanMessage(content="Weather in San Francisco?"),
  AIMessage(content="", tool_calls=[
      {"name": "get_weather", "args": {"city": "San Francisco"}, "id": "call_abc"}]),
  ToolMessage(content="It's always sunny in San Francisco!", tool_call_id="call_abc"),
  AIMessage(content="It's currently sunny in San Francisco."),
]
Key ideaRead the trace like a transcript

Message 2 has empty content, because the model is asking for a tool, not answering. Message 3 shares the same tool_call_id so the model can match result to request. This ran the model twice, exactly like the hand-built loop. Each message also carries prompt, completion and total token counts.

How a function becomes a tool

You pass a plain function. LangChain reads its name, type hints and docstring and builds a schema, roughly the same JSON you wrote by hand in the Foundations book:

{
  "type": "function",
  "function": {
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Get weather for a given city.",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
      "required": ["city"]
    }
  }
}
Beyond the classIllustration, not printed in class

The JSON above is my sketch of roughly what LangChain generates, written to match the schema you hand-wrote in the Foundations book. The class explained that the schema is inferred, but did not print it.

The @tool decorator wraps the function so an agent can call it. Either way, the docstring is the model's only guide to when to use the tool.

from langchain.tools import tool

@tool
def fetch_text_from_url(url: str) -> str:
    """Fetch the plain text of a web page. Use when the user gives a URL."""
    ...
Common trapA vague docstring

A docstring like "Fetch the document" tells the model very little. The agent may skip the tool, or use it for the wrong job. Say what it does and when to use it.

The five-step build pattern

LangChain's quickstart, followed in class, builds an agent in five steps.

  1. Write a detailed system prompt (what the agent is, which tools it has, what not to guess).
  2. Create tools with @tool.
  3. Configure the model with init_chat_model.
  4. Add memory.
  5. Assemble with create_agent and run.
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

model = init_chat_model(
    "openai:gpt-4o-mini",
    temperature=0.5,      # randomness
    timeout=300,          # seconds to wait
    max_tokens=25000,     # cap on output length
)

agent = create_agent(
    model=model,
    tools=[fetch_text_from_url],
    system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    checkpointer=checkpointer,
)
Repo noteModel names in these notes

The repo scripts use openai:gpt-5.5. These notes use gpt-4o-mini as a placeholder. Use any model you have access to, with its matching API key. The repo script also prints .content_blocks (a standard list of content parts), while .content is enough for plain text.

Repo noteThe repo example has a missing piece

The example script passes checkpointer=checkpointer, but the file never defines it, so it fails as written. Create one first (next section).

A real example: the Gatsby research agent

langchain_basics.py points the URL-fetching tool at a hard task: count exact lines in a real ~280 KB book from Project Gutenberg. A model cannot do that from memory, so it must use the tool. The prompt design is the lesson.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a literary data assistant.

## Capabilities
- `fetch_text_from_url`: loads document text from a URL into the conversation.
Do not guess line counts or positions. Ground them in tool results."""

# ...and in the user message:
# "If you cannot VERIFY an exact answer with your tools, do not fabricate numbers.
#  Use null for that field and explain the limitation."
Key ideaGrounding beats guessing

Three habits in one example, all of which come back as guardrails in Chapter 8: 1. Tell the agent what its tool is for in the system prompt. 2. Forbid fabrication and give it an honest way out (null plus an explanation). 3. Ask it to report errors instead of hiding them.

Pro tipTry it yourself

Run it, then count the lines yourself with a text editor or grep -c Gatsby. Does the agent's number match, or did it guess? This is the quickest way to feel the difference between a grounded and an ungrounded answer.

Repo notePreview of the third tier

The same file imports create_deep_agent from deepagents at the top and never uses it. It is a hint of the Deep Agents tier covered in Class 07.

Memory: why the agent forgets

In class, saying "Hi, I am Mayank" in one run and asking "Who am I?" in a second run got no answer. The history lived in the first process, and ended when the script ended.

Beyond the classAdded to fix the repo example

Class 06 made the point that memory is lost when the process ends and needs a store. The checkpointer code below is my addition, because the repo example uses a checkpointer it never defines. Later chapters cover memory properly.

To keep a conversation, plug in a checkpointer and give each conversation a thread id:

from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-4o-mini",
    tools=[get_weather],
    system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant",
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),
)

cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-1"}}
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hi, I am Mayank"}]}, cfg)
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Who am I?"}]}, cfg)   # remembers
NoteStill not permanent

InMemorySaver keeps state only while the Python process runs. For real persistence you need a database-backed checkpointer. Chapters 6 and 10 cover this properly.

Should you cache tool results?

Not always. Match the cache time (TTL) to how fast the data changes.

Data Cache? Reason
Stock price Never Changes every second
Currency rate Minutes Moves slowly within a short window
Weather Hours to a day Changes gradually

From the docs: install, quickstart and choosing a framework

Added from the LangChain overview, install and quickstart pages (read 30 Oct 2026).

Framing. The overview describes create_agent as a minimal, highly configurable agent harness and sums it up as Agent = Model + Harness. You compose an agent from a model, tools, a prompt and middleware.

Which tool for which job (the overview's own comparison):

Option Use it when
LangChain create_agent You want a customisable harness fitted to your data and use case
Deep Agents SDK You want a batteries-included harness (context compression, a virtual filesystem, sub-agents) that you self-host
Managed Deep Agents The same harness, run for you without managing infrastructure
LangGraph You need low-level orchestration mixing deterministic and agentic steps
LangSmith You need to trace, debug and evaluate agents built with any of the above

Four benefits the docs list: one standard interface across providers; a harness you extend step by step with middleware (guardrails, retries, routing, tool policies); built on LangGraph, so durable execution, human-in-the-loop and persistence come with it; and debugging through LangSmith traces.

Install. pip install -U langchain or uv add langchain. Providers are separate packages, installed only when used, for example langchain-openai or langchain-anthropic. LangChain lists integrations for hundreds of models.

Common trapThe docs disagree on the Python version

The install page says Python 3.10 or newer, the quickstart says 3.11 or newer. Use 3.11 or newer and you satisfy all three.

Credentials. Each provider reads its own variable: OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GOOGLE_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, FIREWORKS_API_KEY, BASETEN_API_KEY, OLLAMA_API_KEY, HUGGINGFACEHUB_API_TOKEN. Azure needs AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY, AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT and AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT_NAME. AWS Bedrock needs AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_REGION. A .env file loaded with python-dotenv (load_dotenv()) is the usual way.

The quickstart in one picture. A model string in "provider:model" form, a plain function as a tool (the docstring is the description), a system_prompt, then agent.invoke({"messages": [...]}) and read result["messages"][-1]. It then adds a @tool, init_chat_model settings, an InMemorySaver checkpointer scoped by thread_id, and compares create_agent with create_deep_agent: on the same research task the plain agent replied it had no way to count lines, while the deep agent used its file tools and grep. The docs add that results vary by model and run.

Tracing quickstart. LANGSMITH_TRACING=true plus LANGSMITH_API_KEY, then run as normal .

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Thinking LangChain replaces the API key Authentication error LangChain is free, but you still need a provider key
Wrong env variable name Auth error after switching provider Use the standard name for that provider
Vague docstring Wrong tool or no tool call Say what it does and when to use it
Following Classic tutorials Imports fail, APIs missing Check the tutorial targets LangChain v1 or later
Committing .env Leaked key Use .gitignore and .env.example
Expecting memory across runs Agent forgets Add a checkpointer and reuse the thread_id
Caching volatile data Stale answers Set TTL by how fast the data changes

Hands-on lab

Do this once, with your own hands.

  1. Create a fresh uv project and install the three packages. Add .env, .gitignore and .env.example.
  2. Write get_weather and build the agent with create_agent.
  3. Run it and print result["messages"].
  4. Map each message back to the Foundations loop: which is the user request, the tool request, the tool result, the final answer?
  5. Add InMemorySaver and a thread_id, then prove the agent remembers your name across two invoke calls.
  6. Rewrite the docstring badly, rerun, and see what changes.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

LangChain is a harness around the model loop. create_agent handles tool schemas, message formatting, the call-execute-repeat loop and provider switching, so I can focus on tools, prompts and middleware. I would drop to LangGraph if I needed full control over the workflow, and I understand the raw loop because I built it by hand first.

Basics

What is LangChain and why would you use it?

It is an open-source framework (free to use; you only pay your model provider) that supplies the harness around an LLM: tool handling, message objects, the agent loop, memory hooks and middleware, behind a provider-independent interface.

Why: you stop rewriting plumbing and can swap providers by changing a string.

What does "Agent = Model + Harness" mean?

The model is the reasoning engine. The harness is everything around it: system prompt, tools, memory, context and middleware. Agent quality depends on both. A weak model in a perfect harness is still weak, and the reverse is also true.

LangChain vs LangGraph vs Deep Agents vs LangSmith?
  • Deep Agents: highest level, batteries included (context compression, virtual file system, sub-agents), least control.
  • LangChain: configurable agent harness built on LangGraph.
  • LangGraph: low-level orchestration for custom stateful workflows, most control.
  • LangSmith: observability and tracing, not for building agents.

Trap: LangFuse is not part of this family. It is a separate observability tool.

What does agent.invoke() return?

A dictionary whose messages list holds the whole conversation: the human message, the AI message requesting a tool, the tool message with the result, and the final AI message. The last message is normally the answer.

Intermediate

Walk me through what happens when a user asks "weather in Tokyo?"
  1. invoke sends the user message plus the tool schemas to the model.
  2. The model replies with an AIMessage that has empty content and a tool_calls entry.
  3. The agent runs get_weather("Tokyo").
  4. The result goes back as a ToolMessage with the same tool_call_id.
  5. The model is called again and returns the final text.
  6. The loop ends because there are no more tool calls.
How does LangChain turn a function into a tool?

It reads the function's name, type hints and docstring and generates a JSON schema. The model sees only that schema, never the code. This is why the docstring acts like a prompt.

How do you add memory, and why does the agent forget between runs?

By default the message history exists only in the running process. Adding a checkpointer (such as InMemorySaver) and invoking with a thread_id lets the agent reload that thread's history. InMemorySaver still disappears when the process ends, so production needs a database-backed one.

How would you switch from OpenAI to Anthropic?

Change the model string (for example "anthropic:...") and make sure ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set. The rest of the code stays the same. What can break: a missing or misnamed key, and model-specific features that the new model does not support.

Is the number of loop turns the same in every framework?

No. It varies. Some frameworks cap the loop at around 100 iterations. The hand-built loop in class used 4 as a sensible starting default. Whatever the framework, you want a cap so a confused model cannot loop forever.

Tricky

Isn't LangChain just a wrapper over the OpenAI API?

No. It does wrap provider APIs behind one interface, but it also adds the agent loop, tool schema generation, message types, memory hooks and a middleware system. The honest trade-off: you give up some visibility and some speed in exchange for development speed and standard behaviour.

Why might a LangChain agent be slower than raw Python?

Extra abstraction: generating IDs, building message objects and internal bookkeeping on every step. For most apps it is negligible, but in latency-sensitive systems it can matter, which is a reason some teams write their own loop.

When would you not use LangChain?

When the task is a single model call, when I need tight control over latency or every step, or when the workflow is better expressed as an explicit graph (then I would use LangGraph directly). Knowing the raw loop lets me make that call.

What did the Gatsby example teach about prompting?

That an agent should be told what its tool is for, forbidden from fabricating, and given an honest fallback (null plus an explanation) when it cannot verify an answer. It is a guardrail pattern taught before guardrails had a name.

Should tool results be cached?

Only when it is safe. Cache by how quickly the data changes: never for stock prices, minutes for currency rates, hours for weather. Caching everything because it is easy gives stale answers.

From the course's interview question bank

What is the difference between a chain and an agent?

A chain is a deterministic sequence of steps wired before runtime, running the same way every time. An agent is non-deterministic: a model decides at runtime which tool to call next, looping until it decides the task is done.

A team wants sentiment analysis on support tickets. Would you build a LangChain agent?

Probably not. For narrow classification tasks (sentiment, named-entity recognition) a small purpose-built encoder model is commonly cited as faster, cheaper and more accurate than an LLM chain. Reach for an agent when the task needs reasoning across steps or tools, not for a single fixed label.

Course assignment questions

From Assignment_LangChain_Fundamentals_Landscape_to_Tools.ipynb and its answer-key notebook (Weekend 05, the GreenPlate restaurant scenario). Answers are condensed from the instructor's key.

An agent is "a model calling tools in a loop"; a harness is "everything around the loop". What counts as the harness?

The system prompt (instructions), the tools the model can reach, and the middleware shaping behaviour at each step. create_agent is the harness: configuring it is most of what the course teaches.

Name the four Lang products. Which is different in kind?

LangGraph: low-level orchestration that everything else sits on. LangChain (create_agent): a configurable harness on LangGraph. Deep Agents: a batteries-included harness with planning, a filesystem and subagents pre-wired. LangSmith is different in kind: an observability platform that watches agents built with any of the others, because an agent's runtime decisions cannot be read from its code.

A 2026 tutorial uses AgentExecutor or initialize_agent. What do you conclude?

It predates LangChain v1.0 (October 2025). Those are the legacy pattern, now in the separate langchain-classic package. Use create_agent.

Why does a .env file exist, and what goes wrong if you hard-code a key in a notebook?

.env keeps the key out of the file you commit or share. A hard-coded key is exposed the moment the notebook reaches GitHub, and automated scanners often find and abuse it within minutes.

Plain text, a message-object list, and a dictionary list: when is each natural?

Plain text for one standalone request with no history. Message objects for multi-turn chats, multimodal content and explicit system instructions. Dictionaries do the same job and are natural when the conversation arrives from a database or JSON API.

Part A LangChain core · Chapter 2

The LangChain family and harness engineering

A map of the four "Lang" products, how the framework got here, and how to set up an environment where every later notebook just works.

Class 0718 to 19 July30 min readCode: Weekend 04
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Most confusion later in the course comes from starting to code without a map. Interviewers ask "LangChain vs LangGraph?" constantly, and old tutorials (pre-v1) quietly break on current code. This chapter gives you the map, the timeline, and a working environment.

Key ideaThe sentence to memorise

An agent is a model calling tools in a loop until a task is complete. A harness is everything around that loop.

Nearly everything later (RAG, memory, multi-agent, database agents) is a different configuration of the harness around the same model. The model does not change. What you give it access to, and the rules for using it, do.

Core ideas

1. Model, harness and "harness engineering"

AnalogyEngine, car and harness

The model is the engine. It has extraordinary power but cannot go anywhere alone. The harness (system prompt, tools, memory, middleware, guardrails) turns it into a car you can drive. Even Claude Code and ChatGPT are a brain wrapped in connectors, skills, memory and search.

Harness engineering is a term gaining popularity for exactly this skill: wrapping a raw model with the right prompt, tools, middleware, guardrails and checkpoints so it becomes useful.

Common trap"I used a small model but expected the smartest agent"

The capability of the agent is capped by the brain you chose. A harness improves behaviour, but it cannot make a weak model reason like a flagship one.

The components of an agent, as named in class:

Part Role
Model The reasoning brain
Tools What the agent may reach for
System prompt How it should behave
Memory What it remembers across turns
Context Previous messages, documents
Sub-agents Helpers it can delegate to

create_agent officially exposes the model, tools, system prompt, structured output, invocation and streaming, and later the harness configuration (middleware). Each gets its own chapter.

2. The four "Lang" products

None of these compete. You do not pick one; you use as many as your project needs.

Product One-line job Reach for it when
LangGraph Low-level orchestration: branching, loops, persistence, durable execution, human-in-the-loop You need to wire every step yourself
LangChain create_agent, a configurable harness built on top of LangGraph You want to build agents quickly with a lot of control
Deep Agents create_deep_agent: LangChain plus planning tools, a virtual file system and sub-agents You want those pre-wired
LangSmith Records a trace of every model call, tool call and decision You need to know what an agent actually did
Key ideaLangGraph is underneath, not on top

LangChain's docs say its agents are built on LangGraph, so you get durable execution, human-in-the-loop support and persistence without learning LangGraph first. You are not avoiding LangGraph by using LangChain; you are standing on it.

Why start with LangChain, not Deep Agents? Starting with Deep Agents is like starting a chef's job knowing only how to order delivery. You get food but no control. The intended order is LangChain, then LangGraph, then Deep Agents, because Deep Agents becomes easy once the other two are solid.

Common trapLangFuse is not in the family

It shares the word "Lang" but is an independent, open-source observability platform.

3. LangSmith: the flight's black box

With normal code, a stack trace and the source tell you what happened. An agent decides what to do at runtime, so the code only describes what it could do. A trace is the timestamped record of what it did: each model call, tool call and middleware step.

Two environment variables turn it on:

LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_API_KEY=your-key-here

The reference notebook notes a free Developer tier of 5,000 traces a month as of 2026, plenty for learning. LangSmith also works with OpenTelemetry, so it can watch more than LangChain.

4. The timeline

Date What happened
Oct 2022 LangChain launches with LLM abstractions and chains: fixed sequences like retrieve, then generate
Dec 2022 First general-purpose agents, based on the ReAct paper (Reason plus Act). The model emitted JSON for a tool call and LangChain parsed it by hand
Feb 2024 LangGraph released: streaming, durable execution, short-term memory, human-in-the-loop
Oct 2024 LangGraph becomes the preferred way beyond a single call; most old chains and agents deprecated
20 Oct 2025 LangChain v1.0: one unified agent abstraction on top of LangGraph
15 Mar 2026 Deep Agents released
Repo noteSmall date difference between sources

The class transcript places the ReAct agent in "late 2022 or 2023". The reference notebook says Dec 2022. Treat it as end of 2022.

Common trapOld tutorials: AgentExecutor and initialize_agent

These are the pre-v1 approach. Importing AgentExecutor straight from langchain now raises an ImportError, because that code deliberately lives in a separate langchain-classic package. Seeing it in a 2026 tutorial is a signal the content is outdated, not that your setup is broken.

AnalogyLow-level vs high-level

A low-level layer gives more control and more effort, like having everything on your own desk. A high-level layer hides detail for speed. LangGraph is low-level; LangChain is higher; Deep Agents is higher still.

Setting up the environment

Colab vs VS Code

Google Colab VS Code (local)
Best for Learning line by line Real projects
Setup None, free, works on weak laptops Proper environment, many files, frontend plus backend
Keys Built-in Secrets manager (key icon) .env file

Notebooks are also on GitHub. The instructor's advice: watch live, then practise from the recording rather than coding along. Class also used Pomodoro blocks: 15 to 20 minutes of focus, then a short break.

Local project

uv init langchain-course
cd langchain-course
uv add langchain langchain-openai langchain-community langgraph python-dotenv
uv add langchain-mcp-adapters langchain-chroma chromadb pypdf   # needed in later modules

The second line installs packages for MCP and retrieval that you will need later, so you do not stop mid-course.

Create .env with OPENAI_API_KEY=... and make sure .gitignore contains .env. Then use this check at the top of every notebook:

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()                                  # read .env into the environment
assert os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY"), "Key missing: check .env"
print(os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"][:5])        # first 5 characters only, never the whole key
Pro tipIf you get an authentication error

Two causes cover most cases. (1) .env is not in the folder you are running from. (2) You created .env after starting the notebook session, so restart the kernel so load_dotenv() sees it. A third one seen live: VS Code had the wrong Python interpreter selected. Pick the project's own .venv.

The sanity check

If this runs in both Colab and VS Code, your whole environment is wired correctly:

from langchain.agents import create_agent

def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Get weather for a given city."""
    return f"It's always sunny in {city}!"

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",       # any model you have access to
    tools=[get_weather],
    system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant.",
)
agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in SF?"}]})

How LangChain finds your key

LangChain expects the exact standard variable name per provider (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and so on). Renaming it (say OPENAI_API_KEY_2) or switching provider without the matching variable gives an authentication error. This was shown live by switching to a Claude model without setting ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

Your first model call

init_chat_model is the universal entry point. The string is "provider:model", and the rest of your code does not change when you swap it.

from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

model = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5.5")
response = model.invoke("Tell me what LangChain is")
print(response.content)

Without LangChain you would write different code for OpenAI, Claude, Groq and OpenRouter. LangChain gives one interface. Other frameworks copy the same idea: CrewAI's docs also say "give me any LLM", so learning it here pays off everywhere.

Models differ in capability. Each supports a different mix of tool calling, structured output, multimodality (text plus images) and reasoning. Check the capability sheet of the model you plan to use.

Messages: why a list, not one string

You could send one long string with instructions and the question mixed. The model has no reliable way to tell which part is the instruction. A message list labels each part:

Message Meaning
SystemMessage Instructions for behaviour: the "director's note"
HumanMessage What the user said
AIMessage What the model said earlier
ToolMessage A tool's result, sent back to the model 
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMessage

messages = [
    SystemMessage(content="You are a pirate. Answer everything in pirate language."),
    HumanMessage(content="What is the capital of France?"),
]
print(model.invoke(messages).content)     # a pirate-flavoured answer

The pirate instruction never mixes with the question. That separation is the whole point. ChatModel does not manage or sort chat history for you; that is still on you.

Open vs closed source

Open source Closed source
Weights available Yes: self-host, fine-tune No
Where it runs Your own infrastructure The provider's API only
Cost Often free, plus your hardware Pay per use
Examples GPT-OSS releases Most flagship GPT and Claude models

From the docs: what a harness is made of

Added from the LangChain agents page (read 30 Oct 2026).

The docs define an agent as a model calling tools in a loop until the task is complete, and the harness as everything around that loop: the prompt, the tools and the middleware. Its job is to get the model the right context at the right time.

The agents page groups harness middleware like this, which is a good mental map for Chapters 7 to 9:

Concern Middleware named on the page
Execution environment FilesystemMiddleware (from deepagents) with a backend such as StateBackend
Context management SummarizationMiddleware, MemoryMiddleware, SkillsMiddleware
Planning and delegation TodoListMiddleware, SubAgentMiddleware (sub-agents with isolated context)
Fault tolerance ModelRetryMiddleware, ToolRetryMiddleware
Guardrails PIIMiddleware
Steering (human in the loop) HumanInTheLoopMiddleware

create_deep_agent pre-assembles a harness (filesystem, summarisation, sub-agents, prompt caching) for long-running tasks. Managed Deep Agents builds on create_agent with planning, file tools, sub-agents and memory preassembled.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Following pre-v1 tutorials ImportError on AgentExecutor Use create_agent; only install langchain-classic deliberately
.env created after the kernel started Auth error Restart the kernel
Wrong interpreter in VS Code .env not read, packages missing Select the project's .venv
Renamed API key variable Auth error Use the provider's standard name
Putting instructions in a user string Inconsistent behaviour Use SystemMessage
Expecting a small model to act like a flagship Weak reasoning Choose the model for the job
Mixing up LangFuse and LangChain Wrong tool for the task LangFuse is a separate observability tool

Hands-on lab

  1. Create the project and install the packages above.
  2. Run the key check, then the sanity check, in both Colab and VS Code.
  3. Switch the model string to a second provider and watch the auth error when its key is missing. Fix it.
  4. Send the pirate messages. Then move the instruction into the user message and compare.
  5. Draw the family diagram from memory and say what each box does.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

LangGraph is the low-level engine. LangChain's create_agent is a configurable harness built on top of it. Deep Agents adds planning, a file system and sub-agents on top of that. LangSmith is separate: it traces what an agent actually did. An agent is a model calling tools in a loop; the harness is everything around the loop.

Basics

Define agent and harness.

An agent is a model calling tools in a loop until a task is complete. The harness is everything around that loop: system prompt, tools, middleware, memory and guardrails. The model supplies reasoning; the harness supplies capability and rules.

Is LangChain built on LangGraph, or the other way round?

LangChain is built on top of LangGraph. A common wrong answer is that LangGraph sits on LangChain. LangChain's agents get durable execution, persistence and human-in-the-loop support from LangGraph.

What is LangSmith and why do agents need it?

An observability and evaluation platform. Agents decide at runtime, so reading code does not tell you what happened on one run. A trace records every model call, tool call and decision in order. It is enabled with LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and an API key.

Is LangFuse part of LangChain?

No. It is an independent open-source observability platform that shares the name prefix.

Intermediate

Why learn LangChain before Deep Agents?

Deep Agents is batteries included with little control, and it is built on LangChain agents. If you only know the pre-built version, you cannot customise or debug it. The suggested order is LangChain, LangGraph, then Deep Agents.

A 2026 tutorial uses AgentExecutor. What does that tell you?

It targets pre-v1 LangChain. v1.0 (Oct 2025) unified everything into create_agent, and the old classes now live in the separate langchain-classic package, so importing them from langchain raises ImportError.

How does LangChain find an API key?

From the provider's standard environment variable (for example OPENAI_API_KEY). A different name, or a missing variable after switching provider, gives an authentication error.

Why use a message list instead of one string?

So the model can tell instructions (SystemMessage) from user input (HumanMessage) and earlier replies (AIMessage). It is also the format tool results use (ToolMessage).

Tricky

Does the framework make a weak model smarter?

No. The harness shapes behaviour and adds tools, but reasoning quality is limited by the model. Choose the model for the task and budget.

Why might a notebook fail on an auth error even though .env has the key?

Usually the .env is in a different folder, was created after the kernel started (restart it), or the wrong interpreter is selected. Only after ruling those out would I suspect the key itself.

Open vs closed models: when would you choose each?

Open weights when I need self-hosting, privacy, fine-tuning or no per-call cost, accepting I run the hardware. Closed models when I want top quality with no infrastructure, accepting per-use pricing and no fine-tuning.

From the course's interview question bank

What is the ReAct pattern?

Reasoning plus Acting. The model alternates a thought (reasoning), an action (usually a tool call) and an observation (reading the result), and repeats until it gives a final answer instead of another action. It is the ancestor of today's agentic loop.

Do you know a real security vulnerability in langchain-core?

Yes: CVE-2025-68664, disclosed December 2025, rated CVSS 9.3. It was a serialisation injection in dumps() and dumpd(): they failed to escape the reserved internal key "lc" in free-form dictionaries, so attacker-controlled data (reachable through prompt injection into fields such as model response metadata) could be treated as a trusted internal object when deserialised, potentially exposing secrets from environment variables. It is patched in langchain-core 0.3.81 and 1.2.5 or later. The interviewer is checking that you track security advisories for the frameworks you ship.

Quick revision

From the docs: philosophy, components, LangSmith and deployment

From five LangChain docs pages read in full on 31 Oct 2026: Philosophy, Component architecture, LangSmith Observability, LangSmith Studio and Deployment.

What LangChain believes. LLMs are powerful, better when combined with external data, and applications will become more agentic, but it is early, and a prototype is easy while a reliable production agent is hard. Two focuses: build with the best models (standardise differing provider APIs, parameters and message formats so you can switch models without lock-in), and make it easy to use models to orchestrate flows over other data and computation (tools, parsing and access to unstructured data). You can build with LangChain for maximum control, or with Deep Agents, an opinionated harness with built-in planning, filesystem tools, subagents and context management. Both sit on LangGraph.

A short history, as the page tells it.

When What happened
Oct 2022 v0.0.1, a month before ChatGPT: LLM abstractions plus "chains" (fixed steps, such as retrieve then generate). The name is Language plus Chain
Dec 2022 First general-purpose agents, based on the ReAct paper: the model emitted JSON that was parsed into tool calls
Jan 2023 OpenAI's Chat Completions API moves models from strings to lists of messages; a JavaScript version is released
Mar 2023 OpenAI function calling: the API itself returns tool-call payloads, so LangChain stops parsing JSON
Jun 2023 LangSmith released (observability and evals), since the main problem is reliability
Jan 2024 v0.1.0, the first non-0.0.x
Feb 2024 LangGraph released: the missing low-level orchestration layer (streaming, durable execution, short-term memory, human-in-the-loop)
Jun 2024 700+ integrations, split into partner packages or langchain-community
Oct 2024 LangGraph becomes the preferred way for anything beyond one LLM call; most old chains and agents deprecated
Apr 2025 Multimodal inputs; the message format is extended
20 Oct 2025 v1.0: all old chains and agents replaced by one agent abstraction built on LangGraph; a standard content format for reasoning blocks, citations and server-side tool calls; old code stays available as langchain-classic
Mar 2026 Deep Agents released as an open-source harness on LangGraph

Component architecture. Five layers build on each other: input processing (raw data to documents), embedding and storage, retrieval, generation (models, optionally with tools) and orchestration (agents and memory). The page's category table: models, tools, agents, memory, retrievers, document processing (loaders, splitters, transformers) and vector stores (Chroma, Pinecone, FAISS). Common patterns: RAG, an agent with tools, a multi-agent system.

LangSmith tracing. Agents from create_agent support tracing with no extra code once you set the environment: LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY, plus, in an agent-based workspace, LANGSMITH_AGENT_ID and LANGSMITH_AGENT_ENVIRONMENT (or LANGSMITH_PROJECT in a project-based workspace or self-hosted). A trace records every step: input, model calls, tool calls, decisions and the final response. Trace only some calls with ls.tracing_context(enabled=True), and attach tags and metadata (user id, session id) either in config or in tracing_context.

LangSmith Studio. A free visual interface for running and debugging a local agent. Install langgraph-cli[inmem] (Python 3.11 or newer), put your agent in a file, create a .env (not committed) with the LangSmith key, write a langgraph.json whose graphs key points at your agent (create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph, which is what the key expects), install dependencies and run langgraph dev. The agent is then served at http://127.0.0.1:2024 and opens in Studio, showing prompts, tool arguments and results, tokens, latency and exceptions with their state; the dev server hot-reloads, and you can re-run a thread from any step. Setting LANGSMITH_TRACING=false keeps data local. Safari blocks localhost connections to Studio, so add --tunnel.

Deployment. For production the page offers LangSmith Cloud (managed infrastructure for stateful, long-running agents with persistent state and background execution), plus hybrid, standalone and self-hosted options. The Cloud steps: push a LangGraph-compatible app to GitHub (public or private), create a New Deployment under Deployments in LangSmith and link the repository (about 15 minutes), open it in Studio, copy the API URL, and call it with langgraph-sdk (client.runs.stream(None, "agent", input=..., stream_mode="updates")) or with REST at /runs/stream and an X-Api-Key header. The agent name comes from langgraph.json.
