Part D MCP · Chapter 12

MCP primitives, lifecycle and JSON-RPC

The three primitives in working code, the three-phase MCP lifecycle, JSON-RPC 2.0 as the shared language, and the initialization handshake step by step.

Class 175 September45 min readCode: Weekend 10
Jump to a section

Why it matters

This is the chapter that separates someone who can use an MCP connector from someone who can explain how to build one that scales. Interview questions here are precise: "why JSON-RPC and not REST?", "what are the three handshake steps?", "what does the id field do?" The instructor's stated bar: be able to walk into a Google or Amazon interview and explain it.

Core ideas

1. Quick recap: why, and who talks to whom

People wanted ChatGPT-style AI connected to Google Drive, Slack, GitHub and Gmail. Defining custom tools for each did not scale, and MCP closed the gap. A host (Claude Desktop, VS Code, Cursor, Codex) never talks to a server directly, because they do not share a language. It spins up a client per server, and the client and server communicate in JSON-RPC.

In the Inspector demo, Inspector is both host and client (the interface a person uses, and the thing opening the connection) while server.py is the server. The handshake the instant Inspector connects is a client doing its job.

Key ideaOne-to-one: which direction holds?

Each client connects to exactly one server. That always holds. The reverse depends on the transport. The official docs say: each MCP client maintains a dedicated, 1:1 connection with its server; local servers typically serve a single client, whereas remote servers typically serve many clients at once. A hosted Gmail or Slack MCP server is built for many clients.

Benefits of the 1:1 design (decoupling, safety, scalability, parallelism) were covered in Chapter 11. The safety proof: press Ctrl+C on the server while Inspector is connected and only that connection closes.

2. The three primitives

  • Tools are actions: the one primitive where the AI itself decides to act. Everything else is initiated by someone or something else first. Without a tool the AI can describe sending an email perfectly; with one it can send it.
  • Resources are read-only, near-static data: a repo's README, a database schema file, a team style guide in Google Drive, or (from MCP's own travel-planning example) a passport PDF or visa checklist. Typically the application, not the model, decides to read a resource and feed it in as context. A resource never changes anything.
  • Prompts are predefined templates that help the AI do a task well, not just do it. A bare create_issue call can produce a thin issue. A prompt guides the AI to gather a title, description and reproduction steps first, consistently. Only the form changed, not the model.
Common trapResources and prompts are optional

GitHub's official MCP server ships tools only, no resources or prompts, and that is a completely valid, common design. Tools are effectively the required primitive.

Primitive Functions What they do
Tools list, call list discovers tools and argument schemas; call invokes one
Resources list, read, subscribe list discovers; read retrieves one; subscribing tells a client when a resource changes
Prompts list, get list discovers templates; get retrieves one

The moment a client connects it calls the list functions (tools/list, resources/list, prompts/list). That is how a host learns everything a server offers before using any of it.

3. All three in real code

Starting from the tools-only warm-up server, adding a resource and a prompt takes exactly two more decorators:

@mcp.resource("file://server-notes")
def server_notes() -> str:
    """Read-only notes about this server, straight from a local file."""
    with open("server-notes.txt") as f:
        return f.read()

@mcp.prompt
def structured_escalation(issue_summary: str, what_was_tried: str, customer_sentiment: str) -> str:
    """Guides the AI to log a customer escalation with every required field, in order."""
    return f"""Log this customer escalation with the following structure:
Issue Summary: {issue_summary}
What Was Already Tried: {what_was_tried}
Customer Sentiment: {customer_sentiment}
Recommended Next Action: [determine this from the details above]
"""

In Inspector: greet and add under Tools, file://server-notes under Resources (returning the file's real content), and structured_escalation under Prompts, asking for exactly the three fields. Filled in, it produces:

Issue Summary: Order #4521 arrived damaged
What Was Already Tried: Customer emailed support once, no reply in 3 days
Customer Sentiment: Frustrated, considering a refund request
Recommended Next Action: Escalate to logistics team, offer expedited replacement

Most tutorials stop at tools because tools are the easiest to demo. Resources and prompts are just as easy; they get skipped more often.

4. The lifecycle: three phases, always in this order

Initialization is the handshake and introduction, operation is the conversation, shutdown is saying goodbye. You cannot hold a conversation before anyone has been introduced.

To make it tangible, the instructor opened Claude Desktop's real MCP log (macOS: ~/Library/Logs/Claude/mcp.log; Windows has an equivalent) showing actual JSON-RPC messages with a local Apple Notes server over STDIO. It also explains why a connector can show a warning icon before you use it: at startup Claude initialises every configured server, and if the handshake fails it already knows.

5. JSON-RPC 2.0: the shared language

Two systems need a common language, like two people. For client and server it is JSON-RPC 2.0. JSON is the familiar data format. RPC is Remote Procedure Call: run a function on another machine as if it were local, hiding the network details. Instead of specifying low-level query parameters, the client says "please query the DB with these arguments."

// Request (client to server)
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list", "params": {} }

// Response (server to client)
{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "result": { "tools": [ ] } }
Field Meaning
jsonrpc Always "2.0": the format version both sides must agree on
id Matches a response to its request. Responses can arrive asynchronously and out of order, so without an id you could not tell which answers which
method, params What is being requested
result or error A response has one of these, never both

6. Why JSON-RPC and not plain REST?

An interview-level question, and the reasoning is deliberate.

Reason Meaning
Lightweight Plain, readable JSON without the headers and overhead of REST or XML
Transport-agnostic The same protocol works locally (STDIO) or remotely (HTTP)
Genuinely two-way The biggest departure. In HTTP, only the client initiates and the server replies. In JSON-RPC either side can initiate, so a server can proactively report progress on a long task instead of the client polling
Notifications built in A message with no id means "fire and expect nothing back", which strict request-response does not naturally support
Standard error codes Inherited wholesale, like HTTP's 404 and 500
Key ideaJSON-RPC is not an MCP invention

It is a pre-existing, general-purpose specification used elsewhere in networking. Anthropic adopted it because it already fit MCP's needs.

Common trapTwo-way is not the same as asynchronous, and not a WebSocket

Asynchronous means the client sends a request and carries on, expecting a reply later, but the server still never initiates. Two-way means either side can start a request. And it is not the same as a WebSocket: a WebSocket is a persistent always-open connection, heavier than most MCP interactions need. Two-way capability is a property of the JSON-RPC protocol, not of keeping a permanent socket.

7. The initialization handshake, step by step

  1. The client speaks first with its protocol version, capabilities and client info, tagged with an id (for example 1).
  2. The server responds, matching the id, with its protocol version, its capabilities (tools? resources? prompts?) and its server name.
  3. The client sends an initialized notification: no id, since no reply is expected. This is JSON-RPC notifications in action.

Two rules keep it orderly: the client should send nothing but a ping before the server responds to initialize, and the server should send nothing but a ping before it receives initialized.

8. Version and capability negotiation

The client always sends the latest version it supports, never a list of everything it has ever supported. If the server supports that exact version, it replies with the same one. If not, it replies with the latest it supports, and the client decides whether that is acceptable. With no overlap, they disconnect.

AnalogyWindows and a game negotiating DirectX

Windows supports DirectX 11. A game supports up to DirectX 8. They settle on the highest version both actually share, never a vague "I support all of them."

Real-world consequence, illustrated with WhatsApp: a message deleted in a newer version may not disappear correctly on an older one, because the versions disagree on behaviour. For a client built for a real company, it is not enough to connect to whatever URL is given. A serious implementation decides which historical protocol versions it supports and handles every behavioural difference. That depth is what a strong interview answer shows.

Key pointers to remember

  • MCP solves an integration problem, not an AI capability problem.
  • Host, client, server, always in that order.
  • Client to server is strictly one to one; server to client depends on transport.
  • Two decorators separate a tools-only server from one with all three primitives.
  • Service providers build servers; host developers build clients. Gmail's team builds the Gmail server; Anthropic builds the client in Claude.
  • Every primitive is discovered via its own list.
  • Lifecycle: initialization, operation, shutdown.
  • Handshake: initialize with id, response with the same id, initialized notification with no id.
  • The business case is N times M down to N plus M integrations: any compliant host talks to any compliant server without custom work.

Questions from class worth knowing

Can one MCP server call another?

Yes. A server can act as a client to another server internally, chaining them.

Is FastMCP the only way to build a server?

No. It is the most popular, alongside Anthropic's official MCP SDK. The relationship is like Keras on top of TensorFlow: the official SDK is the base and FastMCP makes building on it easier.

I already have REST APIs and a chatbot. Why build an MCP server?

The scalability maths. Connecting N applications to M tool sets means roughly N times M custom integrations. MCP standardises to about N plus M. It was candidly acknowledged that MCP can feel like needless abstraction over an API call; the value is making access usable by non-technical end users and cutting integration burden at scale.

How does a client know which server to connect to?

The address is given when the client is configured (like pasting a URL into "Add custom connector"). It is not discovered dynamically at connection time.

How does a server know which client a request came from?

That is resolved inside the transport layer: once connected, both sides keep session details internally, like any client-server connection, abstracted from the user.

How do I make my own email domain MCP compatible?

You cannot make an existing product inherently compatible. You build a normal MCP server for it exposing the tools, resources and prompts that make sense.

From the instructor's lifecycle guide and simulator

Added from the MCP Lifecycle guide and the Conversation Simulator on the instructor's Netlify sites (read 30 Oct 2026). The simulator below is rebuilt from the site's own message script.

Interactive demo (needs JavaScript): a play-through of the full MCP conversation, from initialize to shutdown.

Version negotiation is one counter-offer, not a retry loop. The client asks for one version; if the server answers with another, the client checks it once against the list it supports. If it is on the list, it continues; if not, it disconnects. The guide's sketch: a SUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS list, send initialized if the server's version is in it, otherwise disconnect.

Six situations that produce errors: a protocol version mismatch during initialisation, calling a method that was never negotiated, invalid arguments to a real tool, an internal failure on the server, a timeout being exceeded, and a malformed JSON-RPC message. An error is not a crash: it is the same envelope as a success carrying different news.

Code Name Cause
-32700 Parse error Unreadable JSON
-32600 Invalid request Well-formed but not valid
-32601 Method not found Never advertised
-32602 Invalid params Wrong or missing arguments
-32603 Internal error Server logic failed
-32000 and below Server-defined Custom to that server

Ping, timeouts, cancellation and progress. A ping carries no information; its value is keeping a quiet connection from being dropped by a firewall or proxy. Every request should have a timeout; on timeout send a cancellation notification and stop waiting. A progress notification may reset the clock, but a hard maximum should still apply. A progress token rides in _meta on the original call, and the cancellation names the original requestId.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Assuming resources and prompts are required Over-building Tools are the essential primitive
Calling a resource a tool Wrong primitive Resources are read-only
Sending a list of supported versions Wrong negotiation Send only the latest
Forgetting id on a request Cannot match the response Always set it (notifications are the exception)
Replying to a notification Protocol error Notifications expect no reply
Treating two-way as a WebSocket Wrong design Two-way is a protocol property
Ignoring older protocol versions in a custom client Behaviour bugs across servers Decide and handle supported versions
Sending anything but pings before the handshake finishes Out-of-order protocol Wait for the handshake

Run it yourself: all three primitives

The repo's mcp_server_with_primitives.py adds a resource and a prompt to the warm-up server. It reads server-notes.txt from the current folder, so create that file first (the repo version of this folder does not ship one, which makes the resource fail with a file-not-found error until you add it).

mcp_server_with_primitives.py

from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Warm-Up Server")

@mcp.tool
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    """Greet someone by name."""
    return f"Hello, {name}! Welcome to MCP."

@mcp.resource("file://server-notes")
def server_notes() -> str:
    """Read-only notes about this server, straight from a local file."""
    with open("server-notes.txt") as f:
        return f.read()

@mcp.tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """Add two numbers together."""
    return a + b

@mcp.prompt
def structured_escalation(issue_summary: str, what_was_tried: str, customer_sentiment: str) -> str:
    """Guides the AI to log a customer escalation with every required field, in order."""
    return f"""Log this customer escalation with the following structure:
Issue Summary: {issue_summary}
What Was Already Tried: {what_was_tried}
Customer Sentiment: {customer_sentiment}
Recommended Next Action: [determine this from the details above]
"""

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

Then a small checker client. This one is my own example (it follows the pattern of the repo's 02 client); it lists all three primitives and uses each once.

check_primitives.py

"""Connect to mcp_server_with_primitives.py and list all three primitives."""
import asyncio
from fastmcp import Client


async def main():
    async with Client("mcp_server_with_primitives.py") as client:
        tools = await client.list_tools()
        resources = await client.list_resources()
        prompts = await client.list_prompts()
        print("tools    :", [t.name for t in tools])
        print("resources:", [str(r.uri) for r in resources])
        print("prompts  :", [p.name for p in prompts])

        print("greet    :", (await client.call_tool("greet", {"name": "Hitesh"})).data)
        notes = await client.read_resource("file://server-notes")
        print("resource :", notes[0].text.strip())
        msg = await client.get_prompt(
            "structured_escalation",
            {"issue_summary": "Login fails", "what_was_tried": "Reset password",
             "customer_sentiment": "Frustrated"},
        )
        print("prompt   :", msg.messages[0].content.text.splitlines()[0])


asyncio.run(main())

echo "Notes for the warm-up server." > server-notes.txt
python check_primitives.py

Expected output (verified with fastmcp 4.1.4): tools ['greet', 'add'], one resource file://server-notes, one prompt structured_escalation, then the greeting, the file text and the first line of the rendered prompt.

Hands-on lab

  1. Redraw host, client and server from memory, marking where 1:1 applies.
  2. Add @mcp.resource and @mcp.prompt to the warm-up server and confirm all three in Inspector.
  3. Kill the server with Ctrl+C while Inspector is connected and watch it fail contained.
  4. Open your host's MCP log and find the three handshake messages.
  5. Write a JSON-RPC request and response pair by hand for a send_email call with a matching id.
  6. For a service you use daily, list what would be a tool, a resource and a prompt.
  7. Explain out loud why JSON-RPC was chosen over REST.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

Client and server speak JSON-RPC 2.0, chosen over REST because it is lightweight, transport-agnostic, genuinely two-way and has notifications built in. A connection goes through initialization, operation and shutdown. Initialization is three steps: the client sends initialize with an id, the server responds with the same id and its capabilities, and the client sends an initialized notification with no id. A server offers tools, resources and prompts, each discovered with list.

Basics

What are the three MCP lifecycle phases?

Initialization (handshake and capability exchange), operation (the real work) and shutdown (closing the connection, usually initiated by the client).

What are the three handshake steps?

The client sends initialize with an id, protocol version and capabilities. The server responds with the same id, its version, capabilities and name. The client sends an initialized notification with no id, which expects no reply.

What is the id field for?

It matches a response to its request. Responses can arrive asynchronously and out of order, so without an id you cannot tell which answers which.

Which primitive lets the AI act?

Tools. Resources are read by the application and prompts are chosen by the user or app, so the tool is the one the model decides to use.

Intermediate

Why JSON-RPC instead of REST?

Lightweight JSON, transport-agnostic (STDIO or HTTP), two-way so a server can initiate (for example progress on long tasks), notifications with no id, and standard error codes.

JSON-RPC two-way vs asynchronous vs WebSocket?

Async means the client fires and continues but the server never initiates. Two-way means either side can initiate. A WebSocket is a persistent open connection, which is heavier; two-way is a protocol property and does not require it.

How does version negotiation work?

The client sends the latest version it supports. If the server supports it, it echoes it. Otherwise it replies with its latest and the client decides if that is acceptable. With no overlap, they disconnect. Never send a list.

Is JSON-RPC an MCP invention?

No. It is an existing general-purpose spec that Anthropic adopted because it fit.

What does a client do first after connecting?

Calls the list functions (tools/list, resources/list, prompts/list) to learn what the server offers before using any of it.

Tricky

Can a server serve more than one client?

Yes. A client has exactly one server, but a remote server typically serves many clients. Local STDIO servers typically serve one.

Why might a connector show a warning icon before you use it?

At startup the host initialises every configured server. If the handshake fails, it already knows and flags it.

Why must a serious custom client think about older protocol versions?

Versions can behave differently, like WhatsApp message deletion across versions. A production client must decide which versions it supports and handle each behavioural difference, not just connect to any URL.

What can be sent before the handshake completes?

Only pings: the client before the server responds to initialize, and the server before it receives initialized.

What is the business case for MCP in numbers?

N applications by M tool sets means about N times M custom integrations. A standard protocol reduces that to about N plus M, because any compliant host talks to any compliant server.

Part D MCP · Chapter 13

Capability negotiation and the operation phase

Both sides hand over an honest menu, the client discovers and calls tools, the server can ask the user for missing information (elicitation), and a wiretap script lets you watch the real JSON-RPC conversation.

Class 18 (transcript)6 September45 min readCode: Weekend 10
Jump to a section
Repo noteClass numbers differ between the two summary sets

The transcript summaries number this session Class 18 and the short summaries call it Class 17. They are the same 6 September class. The code folder is Weekend 10.

Why it matters

"It just works" is a bad answer in an interview. Things fail at exactly these points in production: capability negotiation, discovery and calls. This chapter shows each step on real systems, plus a tool that makes the hidden JSON-RPC visible. It also covers the question every MCP user eventually asks: are we exposing our data to the LLM?

Core ideas

1. Capability negotiation: an honest menu

Key ideaBoth sides hand over a menu before anyone orders

Client and server each declare what they are capable of, not what they are about to do. That way each side knows what it can ask for later. It is not a commitment; nothing is used until needed.

Side Capability Meaning
Client roots Ability to expose file-system access
Client sampling Supports an LLM sampling request
Client elicitation Can ask the user on the server's behalf
Client tasks, experimental Task support; non-standard features
Server tools, resources, prompts The three primitives
Server logging Can send log messages
Server completions Argument auto-completion
Server experimental Non-standard features

2. Elicitation: the server asks the client

Here the two-way nature of JSON-RPC becomes concrete. Elicitation is how a server requests additional information from the user, through the client, mid-interaction. It does not only reply; it reaches out for something it needs. In LangChain's docs, elicitation surfaces as a LangGraph interrupt: a human answers it and the run resumes.

Common trapElicitation is not Human-in-the-Loop

HITL is an AI-lifecycle safety mechanism layered on tool calls (approve, edit, reject). Elicitation is a native MCP mechanism for a server to ask for information it is missing. Different concept, easy to confuse.

On "deprecated". An older communication pattern is marked deprecated in the newest spec. Deprecated does not mean unused: most servers in the wild still run the older pattern, and migrating an ecosystem takes close to a year.

3. Watching it happen for real

  • VS Code with Context7. Adding the server showed connect then discover tools, automatically, before any request. Context7 is a useful, authentication-free server that returns the latest documentation for a library, solving the problem of a model's training data lagging a fast-moving API. It was named one of the top five most-used MCP servers.
  • Claude Desktop with Apple Notes. The real tool list appeared: list_notes, get_note_content, add_note, update_note_content, with Claude aware of each before any note question.

None of this discovery is written by hand; it is baked into the architecture. You still need to understand every step because production fails at these exact points, and someone who only knows "it just works" cannot diagnose why it stopped.

4. The operation phase: discovery and calling

Operation is exactly two steps.

Step Method When Cost
Discovery tools/list Automatically the instant the handshake completes, before any user question Free: no LLM involved, just the client asking the server what it offers
Calling tools/call Only when a request needs a specific tool Needs a tool name and arguments

A real example. Asked to "list my Apple Notes", the logs showed the real list_notes schema: a folder argument (string, optional, "filter notes by folder") and a limit (number, default 20). Requesting the "Personal" folder sent folder: "Personal" and no limit, so the server's default of 20 applied. Every tool on every server (Gmail, Calendar, Notes) has this same shape: a name, a description and an input schema. The quality of the description decides whether the AI picks the right tool at all.

Key ideaNegotiation says a category exists. Discovery says what is in it.

A student asked why the client calls tools/list if negotiation already said the server "has tools". Negotiation only confirms tools exist as a category. It says nothing about which tools, their names or their arguments. Discovery retrieves that detail.

Errors. Malformed requests fail loudly as a proper JSON-RPC error object using standard codes (a wrong tool name gives a "method not found" style error). This is the same point where the tool-error and retry middleware from Chapter 8 apply.

4b. Three outcomes, not two

Keep these distinct, for the model and for monitoring:

Outcome How to return it Why
Success with data A normal result The model uses it
Success, but empty An explicit empty result, for example {"count": 0, "items": []} The model can truthfully say "no transactions"
Failure A tool result with isError: true and an actionable message, such as "Account not found; call list_accounts first" The model can recover

Invalid requests (bad parameters) are protocol-level JSON-RPC errors, a separate case.

Common trapReturning `{"error": ...}` as a normal result

The model may treat it as data, and your metrics count it as a success. Tool errors also travel as HTTP 200, so status codes will not reveal them. Emit a per-tool metric labelled ok, empty or error. Page a human for infrastructure errors (database down, timeouts); let the model handle user-input errors (unknown account, bad date).

5. The privacy trade-off, head on

"So with MCP, we are exposing our data to the LLM?" Yes. Whatever a tool returns, the client hands to the host, which sends it to the model provider to generate a response. This is real information flow.

  • It is a legitimate reason to lock down which notes, files or folders a connection can see. Apple Notes' lock feature was demoed: a locked note becomes invisible to any MCP call.
  • On the developer's side, middleware (PII detection, guardrails before a model call) controls what the model sees in a custom client or server. See Chapters 7 and 8.

6. Debugging: seeing real JSON-RPC

A third-party "playground" inspector made the lifecycle visible on a two-tool server (getCurrentTime, convertTime). "Convert the current Indian time to Chicago time" produced: an LLM call to understand, tools/call to getCurrentTime, a second LLM call to interpret, tools/call to convertTime, and a final LLM call to answer. The exact request and response bodies were visible, with ids incrementing on every call regardless of primitive.

Common trapClaude Desktop stopped logging full JSON bodies

The repo's wiretap script documents the change. As of 26 June 2026, Claude Desktop's mcp.log and mcp-server-*.log stopped writing the full JSON of each message and now log only a terse one-line summary (method, id, whether params or a result are present). Entries before that date have full JSON; entries after do not. This is the client changing how much it writes to disk, not an MCP protocol version change. Two separate things.

7. The wiretap: sit in the middle of the conversation

Instead of reading logs afterwards, mcp_wiretap.py sits in the conversation. Claude Desktop launches the wiretap instead of the real server, the wiretap launches the real server, and it relays every byte unchanged while printing a pretty copy of each message. Claude Desktop never knows.

In claude_desktop_config.json, change the server entry. Everything after -- is the real command that used to be there:

"filesystem": {
  "command": "python3",
  "args": [
    "/absolute/path/to/mcp_wiretap.py",
    "--log", "/path/to/wiretap-live.log",
    "--", "npx", "-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/you/Desktop"
  ]
}

Fully quit Claude Desktop (Cmd+Q), reopen, and use it normally. The terminal (or log file) shows the handshake, capability discovery, every tool call and shutdown. A --no-color variant exists for piping to a file.

Pro tipGenericise paths before copying

The repo ships claude_desktop_config.example.json with generic paths. Do not copy a real machine's paths into a shared config.

8. Legacy vs modern in the real world

In the debugging tool's connection log, connecting to an older unmigrated server first tried a newer discovery call, got an error because the server did not recognise it, then fell back to the older initialize-first handshake and succeeded. That is version negotiation working in real time.

Realistic migration to a newer MCP version takes 8 months to a year for most servers, with only actively maintained ones (LangChain's, for instance) moving in the first couple of months. A client must support both the modern and legacy handshakes, not only the newest. That separates a demo from something built for a company. Chapter 17 compares them in full.

9. Why MCP and not just function calling (again)

Function calling is fine for a small single-app project. MCP earns its keep once more than one application or team reuses the same tool: a service builds its connector once and every compliant app uses it. It is a free, open, multi-company-governed specification, not a paid Anthropic product, which is why OpenAI and Google support it. Only a shared agreement gets adopted broadly enough to matter.

10. Live project: a no-code AI news updater

Gmail, Google Calendar, Tavily and Apple Notes were connected as live MCP servers through Claude's connector settings. Claude turned a rough flow diagram into a system prompt that researches AI news via Tavily, categorises it, drafts an HTML email, creates a recurring calendar reminder and produces a LinkedIn post and a Substack article.

Key ideaThe brain decides. Tools act.

The model is used every time a decision is needed: which tool, which arguments, how to interpret a result. Data movement happens only through tool calls. A calendar event is created by a tool call once the model picks a time. Search results are woven into a narrative by the model, never by the search tool. Same agentic loop as the start of the course, now across four independent services.

Pro tipA prompt-writing lesson from the same demo

Without telling the model how many headlines to include per category, it made its own undocumented assumption and quietly dropped real stories. The fix is not a framework feature. Be explicit about how much detail you want and test until it holds.

11. An enterprise scenario, worked through

A DevOps architect managing 150+ microservices across AWS, Azure and GCP wanted a vulnerability-remediation agent, but their enterprise Claude account had connector installation locked down to stop data leaving the organisation. The guidance: this is exactly the case for a custom MCP server. A self-hosted server (possibly its own Docker container, fitting the multi-cloud container pipeline) keeps sensitive data inside the organisation, since nothing passes through a third-party connector.

Key pointers to remember

  • Negotiation is an honest menu, not a commitment.
  • Elicitation is a server asking for missing information, native to MCP and different from HITL.
  • Discovery is automatic and free; calling needs a name and arguments.
  • Data returned by a tool really goes to the model provider.
  • A deprecated version still runs most servers; support both handshakes.
  • MCP is a free multi-company specification.
  • The brain decides; tools act.

Questions from class worth knowing

How do we restrict specific tools for specific users in an MCP setup?

That is not an MCP-architecture concern. It is ordinary software engineering, solved with middleware (the guardrail and dynamic tool loading patterns from earlier chapters), not a built-in MCP feature.

Can I create my own MCP server inside Claude?

No. You can connect your own server to Claude, but Claude is not where you build and host one.

Does calling an MCP tool cost LLM tokens?

No. A tool call is a plain client-server transaction. Tokens are spent only when the model is invoked to reason or generate.

Does MCP have built-in caching?

Not by default as far as could be confirmed live. If you want caching, build it separately.

Are Claude's "connectors" the same as MCP servers?

Yes. Claude uses friendlier words ("connectors", "tools") for a general audience to avoid confusing non-technical users.

Should I claim a "production-grade" AI project on my resume if it was not deployed at scale?

Describe it honestly and frame it around the real problem it solved, not the technology. Interviewers care about problem-solving depth, and shallow claims are exposed quickly under questioning.

From the instructor's lifecycle guide: live demo setup and real servers

Added from the MCP Lifecycle guide (read 30 Oct 2026).

Watching traffic in Claude Desktop. The desktop app's own log shows only a one-line summary per message (method, id, whether params or result are present), not the full JSON. The guide's corrected command tails every connected server's log and tags each line with its server and direction (macOS, tail -n0 -f "$HOME/Library/Logs/Claude"/mcp-server-*.log | awk '...'). The log file appears only after Claude Desktop actually connects to a server with that name, so fully quit (Cmd+Q, not just close the window) and reopen after saving the config. With no log setup at all, MCP Inspector (npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector) shows the same traffic in a browser, with full JSON bodies.

Servers you can actually connect to (from the guide's reference page):

Kind Server Run it or URL
Local (stdio) Filesystem npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem <dir>
Local Everything (all three primitives) npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-everything
Local Git uvx mcp-server-git

Local Fetch (URL to markdown) uvx mcp-server-fetch

Pro tipA free transport comparison

DeepWiki publishes both the old SSE URL and the new Streamable HTTP URL for the same service, so you can point at both and watch the transport migration side by side.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Skipping tools/list because negotiation said "tools" Not knowing the tool names or arguments Always run discovery
Thinking discovery uses the LLM Wrong cost estimates It is free; no model involved
Confusing elicitation with HITL Wrong mechanism chosen Elicitation is a server asking for info; HITL approves tool calls
Assuming returned data stays local Privacy surprise It goes to the model provider; restrict and filter
Reading Claude Desktop logs for message bodies Only one-line summaries Use the wiretap
Supporting only the newest handshake Fails against most servers Support legacy and modern
Vague tool description Wrong tool chosen Write a precise description
Not specifying detail level in prompts Silently dropped content State exactly what you want

Hands-on lab

  1. Add Context7 to VS Code and watch discovery happen on connect.
  2. Trigger a tools/list and a tools/call yourself and read both bodies.
  3. Compare an older and a newer entry in your own mcp.log.
  4. Run mcp_wiretap.py in front of a server you already use and read the traffic.
  5. Try the playground inspector on a two-tool server and trace one multi-step request.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

Capability negotiation is each side declaring what it can do, an honest menu, not a commitment. Then the operation phase has two steps: discovery with tools/list, which is automatic and costs no tokens, and calling with tools/call, which needs a name and arguments. Servers can also elicit information from the user through the client. Everything a tool returns is shared with the model provider, so I restrict and filter data deliberately.

Basics

What is capability negotiation?

Both sides declare what they are capable of so each knows what it may ask for later. Client capabilities include roots, sampling, elicitation, tasks and experimental. Server capabilities include tools, resources, prompts, logging, completions and experimental.

What is elicitation?

A server requesting additional information from the user, through the client, mid-interaction. In LangChain it appears as a LangGraph interrupt that a human answers before the run resumes.

What are the two steps of the operation phase?

Discovery (tools/list, automatic and free) and calling (tools/call, needing a tool name and arguments).

Does discovery cost tokens?

No. No LLM is involved. It is just the client asking the server what it offers.

Intermediate

Why call tools/list if negotiation already says there are tools?

Negotiation confirms tools exist as a category. Discovery retrieves which tools, their descriptions and argument schemas.

Elicitation vs HITL?

HITL is an approval layer over tool calls (approve, edit, reject, respond). Elicitation is a native MCP mechanism for the server to request missing information from the client and user.

Are we exposing data to the LLM with MCP?

Yes. Tool results flow client to host to model provider. That is why you restrict what a connection can see (for example locked notes), and use PII middleware and guardrails on custom clients.

What does a good tool definition contain?

A name, a description and an input schema. The description quality decides whether the model picks the right tool.

How should a client handle old and new servers?

Try the newer handshake, fall back to the older one on an error, and explicitly support both. Most servers take 8 months to a year to migrate.

Tricky

Claude Desktop's logs used to show full JSON and now do not. Did the protocol change?

No. The client changed how much it writes to disk (from 26 June 2026 it logs only a terse summary). It is unrelated to the MCP version. The wiretap script recovers the full conversation.

How does the wiretap work?

It sits between Claude Desktop and the real server. Claude Desktop launches the wiretap, which launches the real server and relays every byte unchanged while printing each message. You put the real command after -- in the config.

How would you build a vulnerability agent when connectors are locked down?

A custom self-hosted MCP server, possibly containerised, so sensitive data never leaves the organisation through a third-party connector.

A multi-service no-code workflow dropped some stories. Why?

The model made its own undocumented assumption about how many items to include. Be explicit about the detail wanted in the prompt, and test.

Is "brain decides, tools act" still true across many services?

Yes. The model decides which tool, arguments and how to interpret results. Data movement only happens through tool calls.

Production level

How do you tell tool failures apart from empty results?

Three outcomes: success with data, success but explicitly empty ({"count": 0, "items": []}), and failure as a result with isError: true and an actionable message. Bad parameters are protocol-level JSON-RPC errors. Never return {"error": ...} as a success. Monitor with a per-tool ok, empty, error metric, because tool errors still arrive as HTTP 200.

Part D MCP · Chapter 14

Shutdown, transports and your first real server

Why shutdown depends on the transport layer, how STDIO and Streamable HTTP differ, and how to build a real MCP server the painful legacy way and the easy FastMCP way, then install it into Claude Desktop.

Class 1912 September45 min readCode: Weekend 11
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Shutdown looks like a footnote, but it is the cleanest way to test whether you understand the transport layer. The key fact (no JSON-RPC messages are exchanged during shutdown) catches people out. The second half of this chapter is the first time you build a real server, and the legacy vs FastMCP history is a favourite way for interviewers to separate people who used MCP from people who understand it.

Key ideaLanguage vs connection

JSON-RPC is the language and grammar of what gets said. The transport layer is how the two parties are physically connected in order to say it. Shutdown is about the connection, so it depends entirely on the transport, not on JSON-RPC.

AnalogyWhatsApp vs a phone call

Closing a chat with a friend depends on how you are talking. On WhatsApp, closing the connection means closing your internet. On a phone call, closing your internet does nothing, you have to hang up. Same conversation, different way of ending it.

Core ideas

1. Transport #1: STDIO

STDIO is Standard Input and Output. You have used it for years: any C or C++ program that begins with #include <stdio.h>.

A tiny live demo made the mechanism visible:

name = input("Please tell me your name: ")
print(name)
print("Hello Mayank from Python file")

Run from a terminal, the terminal is the client, the Python file is started as a sub-process and acts as the server, and they are connected by STDIO the instant it runs. What the terminal sends becomes the file's input; what the file prints is what the terminal shows. That three-step pattern (launch a sub-process, share input through stdin, share output through stdout) is exactly what every STDIO MCP connection does, with JSON-RPC messages instead of a name and a greeting.

Benefit Why
Fast Both sides run on the same machine, so no network round trip
Secure Nothing is exposed outside the machine, so almost no attack surface
Simple No server address or network setup; just the command

The trade-off: it only works when both sides can run on the same machine. It does not scale to "anyone on the internet." By default it fundamentally needs a parent and sub-process relationship on one machine (unless proxied through something else).

Shutdown in STDIO:

Key ideaNo JSON-RPC messages are exchanged during shutdown

The whole responsibility shifts to the transport. Closing Claude Desktop sends a plain termination signal to its connected servers: nothing in JSON-RPC, just the process being told to stop.

2. Transport #2: Streamable HTTP

Built on the HTTP everyone knows from the web. Because HTTP already works across the internet, this is what lets a client reach a server running anywhere.

  • The client sends a POST request to a single endpoint, almost always /mcp, carrying the JSON-RPC message in the body, with normal HTTP headers and auth (OAuth or an API key).
  • It replaces the older HTTP plus SSE (server-sent events) pattern, now deprecated, though most existing servers still run the older one because migrating an ecosystem takes the better part of a year.

Seeing it for real. A live connection to an HTTP-based Excalidraw MCP server showed an initialize sent as an actual POST (full headers on screen), then an initialized notification, then tools/list returning 5 tools, then resources/list. The class's own LangChain MCP server URL ended in /mcp too, as every real HTTP MCP server does.

Shutdown in Streamable HTTP: just close the HTTP connection, like closing a browser tab or turning off Wi-Fi. If a server closes unexpectedly mid-connection, something went wrong server-side, and a well-built client should try to reconnect gracefully rather than fail silently.

STDIO Streamable HTTP
Where Same machine, parent and sub-process Anywhere over the internet
How it connects stdin and stdout POST to /mcp
Shutdown Client: stop input, terminate, kill Close the HTTP connection
Speed and risk Fast, tiny attack surface Network latency, needs real auth
Serves Typically one client Typically many clients

With this, all three lifecycle phases (initialization, operation, shutdown) are done.

3. JSON-RPC, one more time

Now that each reason has been seen in practice: lightweight (plain JSON), transport-agnostic (identical over STDIO or HTTP), two-way by design and notifications built in (no id, no reply; exactly what initialized is).

Building a server

4. The legacy way, and why it hurt

The painful original approach was shown deliberately: not to memorise, but to feel its difficulty, and because this style of code still shows up in real companies. With Anthropic's own low-level mcp Python SDK, a simple three-tool server (list_recipes, get_recipe, search_recipes) needed a hand-written list_tools function enumerating every tool plus a large nested if/elif block matching names to implementations. Real, working, verbose and easy to get wrong.

import mcp.types as types
from mcp.server import Server

server = Server("RecipeBox")

@server.list_tools()                      # step 1: describe every tool by hand, as JSON Schema
async def list_tools() -> list[types.Tool]:
    return [
        types.Tool(name="get_recipe",
                   description="Get the full detail for one recipe by id.",
                   inputSchema={"type": "object",
                                "properties": {"recipe_id": {"type": "integer"}},
                                "required": ["recipe_id"]}),
        # ...one types.Tool per tool
    ]

@server.call_tool()                       # step 2: dispatch by name, by hand
async def call_tool(name: str, arguments: dict) -> list[types.ContentBlock]:
    if name == "get_recipe":
        result = RECIPES[arguments["recipe_id"]]
    elif name == "search_recipes":
        ...
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown tool: {name}")
    return [types.TextContent(type="text", text=str(result))]

The description and the dispatch live in two places that must be kept in step by hand. FastMCP generates both from one plain function.

5. The FastMCP way

AnalogyTensorFlow and Keras, all over again

Anthropic released the MCP spec and an official Python SDK that was correct but hard to write. Jeremiah Lowin, a co-founder of Prefect HQ, built standalone FastMCP to make it dramatically easier. It became popular enough that Anthropic folded a version into the official SDK (renaming an internal class to avoid confusion), as Google absorbed Keras's best ideas into TensorFlow. Standalone FastMCP is still what most real servers use.

Common trapFastMCP and FastAPI are unrelated

They are not from the same team or company. They just share a naming style. They are highly compatible in practice, because an MCP tool is conceptually so close to an API endpoint. Do not conflate them in an interview.

from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Recipe Box")

recipes = {
    "123": {"title": "Weeknight Pasta", "minutes": 20, "tags": ["quick", "weeknight"]},
    "124": {"title": "5-Minute Salsa", "minutes": 5, "tags": ["quick", "no-cook"]},
}

@mcp.tool
def list_recipes() -> list[dict]:
    """List all recipe IDs and titles."""
    return [{"id": k, "title": v["title"]} for k, v in recipes.items()]

@mcp.tool
def get_recipe(recipe_id: str) -> dict:
    """Get full details for one recipe by its ID."""
    return recipes[recipe_id]

@mcp.tool
def search_recipes(tag: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Search recipes by tag, e.g. 'quick'."""
    return [{"id": k, "title": v["title"]} for k, v in recipes.items() if tag in v["tags"]]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

What took a hand-written list_tools plus nested if/elif takes one decorator per function. @mcp.tool reads the signature and docstring and handles tools/list and tools/call automatically.

Add a resource and a prompt, no restart needed:

@mcp.resource("recipe://tags")
def valid_tags() -> list[str]:
    """The full list of valid recipe tags, so an LLM knows what it can search for."""
    return ["quick", "weeknight", "no-cook", "vegan", "dessert"]

@mcp.prompt
def plan_weekly_meals() -> str:
    """A template for planning a full week of meals from the recipe box."""
    return "Using the available recipes, plan a balanced set of meals for the next 7 days..."

FastMCP did not need a restart to pick up the resource (reconnect in Inspector, like FastAPI hot reload). The prompt needed a fresh connect and disconnect.

Key ideaWhy the resource matters, concretely

A recipe's tags only exist inside a tool's returned data. A model cannot know which tag values are valid unless it has already called list_recipes or search_recipes. The recipe://tags resource lets it learn the valid tags upfront, so "something for the holidays" can be translated into a tag the server actually understands, rather than the model guessing at something that does not exist.

6. A real debugging moment: port conflicts

npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python3 recipebox_fastmcp.py failed because port 6274 was already in use: MCP Jam happened to be running there. The fix is ordinary debugging: find what occupies the port, then close it or redirect the new one (--client-port 9999 worked). Two things cannot share a port any more than two websites can both be google.com. It is not a sign MCP is broken.

7. Install it into Claude Desktop

uv run fastmcp install claude-desktop recipebox_fastmcp.py

This registers the server in Claude Desktop's own config. After a restart it appears alongside every other connector, usable in a real conversation. The entry it creates:

"RecipeBox_Updated": {
  "command": "/opt/homebrew/bin/uv",
  "args": ["run", "--with", "fastmcp", "fastmcp", "run",
           "/Users/mayank/Complete MCP/first-mcp-server/recipebox_fastmcp.py"],
  "transport": "stdio"
}

Two details: it declares "transport": "stdio" (STDIO is the natural choice for a local server), and the command is uv run --with fastmcp fastmcp run <file>, so Claude Desktop launches the server exactly as you would from a terminal, automated.

8. Preview: making a local server reachable

A server on localhost cannot be reached by anyone else. The answer given was tunnelling, specifically ngrok: it exposes a local port as a real shareable internet URL without deploying to a cloud server. This is what matters once a LangChain agent or another person must reach it. Chapter 16 covers real deployment.

Key pointers to remember

  • Shutdown depends on the transport, not on JSON-RPC. No JSON-RPC messages are exchanged.
  • STDIO is parent and sub-process on one machine: fast, secure, simple, local only. Shutdown: stop input, terminate, kill.
  • Streamable HTTP is POST to /mcp over the internet. Shutdown is closing the connection.
  • @mcp.tool does the work of tools/list and tools/call. The same holds for @mcp.resource and @mcp.prompt.
  • FastMCP and FastAPI are unrelated.
  • A resource can teach a model which values are valid to search for.
  • uv run fastmcp install claude-desktop <file> registers a custom server.
  • Tunnelling (ngrok) bridges "runs on my machine" to "anyone can connect."

Questions from class worth knowing

If an agent talks to a database-backed MCP server, is one tool needed per read operation?

Yes. One tool per meaningful operation (get profile, get transactions), with the model choosing at runtime which best matches the request.

Why does an LLM call list_recipes first instead of get_recipe?

It only learns that get_recipe exists through discovery (tools/list), and it does not know valid ids until it lists them. At real scale there could be thousands of records, not three.

How does an LLM know what kind of file a resource holds?

Through the resource's declared MIME type, the same web concept: plain text, PDF, audio, video and so on.

Should I name frameworks like FastMCP in an interview?

Concepts first. Knowing why MCP is structured as it is, and the legacy vs modern history, separates real understanding from the many who can define an MCP server but cannot explain what happens underneath.

Does the language (Python or Node) matter for a good MCP server?

No. The protocol does not care. The choice comes from your team's stack.

Pro tipInterview feedback from this class

Two learners forwarded for interviews were strong on concepts but weaker on coding. A direct signal: practise writing code, not only explaining it.

From the instructor's lifecycle guide: transports and shutdown

Added from the MCP Lifecycle guide (read 30 Oct 2026).

stdio is just a subprocess and two pipes. The client launches the server, the server reads stdin and writes stdout, messages are newline-delimited, and stderr is free for logging. There is no separate auth layer: credentials come from the environment. The guide proves it with a few lines of plain Python: start server.py with subprocess.Popen (stdin and stdout piped), write one initialize request as a JSON line, flush, and read one line back.

Streamable HTTP uses one endpoint (commonly /mcp) with POST and GET, plain JSON or an upgrade to SSE for long calls, and an optional Mcp-Session-Id header. It replaces the older, deprecated HTTP+SSE transport.

Shutdown has no JSON-RPC message at all. The transport closing is the goodbye.

Transport Client-initiated (common) Server-initiated (rare)
stdio Close stdin and wait; send SIGTERM if it does not exit; SIGKILL as the last resort The server closes its output stream and exits
Streamable HTTP Close the HTTP connection The server closes unexpectedly, so the client should reconnect gracefully

SIGTERM is a polite knock ("please finish up and leave"); SIGKILL forces the door with no chance to clean up.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Looking for JSON-RPC messages in shutdown Cannot find them There are none; the transport handles it
Expecting STDIO to serve remote users Cannot connect Use Streamable HTTP
Hand-writing list_tools and if/elif for new servers Verbose, error-prone Use FastMCP
Confusing FastMCP with FastAPI Wrong in interviews Different projects and teams
Only returning tags inside tool results Model guesses valid values Expose them as a resource
Running two tools on one port Port in use error Free the port or use --client-port
Ignoring an unexpected HTTP close Silent failure Reconnect gracefully
Using HTTP plus SSE for new servers Deprecated Use Streamable HTTP

Hands-on lab

  1. Recreate the input() and print() demo and narrate which part is the client and which is the server.
  2. Trace a real Streamable HTTP connection in Inspector or MCP Jam and find /mcp in the URL.
  3. Build RecipeBox exactly as shown, then add the recipe://tags resource and plan_weekly_meals prompt.
  4. Trigger a port conflict on purpose and fix it with --client-port.
  5. Run uv run fastmcp install claude-desktop <file> and confirm it appears as a connector.
  6. Read about ngrok and explain how it exposes a local port.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

Shutdown depends on the transport layer, not JSON-RPC, so no JSON-RPC messages are exchanged. With STDIO the client stops input, then sends a terminate signal, then kill as a last resort. With Streamable HTTP you simply close the connection, and a client should reconnect gracefully if the server drops. For building, I use FastMCP: one decorator per tool, resource or prompt, instead of the legacy SDK's hand-written list_tools and if/elif dispatch.

Basics

How does MCP shutdown work?

Through the transport layer, with no JSON-RPC messages. STDIO: the client stops sending input, sends a terminate signal and, as a last resort, kill. Streamable HTTP: close the HTTP connection.

STDIO vs Streamable HTTP?

STDIO runs a server as a sub-process on the same machine over stdin and stdout: fast, secure, simple, local only. Streamable HTTP is POST requests to /mcp over the internet: reachable anywhere, serves many clients, needs real auth.

What endpoint does Streamable HTTP use?

A single endpoint, almost always /mcp, with the JSON-RPC message in the POST body.

What does @mcp.tool do?

Registers the function as a tool and handles tools/list and tools/call from its signature and docstring. @mcp.resource and @mcp.prompt do the same for the other primitives.

Intermediate

Why does shutdown depend on the transport and not JSON-RPC?

JSON-RPC defines what is said. Closing the connection is about how the parties are connected. On a phone call you hang up; on WhatsApp you close the internet. Same language, different ending.

FastMCP vs the official SDK?

The official mcp SDK is correct but verbose (hand-written list_tools, nested if/elif). Jeremiah Lowin (Prefect) built FastMCP to make it easy, and a version was folded into the official SDK. Like Keras and TensorFlow.

Is FastMCP from the FastAPI team?

No. Unrelated projects with similar naming. They work well together.

Why add a resource listing valid tags?

A model cannot know valid values that only appear inside tool results. The resource lets it learn them upfront so a vague request maps to a real tag.

What if the HTTP server closes unexpectedly?

It signals something went wrong server-side. A good client attempts to reconnect gracefully rather than failing silently.

Tricky

Why is shutdown "almost always" client-initiated in STDIO?

The client launched the server as a sub-process and owns its lifecycle. The server can close its own output stream and exit, but that is rare.

Can STDIO ever work across machines?

Not by default: it needs a parent and sub-process on one machine. Only if proxied through something else.

How do you get a local server in front of a remote agent?

Tunnel it (for example ngrok) to a real internet URL for testing, or deploy it properly to a cloud host (Chapter 16).

How do you register a custom server in Claude Desktop?

uv run fastmcp install claude-desktop server.py, which writes a config entry with "transport": "stdio" and a uv run --with fastmcp fastmcp run <file> command.

Why show the legacy approach at all?

So its pain is felt, and because that code still appears in real companies.

CLIENT_PORT=9999 npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python3 recipebox_fastmcp.py

Part D MCP · Chapter 15

The Time Tracker project

Wrap a real API in MCP two ways (manual tools and automatic conversion), connect hosts through connectors and config files, and prepare the server for public hosting.

Class 2013 September40 min readCode: Complete MCP, TimeTrackProject
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Real products already have APIs before anyone thinks about MCP. Nothing about Gmail's or Slack's API was designed "for AI". MCP is added afterwards, on top of trusted infrastructure. This chapter is that story end to end, and it answers a real interview question: should you auto-convert an existing API or build tools by hand?

Pro tipAI-assisted coding is expected in this course

The instructor repeated it: the goal is understanding architecture and decisions deeply, not memorising syntax by hand. Pasting code into ChatGPT to understand or debug it is a normal professional habit. What matters is that you can explain and defend the result.

Core ideas

1. Two ways to connect a server to a host

  • Connectors are the discoverable way most people add a server: click "Add", paste a name and a hosted URL. A public, already-hosted server (Firecrawl was the live example) is designed for this.
  • The config file (claude_desktop_config.json on Mac, an equivalent on Windows) powers both methods under the hood. Even a connector added through the UI ends up here. A developer edits it directly to run a locally built server, since a local server has no public URL to paste.
"RecipeBox_Updated": {
  "command": "/opt/homebrew/bin/uv",
  "args": ["run", "--with", "fastmcp", "fastmcp", "run", ".../recipebox_fastmcp.py"],
  "transport": "stdio"
},
"demo-filesystem-wiretapped": {
  "command": "python3",
  "args": ["mcp_wiretap.py", "--log", "wiretap-live.log", "--", "npx", "-y",
           "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "..."]
}
Common trapA bare `uv` often silently fails in the config

Claude Desktop does not necessarily know where uv is installed. Run which uv in a terminal (for example /opt/homebrew/bin/uv) and put the full path in the config's command field. Same for python. This is one of the most common real setup bugs.

The demo-filesystem-wiretapped entry is the wiretap from Chapter 13: a relay that forwards every message while logging the full JSON-RPC.

VS Code is identical in logic: Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P, "MCP: Add Server", choose STDIO, give the command. It writes VS Code's own mcp.json. Every host (Claude, VS Code, Cursor, ChatGPT) runs the same architecture with a different settings screen.

Key ideaThe server never decides which tool to call

A server sits and waits. The client sends a tools/call naming the tool and arguments. All the deciding happens on the model side before the request is sent.

2. The project: Time Tracker

A time-tracking app, the same category as Toggl or Clockify: employees logging real hours against real projects.

Database layer. SQLite with a time_entries table (auto id, employee name, project, entry date, hours, description), seeded on first run so it never starts empty. A row_to_dict helper converts SQLite rows to plain dictionaries.

API layer: FastAPI, deliberately with no MCP yet. This is the REST layer any real product already has:

from fastapi import FastAPI
import database as db

app = FastAPI(title="Time Track")
db.init_db()          # creates the table and seeds sample data if empty

@app.get("/api/entries")
def list_all_entries():
    return db.list_all_entries()

@app.get("/api/projects/{project}/summary")
def get_project_summary(project: str):
    return db.get_project_summary(project)

class NewEntry(BaseModel):
    employee_name: str
    project: str
    entry_date: str
    hours: float
    description: str

@app.post("/api/entries")
def log_time(entry: NewEntry):
    return db.log_time(entry.employee_name, entry.project, entry.entry_date,
                       entry.hours, entry.description)

uv run fastapi dev main.py gave a working Swagger page at /docs and a plain HTML, CSS and app.js front end that logs time and shows project summaries. The browser's network tab showed exactly which REST calls fire when an entry is logged.

3. Two ways to turn an API into an MCP server

Option 1: manual tools, full control.

from fastmcp import FastMCP
import database as db

mcp = FastMCP("Time Tracker")

@mcp.tool
def log_time(employee_name: str, project: str, entry_date: str, hours: float, description: str) -> dict:
    """Log a new time entry for an employee against a project."""
    return db.log_time(employee_name, project, entry_date, hours, description)

@mcp.tool
def get_timesheet(employee_name: str, week_start: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Get all time entries for one employee for a given week."""
    return db.get_timesheet(employee_name, week_start)

@mcp.tool
def get_project_summary(project: str) -> dict:
    """Get total hours and a per-employee breakdown for one project."""
    return db.get_project_summary(project)

@mcp.tool
def list_projects() -> list[str]:
    """List every known project name."""
    return db.list_projects()

@mcp.prompt
def generate_weekly_report(employee_name: str, week_start: str) -> str:
    """A template guiding the AI to pull an employee's week and write a clean summary report."""
    return f"Generate a weekly report for {employee_name} starting {week_start}, using their timesheet and project summaries..."

Inspector showed the same lifecycle as every earlier class: initialize, discovery, a real tools/call. The generate_weekly_report prompt cannot be replicated by a plain API: it guides the AI to combine multiple tool calls into one well-structured output.

Option 2: automatic conversion, speed.

mcp = FastMCP.from_fastapi(app)     # app is the FastAPI instance already defined

Four lines turn every FastAPI endpoint into an MCP tool, confirmed in Inspector: tools mapped straight from the REST routes, no prompts and no resources, since those do not exist in plain REST.

Auto-convert Build by hand
Effort Four lines More
Tool descriptions Whatever the API had AI-friendly, richer
Combine API calls into one tool No Yes
Prompts and resources None Yes
Touches trusted production code No No (a separate layer)
Key ideaWhen to choose which

Auto-convert to make already-working, trusted APIs available to AI quickly, with no interest in reshaping them. Build manually when you need combined calls, richer AI-oriented descriptions than the API ever needed for human developers, or prompts. A practical reason teams go manual: they are reluctant to modify an already-deployed API just to make descriptions AI-friendly, so a separate hand-built MCP layer avoids touching trusted code.

Repo noteThe repo version differs slightly from the class

The repo's main.py has get_timesheet(employee_name, start_date="", end_date="") rather than week_start, and adds a resource timesheet://projects (the current set of known project names). It serves the website and the MCP endpoint from one app, so both see the same data.

4. One app, two front doors (from the repo)

The repo's finished main.py mounts the MCP server inside the FastAPI app: the website for people at /, and the MCP endpoint at /mcp for AI assistants, both using the same database.py.

mcp_app = mcp.http_app(path="/")                     # path="/" here, NOT "/mcp"
app = FastAPI(title="TimeTrack", lifespan=mcp_app.lifespan)   # lifespan AT CONSTRUCTION
...
app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory="static"), name="static")
app.mount("/mcp", mcp_app)
Common trapTwo rules that matter (from the repo README)
  1. Use mcp.http_app(path="/"), not "/mcp". app.mount("/mcp", ...) already adds the prefix, so both would double it into /mcp/mcp.
  2. Pass lifespan=mcp_app.lifespan when constructing FastAPI(...), not afterwards. Otherwise the MCP session manager silently never initialises.
Primitive Name What it does
Tool log_time Logs an entry; appears on the website immediately
Tool get_timesheet One employee's entries, optionally filtered by date
Tool get_project_summary Total hours per project, by employee (a real SQL GROUP BY)
Tool list_projects Every project with at least one entry
Resource timesheet://projects Current known project names
Prompt generate_weekly_report Structures a weekly report request

To connect Claude Desktop to the running server, the repo shows a config with just a URL: {"mcpServers": {"timetrack": {"url": "http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp"}}}.

5. Seeing the raw protocol with curl

The repo includes the handshake as plain curl, which shows that MCP over HTTP really is just POSTs:

curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp/ \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize",
       "params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},
                 "clientInfo":{"name":"test-client","version":"1.0.0"}}}'

# next call reuses the session id returned in the response headers
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp/ \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -H "Mcp-Session-Id: <the id from the first response>" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list"}'

Note the Mcp-Session-Id header: the server hands the client a session id on initialize, and the client sends it back on later calls. That is how the server tells connections apart over HTTP.

6. Going public: Prefect Horizon

Horizon (by Prefect, the company behind FastMCP) is the hosting platform FastMCP's docs recommend. Free tier as noted in class: one developer, up to 200 MCP servers, one-hour log retention, deployed from GitHub so each change redeploys.

The repo's steps:

  1. Create a clean, separate repository with just the server: main.py, database.py, pyproject.toml and uv.lock. Horizon builds from exactly what is in the repo, so notes, scratch files and course material do not belong.
  2. Push to GitHub and sign in at Horizon with that account.
  3. Select the repository and set a server name (for example timetrack) and the entrypoint main.py:mcp.
  4. Optionally verify first with fastmcp inspect main.py:mcp.

The resulting URL can be pasted into any host's connector settings (Claude Desktop, Claude Web, ChatGPT, Cursor), like the Firecrawl connector earlier.

NoteOpen question from the repo README

Whether the website's static routes ship with a Horizon deployment is unconfirmed. Horizon is built for the MCP piece. If the website must be live too, deploy the whole app to a general host (Railway is named as the fallback).

Key pointers to remember

  • A connector and a config-file entry are the same thing; connectors are the UI for it.
  • The server never decides which tool to call.
  • A bare uv path is a top setup bug: use which uv.
  • Real products have APIs before MCP; MCP comes afterward.
  • FastMCP.from_fastapi(app) converts an API in four lines but yields no prompts, no resources and no custom descriptions.
  • Hand-build tools for control; auto-convert for speed and safety.
  • Horizon turns a GitHub repo into a public URL.

Questions from class worth knowing

For deployed production APIs, auto-convert or build manually?

Auto-conversion is the faster, safer start because it does not touch trusted production code. Go manual once you need finer control: better descriptions, combined calls or prompts.

If I have 5 connectors, do they all go in one config file?

Yes. Each connector is its own server entry and the host starts each independently, like multiple servers running side by side.

Is GitHub to Horizon like a Java developer deploying to Kubernetes?

Conceptually yes: take working local code and make it a reachable running service, but through a platform built for MCP servers rather than a general container orchestrator.

Will authorisation be added?

Yes, as a next step once hosted. A publicly reachable time-tracking server for a real company needs real access control.

Is writing code without AI help expected in interviews?

Not in this course. AI-assisted coding is treated as a normal professional skill. What matters is understanding the architecture and decisions well enough to explain and defend them.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Bare uv or python in the config Server does not appear after restart Use the full path from which
http_app(path="/mcp") plus mount("/mcp") Endpoint becomes /mcp/mcp Use path="/"
Setting FastAPI lifespan afterwards MCP sessions silently never start Pass lifespan= at construction
Auto-converting and expecting prompts None exist Add prompts by hand
Vague REST descriptions as tool descriptions Model picks the wrong tool Write AI-friendly descriptions manually
Pushing your whole course folder to Horizon Slow build, leaked files A clean repo with only the server files
Forgetting the Mcp-Session-Id header Server rejects later calls Send the id from the initialize response
Using a local SQLite file on a serverless host Data lost when it goes cold Use a real hosted database

Hands-on lab

  1. Open your host's config file and identify the command and path for one server.
  2. Break a config with a bare uv, then fix it with which uv.
  3. Build a small FastAPI backend with two endpoints over SQLite.
  4. Wrap it both ways: manual @mcp.tool and FastMCP.from_fastapi(app). Compare the tool lists in Inspector.
  5. Add one @mcp.prompt that combines two tools.
  6. Reproduce the handshake with curl and reuse the Mcp-Session-Id.
  7. Read about Horizon's flow from GitHub to a live URL.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

Real products already have APIs, so MCP is a layer added afterwards. I can auto-convert a FastAPI app with FastMCP.from_fastapi for speed and safety, or hand-write tools when I need AI-friendly descriptions, combined calls or prompts, and a separate layer means I never touch trusted production code. Hosts connect through connectors or a config file, which are the same mechanism, and Horizon turns a GitHub repo into a public MCP URL.

Basics

Connectors vs config file?

Connectors are the friendly UI. The config file is what actually holds the entries for both. Developers edit it to run a local server that has no public URL.

Who decides which tool to call?

The model, through the client. The server only executes the tools/call it receives.

How do you auto-convert an API to MCP?

FastMCP.from_fastapi(app) with the existing FastAPI app. Every endpoint becomes a tool.

Intermediate

Auto-convert or manual: how do you choose?

Auto-convert when the goal is quick access to trusted APIs. Manual when you need combined calls, richer AI-oriented descriptions or prompts. Teams often prefer manual so they do not edit deployed APIs.

What does auto-conversion not give you?

Prompts, resources, custom descriptions and tools that combine several calls.

How do you mount an MCP server inside FastAPI?

mcp_app = mcp.http_app(path="/"), create FastAPI(lifespan=mcp_app.lifespan), then app.mount("/mcp", mcp_app).

How do you deploy to Horizon?

Put only the server files (main.py, database.py, pyproject.toml, uv.lock) in a clean GitHub repo, sign in with GitHub, select it, set the entrypoint main.py:mcp, and deploy. The URL looks like your-project.fastmcp.app/mcp.

Tricky

Why might Claude Desktop not show your local server?

Commonly a bare uv or python in the config. Claude does not know where it is installed, so use the full path from which uv.

Why path="/" and not "/mcp"?

app.mount("/mcp", ...) already adds the prefix, so using /mcp in both would double it into /mcp/mcp.

What does the Mcp-Session-Id header do?

The server returns it on initialize, and the client sends it on later requests so the server can tell sessions apart over HTTP.

Why is a hand-built MCP layer sometimes safer in a company?

It leaves already-deployed, trusted API code untouched, while still letting you write richer AI-facing descriptions and prompts.

What breaks if you host with a local SQLite file on a serverless platform?

Data can disappear when the function goes cold. A real hosted database is needed for durability.
