Part D MCP · Chapter 16

Deploying MCP servers and building your own client

Move a server from "works on my machine" to a public URL, understand why the client is a harness, and build the client loop yourself.

Class 2119 September45 min readCode: Complete MCP, TimeTrackProject
Jump to a section

Why it matters

A local server helps only the machine it runs on. Deployment questions are classic interview material: STDIO or HTTP, what does the host platform need, why do local and server databases not sync? And building a client yourself is where "MCP is the same agentic loop" finally clicks. Chapter 15 covered the project and the two main.py rules; this chapter covers what it takes to put it live and to write the other side.

Core ideas

1. STDIO vs HTTP at deployment time

Local STDIO Remote HTTP
Where it runs Your machine, as a sub-process Somewhere else, reachable over the internet
Speed Fast, no network hop A real network round trip on every call
Who can use it Only whatever launched it Many clients, from anywhere, at once
Where the power lives Split across whoever runs it locally Centralised: one genuinely powerful server for everyone
Typical use A personal tool: one person, one machine Team or company-wide shared tools

This is why most serious shared MCP servers run over HTTP. A locally started server, however well built, is not reachable by anyone else.

2. The same file, two transports

uv run fastmcp run main.py
# Starting MCP server 'TimeTrack' with transport 'stdio'

uv run uvicorn main:app --reload
# reachable at http://127.0.0.1:8000, with the MCP endpoint at /mcp
Key idea`fastmcp run` vs `uvicorn`

uv run fastmcp run main.py starts just the MCP server object over STDIO. uv run uvicorn main:app starts the whole application (website, REST API and MCP server mounted together), because app is the FastAPI instance with everything wired in.

3. One app, two front doors

The deployed main.py (Chapter 15 shows the full file) builds the MCP server first, then the FastAPI app with lifespan=mcp_app.lifespan at construction, and app.mount("/mcp", mcp_app). Two rules to remember: http_app(path="/") not "/mcp", and the lifespan passed at construction.

4. A small, honest persistence layer

import os
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

DB_PATH = Path(os.environ.get("TIMETRACK_DB_PATH", "/tmp/timetrack.db"))

def get_connection():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return conn

def log_time(employee_name, project, entry_date, hours, description=""):
    if hours <= 0:
        raise ValueError("hours must be a positive number")
    ...

def get_project_summary(project: str) -> dict:
    rows = conn.execute(
        "SELECT employee_name, SUM(hours) as total_hours FROM time_entries "
        "WHERE project = ? GROUP BY employee_name ORDER BY employee_name", (project,)
    ).fetchall()
    if not rows:
        raise ValueError(f"No time logged against project '{project}'")
    ...
  • log_time validates that hours are positive. Small guardrails like this matter the moment a real tool faces an AI that might send bad input.
  • get_project_summary does a real SQL GROUP BY. The database does the work, not Python after the fact.
  • The database path comes from an environment variable. Class 22 opened with the bug that taught this: a hardcoded path silently failed once deployed to Vercel.

5. Deploying to Prefect Horizon

  1. A clean, separate repo with just the server. The platform builds from exactly what is in the repo. pyproject.toml lists the dependencies and uv.lock pins exact versions, so the platform reproduces the environment exactly.
  2. .gitignore what the server does not need: the virtual environment, local database files, cache and editor folders.
  3. Connect the repo to Prefect Horizon. It is the current name of what was FastMCP Cloud: same team (Prefect, behind FastMCP), same idea. Sign in with GitHub; it detects dependencies from pyproject.toml.
  4. Configure and deploy. Name the server, set the entry point to main.py, pointing at the mcp object specifically, not the whole app. Horizon installs libraries and starts the server, with build logs visible.
  5. Get the live URL, predictable in shape, pasteable into any AI host's connector settings.
Common trapYour local database and the server's database are different files

A .gitignored local database has no relationship to the one created on the hosting platform. They are separate files and separate data. Updating one never touches the other. A local SQLite file on a serverless host can also lose its data when the function goes cold, which is why a real hosted database matters.

NoteHorizon is built for the MCP piece

For a project with more than an MCP server, check whether the website's static routes deploy with it. If not, a general host like Vercel or Railway is the fallback for the full application.

Connect Claude Desktop to the deployed server:

{ "mcpServers": { "timetrack": { "url": "https://your-project-name.fastmcp.app/mcp" } } }

In a real conversation: ask for projects (two found), log 10 hours for "Mayank" on "MCP Mastery", ask again, and the new project now appears. Anyone with the URL can connect and write to the same shared database through their own AI assistant.

6. A second example: no API at all

from fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("Calculator")

@mcp.tool
def add(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    """Add two numbers."""
    return a + b

No API, no database, just a Python function. Deployed the same way, "what is 5 plus 3?" triggers a tools/call to add. MCP has no dependency on a REST API underneath. An MCP server is just a server; what it does inside is up to you.

7. Why you need to build your own client

Claude Desktop and VS Code quietly are MCP clients, so earlier classes took the client for granted. Now picture two separate things: a raw model, reached through a provider's API key, and an MCP server that is capable but cannot decide anything. Neither does anything for the other.

Key ideaHarness engineering

Something has to sit in the middle, connecting the model's intelligence to the server's capabilities. Building that connective layer yourself is harness engineering. Every chat application is a harness around a raw model. Claude Desktop and ChatGPT just build and hide it for you.

from fastmcp import Client
from anthropic import Anthropic

anthropic_client = Anthropic()

async def run_agent(user_message: str):
    async with Client("main.py") as mcp_client:          # connects to the LOCAL server file
        mcp_tools = await mcp_client.list_tools()          # discover
        anthropic_tools = [
            {"name": t.name, "description": t.description, "input_schema": t.inputSchema}
            for t in mcp_tools
        ]
        messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_message}]

        while True:
            response = anthropic_client.messages.create(
                model="claude-sonnet-4-6", messages=messages, tools=anthropic_tools)

            if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
                return response.content                    # final answer: exit the loop

            for block in response.content:                 # the CLIENT executes the tool
                if block.type == "tool_use":
                    result = await mcp_client.call_tool(block.name, block.input)
                    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
                    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [
                        {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id, "content": str(result)}]})
Key ideaAn MCP client is the same agentic loop

Discover the tools, format them for the model provider, send the message, check whether the model asked for a tool, run it, append the result, loop. The model never calls a tool; it only says which one it wants called. The client does. MCP does not change that mechanic. It only standardises how the tool list and the tool call travel between client and server. A framework's "MCP adapter" (LangChain's, for instance) wraps this exact pattern in a few lines, as create_agent wraps the raw loop.

8. The client files in the repo

The repo has nine numbered, self-contained client files (run from the client/ folder):

File What it shows
01_raw_client.py The verbose, three-layer way with the official SDK
02_fastmcp_client_explained.py Builds up step by step to async with
03_fastmcp_client_http.py Connects to the real deployed server on Vercel (needs internet)

Repo noteTwo honest notes from the repo README

File 01 uses the official SDK's low-level stdio_client(), which hangs forever on macOS (documented SDK issue #1452). If it hangs, that is the known issue: move on to file 02.

File 03 was verified live: the public server's list_projects() returned ["Client Onboarding", "Internal Tools", "Website Redesign"] and get_project_summary("Website Redesign") returned 19.0 total hours (13.5 and 5.5), the same seed data as the local server.

9. Where this leaves you

Two honest gaps remain in this project, treated as homework rather than flaws: the database is still a local SQLite file rather than a production-grade one, and every database call is synchronous, so two requests cannot truly run at once. The homework was to make calls async and move to a hosted database (filess.io was demoed: a free 10 MB hosted SQL database with ready-made connection code). The repo also includes a concurrency_showcase.py dev script that measures both problems against a live server: speedup from concurrent calls, and whether every write survives a burst.

10. Running MCP servers in production

These come from the course's MCP interview questions and go beyond what the class demoed.

Scaling to several replicas. On the 2025-11-25 spec, a Streamable HTTP server is stateful by default: initialize returns an Mcp-Session-Id and the session lives in that replica's memory. If the next request lands on another replica, it is rejected.

Option How Trade-off
Run stateless (preferred for request-response tool servers) FastMCP(..., stateless_http=True) You lose server-initiated messages, which most tool servers never use
Sticky routing Route on the Mcp-Session-Id header at the ingress or service mesh Avoid Kubernetes sessionAffinity: ClientIP: all requests from one agent pod pin to one replica, so load is not balanced
Shared session store For example Redis Works, but adds a dependency for little gain

Verify by scaling to two or more replicas and running a multi-turn conversation.

Idempotent sensitive tools. The risk: the database commits, the agent dies before the response arrives, and a retry moves the money twice. MCP has no built-in idempotency, so pass an idempotency key as a tool argument, store it in the same transaction as the transfer (a repeat returns the stored result), and re-check balances at execution time, not at approval time.

Auth. The server acts as an OAuth 2.1 resource server. A 401 with resource metadata sends the client through authorisation code with PKCE. Tokens are short-lived and audience-bound to that one server, never passed through to downstream APIs (use a token exchange). Scope per capability: payments:read is not payments:transfer. Check the scope on every tools/call, filter tools/list by scope, and return 403 insufficient_scope, followed by step-up auth and human approval. Amount, environment and tenant limits live in gateway policy, with an audit log per user and per agent.

Changing a tool contract. Treat the schema and description as an API contract. Make only additive changes in place (new tools, new optional parameters). Ship a breaking change as a new tool name next to the old one and remove the old one when no agent uses it. Agents usually load tools once at startup, so either restart them after a server change or handle notifications/tools/list_changed. Descriptions change routing, so run server changes through the agent eval suite, and snapshot and diff tools/list in CI.

FAQ from class

Is a third-party Postgres MCP server on my laptop really "local"?

Yes. "Local" describes where the MCP server process runs, not where the data lives. A Postgres MCP server started with npx on a laptop is local even though it calls a remote database, like a browser being local while websites are not.

Where do the tools inside a Postgres MCP server come from?

From whoever built it. A vendor or community writes execute and list_tables once, packages them as an MCP server, and everyone who runs it gets them without understanding the driver.

Always MCP, or sometimes a plain tool?

A plain tool is often right for a narrow, fixed action such as sending an email through one channel. MCP earns its place for breadth: supporting a large surface without hand-building dozens of tools.

One setup for several databases (Postgres, Oracle, a mainframe)?

Two options: one custom MCP server with all of them wired in, or an MCP gateway that aggregates several existing servers behind a single entry point so the client connects to one place.

How do I stop an AI from modifying production data?

A common pattern is an environment variable read at startup (for example READ_ONLY=true) that controls which tools the server even registers. Write tools are never exposed, rather than blocked afterwards.

uv vs uvx?

uv works inside your project. uvx runs a tool in an isolated temporary environment without touching the project, like npx. Use uvx for one-off tools.

Does the host platform care whether my server calls an AI model?

No. A call to an LLM provider is just another API call. A generic platform does not distinguish.

How do I keep state per call, per thread and per application?

Application-wide state lives as long as the process. Session state ties to a client-provided session id. Thread-level state is the hardest and has no free built-in mechanism, so you must design how a thread or request owns its context.

Mistake Symptom Fix
Pushing the whole course folder to the host Slow build, leaked files A clean repo with only the server files
Pointing Horizon at app Wrong object deployed Entry point main.py:mcp
Hardcoding the database path Silent failure after deploy Read it from an environment variable
Expecting local and server databases to sync Missing data They are separate files
SQLite file on a serverless host Data lost when cold Use a hosted database
Synchronous database calls Requests cannot overlap Use async
Running file 01 on macOS and waiting Hangs forever Known SDK issue: use file 02
Thinking the model calls the tool Wrong client design The client runs the tool

The persistence layer

database.py

"""
TimeTrack's persistence layer -- SQLite, shared by every tool in this
project. Same tested file from the Persistence video, unchanged.
"""
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

DB_PATH = Path(__file__).parent / "timetrack.db"


def get_connection():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    return conn


def init_db():
    conn = get_connection()
    conn.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS time_entries (
            id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
            employee_name TEXT NOT NULL,
            project TEXT NOT NULL,
            entry_date TEXT NOT NULL,
            hours REAL NOT NULL,
            description TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''
        )
    """)
    count = conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM time_entries").fetchone()[0]
    if count == 0:
        seed = [
            ("Asha Patel", "Website Redesign", "2026-09-08", 6.5, "Homepage layout"),
            ("Asha Patel", "Website Redesign", "2026-09-09", 7.0, "Mobile responsive fixes"),
            ("Asha Patel", "Client Onboarding", "2026-09-10", 3.0, "Kickoff call + notes"),
            ("Rahul Mehta", "Website Redesign", "2026-09-08", 5.5, "API integration"),
            ("Rahul Mehta", "Internal Tools", "2026-09-09", 8.0, "Dashboard bug fixes"),
        ]
        conn.executemany(
            "INSERT INTO time_entries (employee_name, project, entry_date, hours, description) "
            "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
            seed,
        )
        conn.commit()
    conn.close()


def _row_to_dict(row) -> dict:
    return {
        "id": row["id"],
        "employee_name": row["employee_name"],
        "project": row["project"],
        "entry_date": row["entry_date"],
        "hours": row["hours"],
        "description": row["description"],
    }


def list_all_entries() -> list[dict]:
    conn = get_connection()
    rows = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM time_entries ORDER BY entry_date DESC, id DESC").fetchall()
    conn.close()
    return [_row_to_dict(r) for r in rows]


def log_time(employee_name: str, project: str, entry_date: str, hours: float, description: str = "") -> dict:
    if hours <= 0:
        raise ValueError("hours must be a positive number")
    conn = get_connection()
    cursor = conn.execute(
        "INSERT INTO time_entries (employee_name, project, entry_date, hours, description) "
        "VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)",
        (employee_name, project, entry_date, hours, description),
    )
    conn.commit()
    new_id = cursor.lastrowid
    row = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM time_entries WHERE id = ?", (new_id,)).fetchone()
    conn.close()
    return _row_to_dict(row)


def get_timesheet(employee_name: str, start_date: str | None = None, end_date: str | None = None) -> list[dict]:
    conn = get_connection()
    query = "SELECT * FROM time_entries WHERE employee_name = ?"
    params: list = [employee_name]
    if start_date:
        query += " AND entry_date >= ?"
        params.append(start_date)
    if end_date:
        query += " AND entry_date <= ?"
        params.append(end_date)
    query += " ORDER BY entry_date"
    rows = conn.execute(query, params).fetchall()
    conn.close()
    return [_row_to_dict(r) for r in rows]


def list_projects() -> list[str]:
    conn = get_connection()
    rows = conn.execute("SELECT DISTINCT project FROM time_entries ORDER BY project").fetchall()
    conn.close()
    return [r["project"] for r in rows]


def get_project_summary(project: str) -> dict:
    conn = get_connection()
    rows = conn.execute(
        "SELECT employee_name, SUM(hours) as total_hours FROM time_entries "
        "WHERE project = ? GROUP BY employee_name ORDER BY employee_name",
        (project,),
    ).fetchall()
    conn.close()
    if not rows:
        raise ValueError(f"No time logged against project '{project}'")
    by_employee = {r["employee_name"]: r["total_hours"] for r in rows}
    return {
        "project": project,
        "total_hours": sum(by_employee.values()),
        "by_employee": by_employee,
    }

The server (note slow_tool, log_time_with_confirmation and summarize_week, which Chapter 17 uses)

main.py

"""
main.py -- the COMPLETE TimeTrack server used by every file in client/.

This is one file with everything already in it: the four original tools,
the resource, the prompt, and the two "advanced" tools (summarize_week and
log_time_with_confirmation) plus one deliberately slow tool for the
timeout/progress demos. You do not need to copy anything into this file --
it already has it all.

Run it on its own to sanity-check it starts:
    python3 main.py
(it will just sit there waiting for a client -- that's correct. Ctrl+C to stop.)
"""
import os
from fastmcp import FastMCP, Context
from anthropic import Anthropic
import database as db

# Make sure the database file and its table exist before anything else runs
db.init_db()

mcp = FastMCP("TimeTrack")
anthropic_client = Anthropic(api_key=os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", ""))


# ============================================================
# THE ORIGINAL FOUR TOOLS -- unchanged from the Persistence video
# ============================================================

@mcp.tool
def log_time(employee_name: str, project: str, entry_date: str, hours: float, description: str = "") -> dict:
    """Log a time entry. entry_date must be YYYY-MM-DD."""
    return db.log_time(employee_name, project, entry_date, hours, description)


@mcp.tool
def get_timesheet(employee_name: str, start_date: str = "", end_date: str = "") -> list[dict]:
    """Get one employee's logged entries, optionally filtered to a date range (YYYY-MM-DD)."""
    return db.get_timesheet(employee_name, start_date or None, end_date or None)


@mcp.tool
def get_project_summary(project: str) -> dict:
    """Get total hours logged against a project, broken down by employee."""
    return db.get_project_summary(project)


@mcp.tool
def list_projects() -> list[str]:
    """List every project that has at least one logged time entry."""
    return db.list_projects()


@mcp.resource("timesheet://projects")
def known_projects() -> list[str]:
    """The current set of projects with logged time."""
    return db.list_projects()


@mcp.prompt
def generate_weekly_report(employee_name: str, week_start: str) -> str:
    """Guides the AI to build a structured weekly hours report."""
    return f"""Build a weekly report for {employee_name}, starting {week_start}.

1. Call get_timesheet with employee_name='{employee_name}', start_date='{week_start}'
2. Group the results by project
3. Present it as a clean report with a total

If no entries are found for that week, say so plainly instead of inventing data.
"""


# ============================================================
# NEW: a tool that generates a natural-language summary by
# calling an LLM provider directly. (MCP client-side "sampling"
# -- where the server borrows the CONNECTED CLIENT's LLM via
# ctx.sample() -- was deprecated in the MCP spec (SEP-2577) and
# FastMCP 4.x removed Context.sample() entirely. Tools now talk
# to a provider themselves instead of routing through the client.)
# ============================================================

@mcp.tool
async def summarize_week(employee_name: str, week_start: str) -> str:
    """Summarize one employee's week in plain language, using an LLM."""
    # Step 1: get the real data, same as any other tool would
    entries = db.get_timesheet(employee_name, start_date=week_start)
    if not entries:
        return f"No entries found for {employee_name} starting {week_start}."

    # Step 2: turn the raw rows into readable lines for the prompt
    entries_text = "\n".join(
        f"- {e['project']}: {e['hours']}h ({e['description']})" for e in entries
    )

    # Step 3: call the LLM provider directly to generate the text.
    response = anthropic_client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5",
        max_tokens=256,
        messages=[{
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"Summarize this week's work for {employee_name} in two friendly sentences:\n\n{entries_text}",
        }],
    )
    text = "".join(block.text for block in response.content if block.type == "text")
    return text or "Could not generate a summary."


# ============================================================
# NEW: a tool that uses ELICITATION -- the server pauses and
# asks the human, through the client, before doing something
# that looks unusual.
# ============================================================

@mcp.tool
async def log_time_with_confirmation(
    employee_name: str, project: str, entry_date: str, hours: float, description: str, ctx: Context
) -> dict:
    """Log time, but pause to confirm first if the hours look unusually high."""
    # Only ask when something actually looks worth double-checking --
    # this is a deliberate choice, not every tool call should interrupt
    if hours > 10:
        # This PAUSES the tool and waits for a real answer from whoever
        # is on the other end of the connection.
        result = await ctx.elicit(
            f"{hours} hours in one day is unusually high -- log it anyway?",
            response_type=bool,
        )
        if result.action != "accept" or not result.data:
            # The user said no (or didn't answer) -- stop here, log nothing
            return {"status": "cancelled", "reason": "not confirmed by user"}
    return db.log_time(employee_name, project, entry_date, hours, description)


# ============================================================
# NEW: one deliberately slow tool, used ONLY to demonstrate
# timeouts, cancellation, and progress notifications for real.
# ============================================================

@mcp.tool
async def slow_tool(ctx: Context) -> str:
    """Takes about 5 seconds on purpose, reporting progress the whole way -- for demoing timeouts and progress."""
    import asyncio
    total_steps = 5
    for step in range(1, total_steps + 1):
        await asyncio.sleep(1)
        await ctx.report_progress(progress=step, total=total_steps, message=f"Step {step} of {total_steps}")
    return "Finished all 5 steps."


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

Client 01: the raw, official-SDK client

The most explicit way: you build the stdio connection, wrap a session around the two streams, run the handshake, list tools and call one, all by hand. The file warns that stdio_client() hangs forever on macOS (SDK issue #1452). I ran it on Linux and it worked: it printed the handshake line, the seven tool names and the list_projects result. Note that it starts the server with the command python3, so run it in the environment where fastmcp is installed (I put my virtual environment first on PATH).

"""
01 -- THE RAW CLIENT
=====================
The most explicit, most verbose way to talk to an MCP server. Nothing
here is hidden -- every step the protocol actually needs is written out
by hand, so you can see exactly what happens.

!! KNOWN BUG, PLEASE READ BEFORE RUNNING !!
There is a real, currently open bug where the line `stdio_client(...)`
below hangs FOREVER on macOS specifically (official SDK issue #1452).
If this script just sits there and never prints anything, that is why --
it is not a mistake in this code. Skip straight to 02, which does the
exact same thing safely.

SETUP:
    pip install mcp

RUN:
    python3 01_raw_client.py
"""
import asyncio
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

# This describes HOW to start the server -- it does not start it yet.
server_params = StdioServerParameters(
    command="python3",
    args=["../main.py"],
)


async def main():
    # STEP 1: open the connection.
    async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read_stream, write_stream):
        # STEP 2: wrap a "session" around those two raw streams.
        async with ClientSession(read_stream, write_stream) as session:
            # STEP 3: the handshake.
            await session.initialize()
            print("Connected! Handshake complete.")

            # STEP 4: ask what tools exist.
            tools_response = await session.list_tools()
            tool_names = [t.name for t in tools_response.tools]
            print("Tools this server offers:", tool_names)

            # STEP 5: call one of them for real.
            result = await session.call_tool("list_projects", arguments={})
            print("Result of calling list_projects:", result)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Client 05: summarize_week, where the server calls the model itself

Despite its file name this is not a sampling demo any more: sampling was removed (Chapter 17), so the server's summarize_week tool calls the Anthropic API directly and the client is an ordinary tool call. The one lesson worth keeping is the environment variable: the default stdio transport forwards only a minimal safe set of variables to the server subprocess, so Client("../main.py") would start the server without your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. The file builds a PythonStdioTransport and passes the key by hand. (I checked its syntax only; running it needs a real key.)

"""
05 -- SUMMARIZE_WEEK: THE SERVER CALLS AN LLM DIRECTLY
=======================================================
main.py's "summarize_week" tool calls the Anthropic API itself to turn
raw timesheet rows into a friendly two-sentence summary, then returns
plain text like any other tool.

A NOTE WORTH KNOWING: MCP used to support "sampling" -- a server tool
could call ctx.sample(...) to PAUSE and ask the CONNECTED CLIENT to run
the LLM call on its behalf (the client would supply a sampling_handler
to answer it). That pattern is now deprecated in the MCP spec
(SEP-2577), and FastMCP 4.x removed Context.sample() entirely -- there
is no back-channel for it anymore. Tools are expected to call an LLM
provider directly, which is what summarize_week does now. This client
file is just a normal tool call; no sampling_handler needed.

SETUP:
    pip install fastmcp anthropic
    export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-key-here   # needed by the SERVER now, not the client

RUN:
    python3 05_sampling_demo.py

A NOTE ON THE ENV VAR: the server runs as a stdio subprocess, and FastMCP's
default stdio transport only forwards a minimal safe set of environment
variables to it (PATH, HOME, etc.) -- NOT your whole shell environment. So
we build an explicit PythonStdioTransport here and pass ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
through by hand; just running Client("../main.py") would spawn the server
without the key and it would fail to authenticate with Anthropic.
"""
import asyncio
import os
from fastmcp import Client
from fastmcp.client.transports import PythonStdioTransport

transport = PythonStdioTransport(
    "../main.py",
    env={"ANTHROPIC_API_KEY": os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", "")},
)


async def main():
    async with Client(transport) as client:
        result = await client.call_tool(
            "summarize_week",
            {"employee_name": "Asha Patel", "week_start": "2026-09-08"},
        )
        print("Summary, written by the server's own LLM call:")
        print(result)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Client 02: the same five steps, built up gradually

client/02_fastmcp_client_explained.py

"""
02 -- THE EASY CLIENT, EXPLAINED STEP BY STEP
================================================
Before jumping into the one-line pattern you'll see everywhere in this
course -- "async with Client(...) as client:" -- let's break down
exactly what a client needs to do, in plain English, one step at a time.

WHAT A CLIENT ACTUALLY NEEDS TO DO (five steps, nothing more):
  1. START the server (or connect to one already running)
  2. SAY HELLO -- the handshake from the Lifecycle video
  3. ASK what tools exist
  4. USE one of them
  5. SAY GOODBYE -- close the connection cleanly, even if something broke

That's the whole job. Everything below is just two different ways of
writing those same five steps.

WHY DOES THE CODE LOOK LIKE "async with Client(...) as client:"?
--------------------------------------------------------------------
You could write this the "manual" way, spelling out every step:

    client = Client("../main.py")
    await client.__aenter__()          # steps 1 + 2: start + handshake
    try:
        ... use the client here ...     # steps 3 + 4
    finally:
        await client.__aexit__(None, None, None)   # step 5 -- ALWAYS runs

That works. But it's easy to get wrong -- forget that "finally" block,
and a script that crashes halfway through leaves the server subprocess
running in the background forever, with nobody around to close it.

Python's "async with" does exactly that manual version FOR you,
automatically, and it GUARANTEES step 5 happens no matter what:

    async with Client("../main.py") as client:
        ... use the client here ...
    # step 5 already happened here automatically, even if something above failed

So "async with" isn't a new concept to learn -- it's just "always clean
up properly," written in one line instead of five. Both versions below
do the identical five steps. Run this file and watch them do the same
thing, two different ways.
"""
import asyncio
from fastmcp import Client


async def the_manual_way():
    """Not how you'll normally write this -- shown once, so 'async with' stops looking like magic."""
    print("--- THE MANUAL WAY (for understanding only) ---")
    client = Client("../main.py")

    await client.__aenter__()  # steps 1 + 2: start the server, do the handshake
    try:
        tools = await client.list_tools()  # step 3: ask what's available
        print("Tools:", [t.name for t in tools])

        result = await client.call_tool("list_projects", {})  # step 4: use one
        print("Result:", result)
    finally:
        await client.__aexit__(None, None, None)  # step 5: ALWAYS runs, even on error
        print("Cleaned up properly -- even without 'async with'.")


async def the_real_way():
    """This is what you'll actually write, every time, from here on in this course."""
    print("\n--- THE REAL WAY (what every later file actually uses) ---")
    async with Client("../main.py") as client:  # steps 1, 2, AND 5 (cleanup), handled for you
        tools = await client.list_tools()  # step 3
        print("Tools:", [t.name for t in tools])

        result = await client.call_tool("list_projects", {})  # step 4
        print("Result:", result)
    # step 5 (cleanup) already happened here, automatically, the instant the block ended


async def main():
    await the_manual_way()
    await the_real_way()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Client 03: the same client pointed at a deployed server

client/03_fastmcp_client_http.py

"""
03 -- CONNECTING TO A REAL, DEPLOYED SERVER OVER HTTP
========================================================
Every file so far launched main.py as a LOCAL subprocess over stdio.
This file connects to the EXACT SAME TimeTrack server -- except this one
is already running, permanently, on the actual internet. It was deployed
earlier in this course and is live right now at the URL below.

THE ONLY THING THAT CHANGES: you pass a URL instead of a file path.
FastMCP detects the difference automatically and switches from stdio to
Streamable HTTP -- same tools, same behavior, completely different road,
exactly like the Transport Layer video explained.

No local server to start. No subprocess. Just a URL, reachable from
anywhere, by anyone -- not just you.

SETUP:
    pip install fastmcp

RUN:
    python3 03_fastmcp_client_http.py
"""
import asyncio
from fastmcp import Client

# This exact URL is live -- verified directly before this file was
# written by calling it for real:
#   list_projects()        -> ["Client Onboarding", "Internal Tools", "Website Redesign"]
#   get_project_summary("Website Redesign")
#                           -> total_hours: 19.0, Asha Patel: 13.5, Rahul Mehta: 5.5
SERVER_URL = "https://time-track-mcp-server.vercel.app/mcp"


async def main():
    # Same five steps as every previous file -- start, handshake, ask,
    # use, clean up. The ONLY difference from 02's "the_real_way()" is
    # what's inside Client(...): a URL instead of "../main.py".
    async with Client(SERVER_URL) as client:
        print(f"Connected to {SERVER_URL}")
        print("(over the real internet -- no subprocess was started)")

        tools = await client.list_tools()
        print("\nTools this remote server offers:", [t.name for t in tools])

        projects = await client.call_tool("list_projects", {})
        print("\nProjects, straight from the live deployment:", projects)

        summary = await client.call_tool("get_project_summary", {"project": "Website Redesign"})
        print("Live project summary:", summary)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Client 04: a real agent loop with no framework

Read this one slowly. It is the whole agent idea in about 60 lines: ask the model, check stop_reason, run the tool yourself through MCP, append the result, repeat. The model never runs anything.

client/04_agent_loop.py

"""
04 -- A REAL AGENT LOOP, NO FRAMEWORK
=======================================
This is what "an AI agent using MCP" actually is, underneath every
framework that promises to do it for you. No LangChain, nothing hidden --
just: ask the LLM, check if it wants a tool, call it for real through
MCP, hand the result back, repeat.

SETUP:
    pip install fastmcp anthropic
    export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-key-here

RUN:
    python3 04_agent_loop.py
"""
import asyncio
import os
from fastmcp import Client
from anthropic import Anthropic


def mcp_tools_to_anthropic_format(mcp_tools) -> list[dict]:
    """
    MCP describes a tool one way. Anthropic's API wants it described a
    slightly different way. This is the ONLY translation a framework-free
    agent loop actually needs to do by hand.
    """
    return [
        {
            "name": tool.name,
            "description": tool.description or "",
            "input_schema": tool.inputSchema,
        }
        for tool in mcp_tools
    ]


async def run_one_tool_call(mcp_client: Client, block) -> dict:
    """Actually calls one tool through MCP, and packages the result the
    way Anthropic's API expects it to come back."""
    print(f"  -> calling {block.name} with {block.input}")
    result = await mcp_client.call_tool(block.name, block.input)
    return {
        "type": "tool_result",
        "tool_use_id": block.id,
        "content": str(result),
    }


async def run_agent_loop(user_message: str):
    anthropic_client = Anthropic(api_key=os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"])

    async with Client("../main.py") as mcp_client:
        mcp_tools = await mcp_client.list_tools()
        anthropic_tools = mcp_tools_to_anthropic_format(mcp_tools)

        # This list is the entire "memory" of the conversation. Every
        # question, every tool result, gets appended here and sent back
        # on the NEXT request -- the LLM itself remembers nothing between
        # calls; this list is doing all the remembering.
        messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_message}]

        while True:
            response = anthropic_client.messages.create(
                model="claude-sonnet-4-5",
                max_tokens=1024,
                tools=anthropic_tools,
                messages=messages,
            )

            if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
                final_text = "".join(
                    block.text for block in response.content if block.type == "text"
                )
                print("\nFinal answer:", final_text)
                return

            messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

            tool_results = [
                await run_one_tool_call(mcp_client, block)
                for block in response.content
                if block.type == "tool_use"
            ]

            messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(run_agent_loop(
        "Hi."
    ))

Run it yourself: scopes and roles (auth)

The warm-up folder also has server_with_auth.py, which uses a development-only StaticTokenVerifier with three fixed tokens (user-token, analyst-token, admin-token) and per-tool require_scopes(...). Here is the complete file.

server_with_auth.py

from fastmcp import FastMCP
from fastmcp.server.auth import require_scopes
from fastmcp.server.auth.providers.jwt import StaticTokenVerifier
from fastmcp.server.dependencies import get_access_token


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# AUTHENTICATION
# ---------------------------------------------------------

# DEVELOPMENT ONLY
#
# Each token represents a different user/role.
#
# user-token    -> user role
# analyst-token -> analyst role
# admin-token   -> admin role

auth = StaticTokenVerifier(
    tokens={
        "user-token": {
            "client_id": "normal-user",
            "scopes": ["user"],
        },

        "analyst-token": {
            "client_id": "data-analyst",
            "scopes": ["user", "analyst"],
        },

        "admin-token": {
            "client_id": "administrator",
            "scopes": ["user", "analyst", "admin"],
        },
    }
)


mcp = FastMCP(
    "Warm-Up Server",
    auth=auth
)


# =========================================================
# USER TOOLS
# =========================================================

@mcp.tool(auth=require_scopes("user"))
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    """
    Greet someone by name.

    Role:
        user
        analyst
        admin
    """

    return f"Hello, {name}! Welcome to MCP."


@mcp.tool(auth=require_scopes("user"))
def add_numbers(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    """
    Add two numbers.

    Role:
        user
        analyst
        admin
    """

    return a + b


# =========================================================
# ANALYST TOOLS
# =========================================================

@mcp.tool(auth=require_scopes("analyst"))
def query_db(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> int:
    """
    Query database example.

    Role:
        analyst
        admin
    """

    return a + b + c


@mcp.tool(auth=require_scopes("analyst"))
def calculate_average(numbers: list[float]) -> float:
    """
    Calculate average of numbers.

    Role:
        analyst
        admin
    """

    if not numbers:
        return 0

    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)


@mcp.tool(auth=require_scopes("analyst"))
def sales_report(month: str) -> dict:
    """
    Return a mock sales report.

    Role:
        analyst
        admin
    """

    return {
        "month": month,
        "revenue": 125000,
        "orders": 430,
        "customers": 310,
    }


# =========================================================
# ADMIN TOOLS
# =========================================================

@mcp.tool(auth=require_scopes("admin"))
def list_users() -> list[dict]:
    """
    List users.

    Role:
        admin only
    """

    return [
        {
            "id": 1,
            "name": "Mayank",
            "role": "admin",
        },
        {
            "id": 2,
            "name": "Alice",
            "role": "analyst",
        },
        {
            "id": 3,
            "name": "Bob",
            "role": "user",
        },
    ]


@mcp.tool(auth=require_scopes("admin"))
def delete_user(user_id: int) -> str:
    """
    Delete a user.

    Role:
        admin only
    """

    return f"User {user_id} deleted successfully."


# =========================================================
# OPTIONAL TOOL - SEE CURRENT AUTH USER
# =========================================================

@mcp.tool(auth=require_scopes("user"))
def who_am_i() -> dict:
    """
    Show information about the authenticated client.
    """

    token = get_access_token()

    return {
        "client_id": token.client_id,
        "scopes": token.scopes,
    }


# ---------------------------------------------------------
# RUN SERVER
# ---------------------------------------------------------

if __name__ == "__main__":


    mcp.run(
        transport="http",
        host="127.0.0.1",
        port=8000,
    )

Start it with python server_with_auth.py, then run this checker. It is my own example, and I ran it against the server above.

check_auth.py

"""Start server_with_auth.py first:  python server_with_auth.py
Then run this file. Each token carries different scopes."""
import asyncio
from fastmcp import Client

URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp"


async def try_role(token: str):
    async with Client(URL, auth=token) as client:
        names = [t.name for t in await client.list_tools()]
        print(f"{token:14} sees:", names)
        print(f"{'':14} who_am_i:", (await client.call_tool("who_am_i", {})).data)
        try:
            await client.call_tool("delete_user", {"user_id": 3})
            print(f"{'':14} delete_user: ALLOWED")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"{'':14} delete_user: refused ({type(e).__name__})")


async def main():
    for token in ("user-token", "analyst-token", "admin-token"):
        await try_role(token)


asyncio.run(main())

What it shows (verified): the user-token sees only greet, add_numbers and who_am_i; the analyst adds the three analyst tools; the admin also sees list_users and delete_user. A scope does not only block a call, it hides the tool from tools/list, so the model never even learns that a forbidden tool exists. delete_user was refused for user and analyst and allowed for admin.

Common trapStatic tokens are for demos only

Fixed strings in source code are not authentication you can ship. In production you verify real signed tokens (JWT or OAuth) from an identity provider, and you keep scopes narrow, as in the production section above.

Spot the bug: deployment mistakes

Each pair is a mistake from this chapter and the fix. Cover the right side and try to find the problem first.

1. Doubled path

# BROKEN: the URL becomes /mcp/mcp and clients get 404
mcp_app = mcp.http_app(path="/mcp")
app = FastAPI(lifespan=mcp_app.lifespan)
app.mount("/mcp", mcp_app)

# FIXED: the mount supplies /mcp, so the inner app lives at "/"
mcp_app = mcp.http_app(path="/")
app = FastAPI(lifespan=mcp_app.lifespan)
app.mount("/mcp", mcp_app)

2. Lifespan attached too late

# BROKEN: the MCP app's startup never runs, so sessions fail on the first request
app = FastAPI()
app.router.lifespan_context = mcp_app.lifespan   # set after construction

# FIXED: pass it when you construct the app
app = FastAPI(lifespan=mcp_app.lifespan)

3. Treating the model as the one that runs tools

# BROKEN: the response is only a REQUEST to call a tool; nothing has run
response = client.messages.create(model=..., tools=tools, messages=messages)
print(response.content)          # tool_use block, no result

# FIXED: run it through MCP, send the result back, loop until stop_reason != "tool_use"
if response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    result = await mcp_client.call_tool(block.name, block.input)
    messages.append({"role": "user",
                     "content": [{"type": "tool_result",
                                  "tool_use_id": block.id,
                                  "content": str(result)}]})

Hands-on lab

  1. Run the same main.py with fastmcp run and then uvicorn and note what each starts.
  2. Make the database path an environment variable and confirm writes work.
  3. Deploy to Horizon with a clean repo and entry point main.py:mcp.
  4. Connect Claude Desktop to your URL and log an entry through chat.
  5. Build the client loop (list tools, send with tools, check stop_reason, call the tool, append the result).
  6. Run 03_fastmcp_client_http.py against the public server.
  7. Do the homework: async calls and a hosted database.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

To go live I put only the server files in a clean repo, deploy to a platform like Horizon with entry point main.py:mcp, and read the database path from an environment variable, because the server's database is a separate file from my local one. A client is just the agentic loop: it lists the server's tools, gives them to the model, runs whichever tool the model asks for, appends the result and loops. The model never calls the tool.

Basics

Why do shared MCP servers run over HTTP?

A STDIO server is only usable by whatever launched it. HTTP is reachable by many clients from anywhere, at the cost of a network round trip.

fastmcp run vs uvicorn main:app?

fastmcp run starts only the MCP server over STDIO. uvicorn main:app starts the whole app (website, API and mounted MCP endpoint).

What does a hosting platform need from your repo?

main.py, database.py, pyproject.toml and uv.lock: the code plus the dependency list and exact pinned versions.

Does MCP need an API underneath?

No. A calculator with a plain add function is a valid MCP server.

Intermediate

Why is your local database unaffected by the deployed one?

They are separate files and separate data. A .gitignored local database never ships, and the server creates its own.

Why must the client, not the model, call the tool?

The model only emits which tool and arguments. The client holds the connection to the server, so it executes call_tool and feeds the result back. MCP standardises how that travels; it does not change who does it.

What is harness engineering?

Building the layer that connects a raw model to tools: the loop, tool formatting, execution and message handling. Every chat application is one.

How do you let several databases sit behind one MCP entry point?

Either one custom server wiring them all, or an MCP gateway that aggregates existing servers behind one endpoint.

Tricky

How do you stop an agent from writing to a production database?

Register only read tools at startup when a flag such as READ_ONLY=true is set, so write tools are never offered.

Is a Postgres MCP server running on my laptop local or remote?

Local: the server process runs on your machine. The data it queries may be remote.

Why might a deployed server lose data?

SQLite on a serverless host can lose its file when the function goes cold, and it is a local file rather than a shared database. Use a hosted database.

What are the two honest gaps in this project?

A local SQLite file instead of a hosted production database, and synchronous database calls so two requests cannot run at the same time.

Plain tool or MCP?

A plain tool for a narrow fixed action. MCP for breadth where you would otherwise hand-build and maintain many tools.

Production level

How do you run an MCP server with several replicas when sessions are stateful?

Prefer running stateless (stateless_http=True) so any replica serves any request. Otherwise use sticky routing on Mcp-Session-Id at the ingress (not sessionAffinity: ClientIP), or a shared session store such as Redis. Test with two or more replicas and a multi-turn conversation.

How do you make a money-moving tool safe across retries and crashes?

An idempotency key as a tool argument, stored in the same database transaction as the transfer so a repeat returns the stored result, and balances re-checked at execution time rather than at approval.

How do you scope OAuth for sensitive tools?

One tool, one scope (payments:read differs from payments:transfer). Check the scope on every call, filter tools/list by scope, return 403 insufficient_scope and trigger step-up plus human approval. Tokens are short-lived and audience-bound to one server; downstream APIs get a token exchange, never passthrough.

A server changes a tool's parameters. How do you avoid breaking agents?

Only additive changes in place; breaking changes ship as a new tool name alongside the old. Restart agents or handle tools/list_changed, run the eval suite because descriptions change routing, and diff tools/list snapshots in CI.

Quick revision

Practice project: Your own MCP server

Goal: wrap a small API or database as an MCP server and put it on a public URL.

  • FastMCP with at least one tool, one resource and one prompt. Test in Inspector.
  • Mount it in FastAPI (path="/", lifespan at construction), keep the database path in an environment variable, deploy a clean repo to Horizon.
  • Stretch: compare FastMCP.from_fastapi with hand-written tools, and make database calls async.
  • Interview story: auto-convert versus manual, and the deployment bug you hit.

Part D MCP · Chapter 17

Legacy vs modern MCP

What changed between the legacy session-based MCP this course taught and the stateless spec finalised on 28 July 2026, why, and how real client features (sampling, elicitation, ping, timeouts) behave now.

Class 2220 September45 min readCode: Complete MCP, mcp-client-and-advanced
Jump to a section

Why it matters

The first thing to know: everything built in this course still runs, unchanged, today. Nothing was wasted. But "legacy vs modern MCP" is the question that separates people who learned a tutorial from people who can reason about the protocol. It also explains real errors you will hit on a fresh install.

Key ideaThe one idea behind every change

Legacy remembers you. Modern makes every message carry everything about itself. Everything that follows is a consequence of that single idea, not a list of arbitrary new rules.

Core ideas

1. The real timeline

Adoption of the modern spec is opt-in. Nothing forced existing servers to change on that date. There is no blanket migration deadline, only a handful of named features carrying their own twelve-month clock. Real ecosystems move slowly (rewriting a working system is real engineering), so most servers, local or hosted, still run the legacy architecture and will for a while.

2. "Remember me" vs "tell me every time"

AnalogyTwo co-working buildings

In one building the same receptionist greets you each morning and waves you through because she recognises your face. That is the legacy Mcp-Session-Id. In the other, everyone taps an ID badge at every door (entrance, lift, meeting room), because nobody is keeping track of who is who. Slightly more tapping, but any door can let you through, on any day, whoever is working it.

A live demo made the legacy side concrete: start a server with uv run uvicorn main:app, send a raw curl initialize from a second terminal, and the response returns the Mcp-Session-Id the server uses to remember that client. (The curl commands are in Chapter 15.)

Why give that up? A system that must remember a specific person can only be handled by whoever met them first. A system that reads a badge each time can be handled by any server, so a busy application can open more servers behind the scenes without any of them having "met" the client. Stateless, self-contained requests make horizontal scaling easy.

AnalogySupport call vs support ticket

A call connects you to one agent who remembers the conversation, but if the call drops, you start over with someone who knows nothing. A ticket has everything written in it, so any agent can pick it up. Modern MCP has no session id. The full context travels with every request. Slightly more data per call, but freedom to scale without anyone remembering a client.

3. How a server asks a question mid-task now

If nothing is remembered, how does a server ever ask a clarifying question?

AnalogyThe restaurant kitchen rule

A kitchen can send a waiter back to ask "how spicy?" while your order is already being cooked. It cannot walk up to an empty table and start asking cooking questions before anyone has ordered.

Rule In plain words
Already cooking A server can only ask a question while actively handling something the client already requested
Real question The reply must contain an actual question, never a vague "something is needed"

Example: a TimeTrack tool asked to log 14 hours in a day comes back with "that seems unusually high, log it anyway?" It pauses mid-task and does not appear unprompted.

Confirming and continuing: the OTP pattern. At checkout the app asks for a code sent to your phone. You are not stuck waiting. You fetch the code, return, and submit it with your order reference. The order can complete on a different backend server, because the ticket carries everything needed. The assistant that asked is free to do something else meanwhile, and whoever is free when the answer arrives can pick it up.

4. The small stuff that helps

Change What it does Analogy
Faster routing Every request carries Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name labels in its HTTP headers, so a load balancer can route by glancing at two labels A coloured tag on a boarding pass
Smarter caching A server can set ttlMs (how long an answer stays fresh, in milliseconds) and cacheScope (safe to share across users, or private to one) A weather app caching a forecast for an hour
Finding what broke Built on the W3C tracing standard, a request carries a tracking context across every hop, so a failure three services deep is traceable One tracking number following a package across carriers

5. Gone vs going away

MCP's own policy gives anything deprecated a minimum of twelve months from its announcement (started July 2026) before removal is even eligible. That is a floor, not a countdown to breakage.

Common trapThe twelve months is the spec's promise, not every library's

A specific SDK's maintainers can drop a deprecated feature's code sooner. That is what happened with sampling in a recent FastMCP release. Spec timeline and library behaviour are two different things.

Building a client against the current library

6. The five steps every client performs

Two ways to write it in Python: a manual try/finally, or async with client as client. They are the same five steps. async with does the manual version automatically and guarantees step 5 happens no matter what. It is not a new concept; it writes "always clean up properly" in one line instead of five.

7. Why the demos broke: the root cause

The repo's MCP_PROTOCOL_CHANGES_SUMMARY.txt explains it. The installed fastmcp 4.0.5 negotiates protocol revision 2026-07-28 by default. The older demos were written for the session-based protocol, where one persistent connection let both sides send requests at any time. That back-channel let a server tool pause and ask the client to call an LLM, ask the human a question or answer a ping. The new revision is stateless: every request is a single self-contained exchange with no persistent back-channel. Every "server asks, client answers, mid-tool-call" feature breaks:

Feature On the modern connection
ctx.sample() AttributeError: the method was deleted
ctx.elicit() "unavailable on 2026-07-28 connections"
client.ping() "Method not found"

Two kinds of fix were needed because the features are in different states.

Class A: fully deleted, no flag brings it back. Sampling. FastMCP 4.x removed Context.sample() entirely. (The repo confirmed it by installing fastmcp 2.14.7 in a scratch environment, where it still exists.)

Class B: exists, but needs the classic handshake. Elicitation and ping. Pass mode="legacy" when constructing the Client to force the classic initialize handshake and restore the back-channel.

8. Sampling: genuinely removed

Sampling lets a server borrow the client's connected model instead of holding its own API key.

The fix in summarize_week: stop taking a ctx, call the provider directly with the server's own key.

# before: asked the connected client's model
# text = await ctx.sample(prompt_text)

# after: the server talks to the provider itself
anthropic_client = Anthropic(api_key=os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", ""))
response = anthropic_client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-5", ...)

This is also the migration path the spec recommends ("servers call a provider directly"), not a downgrade. Practical effect: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY must now be available to the server process. The stdio subprocess needs it passed explicitly, so the demo builds a PythonStdioTransport("../main.py", env={...}) rather than the string-inferred Client("../main.py"), because of stdio subprocess environment isolation.

9. Elicitation: still there, behind mode="legacy"

client = Client(
    "main.py",
    elicitation_handler=elicitation_handler,
    mode="legacy",        # restores the classic handshake the course taught
)

async def elicitation_handler(message, response_type, params, context):
    print(f"Server is asking: {message}")
    confirm = input("Type Y to confirm, anything else to cancel: ")
    return confirm.strip().lower() == "y"

Run twice: logging 4 hours triggered no question (under the tool's 10-hour threshold). Logging 14 hours triggered "14 hours in one day is unusually high, log it anyway?" and branched on the typed reply: Y completed the log, anything else returned "cancelled, not confirmed by user."

NoteThe modern replacement exists

The repo notes elicitation has a modern native replacement: a tool returns an InputRequiredResult and is re-invoked later with the human's answer (a guard-and-return pattern for stateless connections). The class chose mode="legacy" because the native pattern needs the tool restructured as a re-entrant, resumable function, a much bigger rewrite.

10. Ping, timeout, cancellation and progress

  • Ping is the simplest check: "are you still there?" It is removed in the strictest modern sense (nothing persistent to ping), but client.ping() works in legacy mode and returned True.
  • Timeout and cancellation. A deliberately slow tool (sleeping 5 seconds) with a client timeout of 1 second was cancelled with a clear "tool call timeout" error instead of hanging. Raising the timeout above the tool's delay let it succeed.
  • Rule: every request should have a timeout. A cancellation notification stops waiting, and a progress notification can reset that clock if the server is genuinely still working.

11. How this connects to LangChain

When LangChain is the host, its agent is the host, and LangChain creates the MCP client itself using the LangChain MCP Adapters package, which is built on FastMCP underneath. MultiServerMCPClient with a config dictionary still goes through the same initialisation and tool discovery.

Any MCP server, whichever library wrote it, rests on the same official protocol. FastMCP and the adapters are abstractions that make the code easier; everything executes down to the same base. For an agent framework, MCP is just a connection to a set of tools, nothing more exotic than tools covered many classes ago, sourced from a standard protocol. LangChain's MCP support is for consuming existing servers as tool sources, not building new ones. That is FastMCP's job. Chapter 18 shows it in code.

12. What the 2026-07-28 spec changes in practice

From the course's MCP interview questions:

  • No initialize handshake. The protocol version and capabilities travel in _meta on every request.
  • No sessions. Mcp-Session-Id is gone, so any replica serves any request and you need no sticky routing.
  • State moves into tools. Cross-call state becomes a handle the tool returns (for example a basket_id) that the client passes back.
  • Most production servers still run 2025-11-25, where sessions are optional but stateful by default.
Deprecated What replaces it
Roots Pass paths as tool parameters
Sampling Call the LLM provider's API directly
Logging OpenTelemetry or stderr
HTTP plus SSE transport Streamable HTTP
Dynamic Client Registration Client ID Metadata Documents

Client-side settings live on the client. In the repo's demos, timeout and progress_handler are set when you create the client, not per call:

async with Client("../main.py", timeout=1.0) as client:          # times out a ~5-second tool
    ...

async def on_progress(progress: float, total: float | None, message: str | None):
    print(f"{progress}/{total}: {message}")

async with Client("../main.py", progress_handler=on_progress) as client:
    await client.call_tool("slow_tool", {})

On the server, a tool reports progress with await ctx.report_progress(progress=step, total=total_steps, message=...).

Key pointers to remember

  • Nothing you built breaks. Modern MCP is opt-in.
  • Legacy remembers you via a session; modern makes every message self-contained.
  • A server can only ask a question while handling a request you sent.
  • Sampling is gone in current FastMCP. Call a provider directly.
  • Elicitation and ping need mode="legacy", or the new InputRequiredResult pattern for elicitation.
  • Every request should have a timeout.
  • Deprecated means twelve months minimum before removal is eligible. Libraries may drop code sooner.
  • LangChain's adapters build the client on FastMCP.

Questions from class worth knowing

Should I worry about mastering every previous MCP version?

No. Modern adoption will take time, and understanding legacy deeply is what makes the modern one make sense.

Is sampling controlled by my code or called automatically?

By the tool's own code. If its logic needs a completion, it calls the provider (now directly). The framework does not trigger it automatically.

Are sampling and elicitation MCP concepts or framework features?

Both are part of the MCP specification. A framework like FastMCP provides the implementation.

Does LangChain's MCP support let me create servers?

No. It only consumes existing servers as a tool source for an agent. Creating servers is for libraries like FastMCP.

Does LangChain-as-host still do the handshake?

Yes. The adapter builds the harness and client for you, but the same handshake and discovery happen underneath.

Will an OpenRouter key work for the client exercises?

Yes, with a small change to point at the right endpoint and model string. The pattern does not change.

Try it: remember me, or tell me every time

From the instructor's "What is actually changing" site (read 30 Oct 2026). Its timeline and the removed-versus-deprecated points are already in the sections above; this adds the toggle and the OTP walk-through.

Interactive demo (needs JavaScript): switch between the legacy and modern models and play the confirm-and-continue sequence.

The site adds one more way to tell the two fixes apart. If Python says the method does not exist at all (an AttributeError), it is Class A, genuinely gone (sampling): rewrite the tool. If the method exists but complains about the connection type when called, it is Class B, still there but asleep (elicitation and ping): ask for the old connection with mode="legacy". Its one-line mental model: the modern protocol has no back-channel, so a server can no longer interrupt a client mid-task, and everything that depended on that was either removed or sits behind the legacy counter.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Using ctx.sample() on fastmcp 4.x AttributeError Call the LLM provider directly in the tool
Using ctx.elicit() on a modern connection "unavailable on 2026-07-28 connections" mode="legacy", or the InputRequiredResult pattern
client.ping() on a modern connection "Method not found" mode="legacy"
Provider key only in the client Server cannot call the LLM Provide it to the server process (and the stdio env)
No client timeout Calls hang Set a timeout on every request
Treating deprecated as removed today Rushed rewrites Twelve-month floor; check your library
Assuming the spec timeline equals the SDK timeline Surprise breakage Read the library's changelog
Writing manual cleanup everywhere Leaked connections on errors async with client as client

Run it yourself: the four advanced clients

Complete, unmodified files from the repo. Run them from the client/ folder next to ../main.py (the server and database.py are printed in Chapter 16). I ran all four against fastmcp 4.1.4.

06: elicitation (mode="legacy" and a handler). With 4 hours no question is asked; with 14 hours the server asks "log it anyway?" and the handler answers.

client/06_elicitation_demo.py

"""
06 -- ELICITATION: THE SERVER ASKS A REAL QUESTION
=====================================================
main.py's "log_time_with_confirmation" tool calls ctx.elicit(...)
whenever hours look unusually high. That call PAUSES the tool, mid-way
through, and waits for a real answer from the client. This file
provides that answer.

A NOTE WORTH KNOWING: the newest MCP protocol revision (2026-07-28) is
stateless -- it has no back-channel at all for server-initiated requests,
so ctx.elicit() raises an error on a connection negotiated at that
version. Elicitation itself isn't gone (there's a modern "return an
InputRequiredResult and get re-invoked" pattern for it), but the simple
imperative ctx.elicit() this demo relies on only works on the classic,
session-based handshake. So we pin the client to mode="legacy" below to
force that older handshake and keep this demo working as written.

SETUP:
    pip install fastmcp

RUN:
    python3 06_elicitation_demo.py
"""
import asyncio
from fastmcp import Client


async def elicitation_handler(message: str, response_type, params, context):
    """
    Called BY the server, through the client, whenever a tool calls
    ctx.elicit(). In a real app with a UI, this is where you'd show a
    real dialog box. For this demo, we print the question and auto-confirm.
    """
    print(f"\n[The server is asking]: {message}")
    print("[Auto-confirming for this demo -- swap this for real input() or a UI in your own client]")
    return True


async def main():
    async with Client(
        "../main.py", elicitation_handler=elicitation_handler, mode="legacy"
    ) as client:
        print("--- Logging 4 hours (normal -- watch: NO question gets asked) ---")
        normal_result = await client.call_tool(
            "log_time_with_confirmation",
            {"employee_name": "Asha Patel", "project": "Website Redesign",
             "entry_date": "2026-09-12", "hours": 4.0, "description": "A normal day"},
        )
        print("Result:", normal_result)

        print("\n--- Logging 14 hours (unusual -- watch: a real question appears) ---")
        high_result = await client.call_tool(
            "log_time_with_confirmation",
            {"employee_name": "Asha Patel", "project": "Website Redesign",
             "entry_date": "2026-09-12", "hours": 14.0, "description": "Crunch day"},
        )
        print("Result:", high_result)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Verified output shape: the 4-hour call returns a new row straight away; the 14-hour call prints [The server is asking]: 14.0 hours in one day is unusually high -- log it anyway?, auto-confirms, and then logs the row.

07: ping and a real error

client/07_ping_and_errors.py

"""
07 -- PING AND A REAL ERROR
=============================
Two of the "special cases" from the Lifecycle video, now actually
happening instead of being a JSON example on a slide.

A NOTE WORTH KNOWING: `ping` is removed as of the newest MCP protocol
revision (2026-07-28) -- it only works under the classic, session-based
handshake. So, same as the elicitation demo, we pin mode="legacy" here
to keep client.ping() working as written.

RUN:
    python3 07_ping_and_errors.py
"""
import asyncio
from fastmcp import Client


async def demo_ping():
    print("--- PING: just checking the connection is alive ---")
    async with Client("../main.py", mode="legacy") as client:
        result = await client.ping()
        print("Server responded:", result)


async def demo_real_error():
    print("\n--- A REAL ERROR, TRIGGERED ON PURPOSE ---")
    async with Client("../main.py", mode="legacy") as client:
        try:
            # "Nonexistent Project" was never logged against -- this makes
            # get_project_summary's own ValueError fire for real, surfacing
            # back to us as a genuine protocol error.
            await client.call_tool("get_project_summary", {"project": "Nonexistent Project"})
        except Exception as e:
            print("Caught a real error response:", e)


async def main():
    await demo_ping()
    await demo_real_error()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Verified: ping succeeds, and the missing project comes back as an error that the client catches (No time logged against project 'Nonexistent Project'). Remember the server also prints a long traceback to its own stderr; that noise is the server's log, not your client failing.

08: timeout and cancellation

client/08_timeout_and_cancellation.py

"""
08 -- TIMEOUT, WHICH TRIGGERS A REAL CANCELLATION
====================================================
main.py's "slow_tool" deliberately takes about 5 seconds. Here, we
connect with a much shorter timeout on purpose, so it actually times
out -- and watch what that triggers.

NOTE: "timeout" is set when you CREATE the Client, not as an argument
to call_tool() itself -- verified against FastMCP's own current
documentation.

RUN:
    python3 08_timeout_and_cancellation.py
"""
import asyncio
from fastmcp import Client


async def main():
    print("--- Connecting with a 1-second timeout, calling a ~5-second tool ---")
    async with Client("../main.py", timeout=1.0) as client:
        try:
            await client.call_tool("slow_tool", {})
        except Exception as e:
            print("Timed out and was cancelled, exactly as expected:", e)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Verified: the 5-second slow_tool is cut off by the 1-second client timeout and the client reports Request 'tools/call' timed out.

09: progress notifications

client/09_progress_notifications.py

"""
09 -- PROGRESS NOTIFICATIONS, WATCHED LIVE
=============================================
main.py's "slow_tool" reports its progress as it works. Here we give the
client a progress_handler, so every update prints the moment it arrives
-- instead of the client just sitting there for 5 seconds wondering if
anything is happening.

NOTE: "progress_handler" is also set when you CREATE the Client, not
per-call -- same rule as timeout in the previous file.

RUN:
    python3 09_progress_notifications.py
"""
import asyncio
from fastmcp import Client


async def on_progress(progress: float, total: float | None, message: str | None):
    print(f"  progress update: {progress}/{total} -- {message}")


async def main():
    print("--- Calling the 5-second tool, watching progress arrive live ---")
    async with Client("../main.py", progress_handler=on_progress) as client:
        result = await client.call_tool("slow_tool", {})
        print("Final result:", result)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Verified: five updates arrive as 1.0/5.0 -- Step 1 of 5 up to 5.0/5.0, then the final result.

Spot the bug: client mistakes

1. Elicitation with no handler or legacy mode

# BROKEN: no handler, so the client has no way to answer the server's question
async with Client("../main.py") as client:
    await client.call_tool("log_time_with_confirmation", {...})

# FIXED: give the client a handler and the legacy mode the demo needs
async with Client("../main.py", elicitation_handler=handler, mode="legacy") as client:
    ...

2. Expecting sampling to still work

# BROKEN on current fastmcp: ctx.sample() was removed
summary = await ctx.sample("Summarise this week")

# FIXED: call your model provider directly from the tool
msg = anthropic_client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-4-5", max_tokens=500, messages=[...])

3. Progress handler with the wrong signature

# BROKEN: the client passes progress, total and message, so a one-argument handler does not match
async def on_progress(progress):
    print(progress)

# FIXED: match the signature the repo uses
async def on_progress(progress: float, total: float | None, message: str | None):
    print(f"{progress}/{total} -- {message}")

  2. Rewrite a tool that used sampling so it calls a provider directly.
  3. Build the elicitation demo with mode="legacy" and test both branches (under and over the threshold), confirming and cancelling separately.
  4. Set a client timeout shorter than a slow tool and trigger cancellation.
  5. Make your TimeTrack database path dynamic with an environment variable and confirm writes after deployment.
  6. Read the repo's MCP_PROTOCOL_CHANGES_SUMMARY.txt and match each error to its cause.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

Legacy MCP is session-based: you handshake once and the server remembers you through a session id. The modern spec, finalised 28 July 2026, is stateless: every request is self-contained, so any server can handle any request and you can scale horizontally. The cost is a little more data per call, and server-to-client features like sampling and elicitation lose their back-channel. Adoption is opt-in and deprecated features get at least twelve months, so existing servers keep working.

Basics

What is the central difference between legacy and modern MCP?

Legacy remembers the client with a session handshake and Mcp-Session-Id. Modern has no session: every message carries its own context, so any server can handle it.

Will my existing servers break?

No. Modern adoption is opt-in and legacy keeps working. Deprecated features have a twelve-month minimum before removal is even eligible.

What do Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name do?

They are HTTP headers on each request that let load balancers route by glancing at the method and name, instead of reading the body.

Intermediate

Why did elicitation, ping and sampling break?

They relied on the persistent two-way session. The modern revision is stateless with no back-channel, so a server cannot send an unsolicited request to the client.

How do you fix each?

Sampling was deleted: have the tool call the LLM provider directly. Elicitation and ping: create the client with mode="legacy", or for elicitation use the modern InputRequiredResult re-invocation pattern.

When can a server ask the user a question in modern MCP?

Only while handling a request the client already sent, and the reply must contain a real question. Think of the kitchen sending a waiter back, not asking an empty table.

How does a question get answered if a different server picks up the reply?

Like an OTP at checkout: the answer is submitted with a reference that carries everything needed, so any backend can complete the order.

What do ttlMs and cacheScope do?

ttlMs sets how long a server's answer stays fresh in milliseconds. cacheScope says whether it is safe to share across users or private to one.

Tricky

Why is stateless better for scale?

A stateful system can only be handled by whoever met the client first. Stateless requests can go to any server, so you can add servers behind a load balancer without anyone needing to remember a client.

Deprecated vs removed?

Removed means gone (old handshake, ping, logging/setLevel, the old session header). Deprecated still works on a timeline (Roots, Sampling, Logging, HTTP plus SSE) with a minimum twelve months.

The spec says twelve months but my SDK dropped a feature. Contradiction?

No. Twelve months is the spec's promise. A specific library's maintainers can remove the code sooner, as FastMCP did with sampling.

What does async with client as client guarantee?

That the connection is closed (step 5) no matter what, including on an error. It is the same five steps as a manual try/finally, in one line.

Where does ANTHROPIC_API_KEY need to live after the sampling change?

In the server process, because the tool now calls the provider itself. For a stdio subprocess, pass it explicitly in the transport's env, because the subprocess environment is isolated.

How does LangChain relate to FastMCP and the SDK?

LangChain MCP Adapters build the client on FastMCP, which sits on the official MCP Python SDK. LangChain only consumes servers; it does not build them.

Production level

What changed in the latest MCP spec, and how does it affect running servers?

The 2026-07-28 spec is stateless: no initialize handshake (version and capabilities travel in _meta on every request), no Mcp-Session-Id, so any replica serves any request, and cross-call state becomes a handle returned by tools. Roots, sampling, logging, HTTP plus SSE and dynamic client registration are deprecated, replaced by tool parameters, direct provider calls, OpenTelemetry or stderr, Streamable HTTP and Client ID Metadata Documents. Most production servers still run 2025-11-25.

Quick revision

Key ideaSampling is being deprecated

The Craft card for the lifecycle simulator notes that roots, sampling and logging are being deprecated in the newest spec revision (SEP-2577). That matches this chapter: ctx.sample() is removed from the current FastMCP, and the TimeTrack server calls the model provider directly instead.
