Part E Advanced · Chapter 18

MCP inside LangChain

Use MCP servers as a tool source for a LangChain agent: load tools, call them directly, handle errors, require approval for destructive tools, answer elicitations, connect several servers and authenticate.

Weekends 13 and 14Notebook-based, no class summary45 min readCode: Weekend 14
Jump to a section
Repo noteThis chapter comes from notebooks, not a class write-up

There is no written summary for these sessions. The content is built from the repo's notebooks (MCP_in_Langchain.ipynb, MCP_MultiServer_Live_Demo.ipynb, Langchain MCP.ipynb). The Weekend 13 folder has an empty README.md and a short langchain.py. The notebooks target a beta built-in module, so API names may change. Check them against your installed version.

Why it matters

Chapters 11 to 17 treated MCP on its own. In practice you will use MCP servers as a tool source for an agent. This chapter shows how LangChain consumes them, and the honest trade-offs between the new built-in module and the older adapter package. It is also where MCP meets the middleware you learned earlier: human approval, error handling and elicitation all reappear.

Key ideaFor an agent framework, MCP is just a source of tools

Nothing about the agentic loop changes. An MCP server is "a connection to a set of tools". LangChain builds the client for you (the agent is the host) and hands the tools to create_agent like any other tools. LangChain's MCP support consumes servers. Building servers is still FastMCP's job (Chapter 17).

Core ideas

1. Install and the first connection

pip install "langchain[mcp]>=1.4.0"        # the built-in module, no separate package

from pathlib import Path
from langchain.mcp import MCPAdapter
from fastmcp.client.transports import PythonStdioTransport

cinebot_transport = PythonStdioTransport(
    script_path=Path("cinebot_mcp_server.py"),
    log_file=Path("cinebot_mcp_server.log"),
)

async with MCPAdapter(cinebot_transport) as adapter:
    tools = await adapter.list_tools()
    print([t.name for t in tools])

MCPAdapter is an async context manager (so cleanup is guaranteed, as with async with client). It accepts a transport, a bare URL, a fastmcp Client, a config dictionary or a client group. list_tools() returns ordinary LangChain tools. Once you have them, they are used like any other tool.

Repo noteNotebook paths are machine-specific

One cell hard-codes an absolute path on the author's Mac (/Users/mayank/...). Replace it with a relative Path("cinebot_mcp_server.py").

2. Call a tool with no AI at all

async with MCPAdapter(cinebot_transport) as adapter:
    tools = await adapter.list_tools()
    showtime_tool = next(t for t in tools if t.name == "check_showtimes")
    direct = await showtime_tool.ainvoke({"movie_title": "interstellar"})   # no model involved

    agent = create_agent(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", tools=tools)           # or give them to an agent
    result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [("user", "What are the showtimes for Interstellar?")]})

Calling the tool directly proves the server works before you add a model. Then the same tools list goes into create_agent.

3. Tool output: content blocks and structured data

An MCP tool result is not limited to text. The adapter converts what the server sends into standard LangChain content blocks, so the model sees one shape regardless of the server.

MCP content type Becomes
TextContent text content block
ImageContent image block (base64 plus mime type)
ResourceLink (image mime type) image block (by URL)
ResourceLink (other) file block
EmbeddedResource (text) text block
EmbeddedResource (blob) image or file block, by mime type
AudioContent not yet supported: raises NotImplementedError

Two audiences for one result. The ToolMessage carries .content (what the model reads) and .artifact (data your code can use). For structured content the adapter puts it in artifact["structured_content"]:

message = await seat_map_tool.ainvoke({"name": "get_seat_map", "args": {"movie_title": "Interstellar"},
                                        "id": "unique_call_id_12345", "type": "tool_call"})
print(message.content)                                         # text the model reads
print(message.artifact["structured_content"]["available_rows"])  # structured data for your code

This is the same content and artifact split from Chapter 3, now applied to MCP results.

4. Error handling: two very different failures

Failure What happened What the agent sees
Tool ran and reported failure (isError=True) The tool executed, then explicitly failed (bad input, business rule) A ToolMessage with status="error". The agent can read it and self-correct, like any tool error
Transport or session failure The connection dropped, the server crashed, the process could not start Raises an exception. There is no error message for the model, because nothing came back to convert 
@mcp.tool()
def risky_lookup(booking_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up a booking. Fails if the ID format is wrong."""
    if not booking_id.startswith("BK"):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid booking ID format: {booking_id!r}. Expected it to start with 'BK'.")
    return f"Booking {booking_id}: confirmed."

Calling it with 12345 returns a ToolMessage with an error status the model can read. Use Chapter 8's tool error and retry middleware for the layer around it.

5. Destructive tools get human approval, automatically

Servers can mark tools with annotations such as destructive_hint. The adapter surfaces them under tool.metadata["mcp"]["tool"]["annotations"]. Build the human-in-the-loop config from that, so the server decides what is dangerous:

def is_destructive_tool_call(tool):
    meta = (tool.metadata or {}).get("mcp", {}).get("tool", {}).get("annotations", {})
    return bool(meta.get("destructive_hint"))

async with MCPAdapter(cinebot_transport) as adapter:
    tools = await adapter.list_tools()
    interrupt_on = {
        t.name: {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}
        for t in tools if is_destructive_tool_call(t)
    }
    hitl_middleware = HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on=interrupt_on)
    cinebot_guarded = create_agent(model="openai:gpt-5-mini", tools=tools, middleware=[hitl_middleware])

One HITL configuration, built dynamically from whatever the server marked destructive. On the server the tool is declared with @mcp.tool(annotations=ToolAnnotations(destructive_hint=True)), as for cancel_booking.

Common trapVerify the filter against your own server

The notebook's saved output for cancel_booking shows destructive_hint: True inside the raw metadata, yet the line printed by the helper in that same cell says Destructive: False. The notebook does not explain the mismatch (it may be stale output from an earlier version of the helper). Do not assume the filter works: print tool.metadata and the helper's result for your server and confirm the dangerous tool is actually selected. A guard that silently matches nothing is worse than none.

6. Elicitation becomes an interrupt, automatically

Some tools need clarification mid-call ("confirm you want to proceed?"). langchain.mcp answers with a LangGraph interrupt(). Every client the adapter builds is armed for it by default, with no extra code.

@mcp.tool()
async def cancel_booking_confirm(booking_id: str, ctx: Context) -> str:
    """Cancel a booking, but ask the caller to confirm first."""
    result = await ctx.elicit(f"Confirm cancellation of booking {booking_id}?", response_type=bool)
    if result.action != "accept":
        return f"Cancellation of {booking_id} aborted ({result.action})."
    if not result.data:
        return f"Cancellation of {booking_id} aborted (user said no)."
    return f"Booking {booking_id}: cancelled."

Called outside a graph, the tool returns a status you can inspect. Inside an agent, the interrupt pauses the graph and a human answers with Command(resume={"responses": {key: answer}}). It connects Chapter 13 (elicitation), Chapter 10 (interrupts and Command) and Chapter 17 (the modern protocol changes how this works on the wire).

7. Connecting several servers

Real deployments rarely use one server. Two patterns, with a real trade-off:

Pattern What it does Tool naming Protocol negotiation
MCPConfig dict One aggregate connection across several servers Prefixed by the config key you choose Shared: the whole fleet negotiates down to the oldest protocol era any member needs
ClientGroup Independent connections, one per server Namespaced {server}_{tool} automatically Independent: each member keeps its own protocol era and auth 
from fastmcp.client import Client
from fastmcp.client.group import ClientGroup

group = ClientGroup({
    "cinebot": Client(Path("cinebot_mcp_server.py")),
    "errors": Client(Path("cinebot_error_server.py"), mode="legacy"),    # an older-era server
    "time_track_server": Client("https://time-track-mcp-server.vercel.app/mcp/"),
})
async with MCPAdapter(group) as adapter:
    group_tools = await adapter.list_tools()

Because MCPConfig forces the fleet to the oldest protocol era any member needs, a mixed legacy and modern fleet is the case for ClientGroup. This is Chapter 17's legacy and modern split showing up in practice.

The live multi-server demo connects each server in its own try/except and merges whichever tool lists succeed (a local CineBot over STDIO, the free public Context7 server over HTTPS, and your own deployed Time Tracker). For a live audience, one server being down does not take out the demo: you show "what we got from the reachable servers" instead of a crashed cell, with a status line per server.

8. Authentication

Auth is configured on the FastMCP client, not on MCPAdapter, which just wraps whatever client you hand it.

Need Pattern
Bearer token Client(url, auth=token)
OAuth 2.1 (discovery, browser redirect, token exchange) Client(url, auth="oauth")
OAuth persisted across runs Client(url, auth=OAuth(mcp_url=url, token_storage=...))
Different auth per server ClientGroup with a different auth= on each member client
Per-user auth in a deployment A custom auth handler resolves the caller server-side; the graph factory mints or exchanges a token per user 
async def load_tools_with_bearer(url: str, token: str):
    async with MCPAdapter(Client(url, auth=token)) as adapter:
        return await adapter.list_tools()

The demo server checks a static bearer token with a StaticTokenVerifier. A bearer check only applies at a network boundary, so that server then serves over HTTP (port 8000), not STDIO.

Common trapNever put a real key in a notebook

A bearer token like the demo's is fine as a labelled example. But one notebook in the course repo has what looks like a real third-party API key passed as a variable name to os.environ.get(...), which means the key sits in the code. Do not copy it anywhere. Anyone who owns such a repo should rotate that key. Read secrets from environment variables, as in Chapter 1.

9. langchain.mcp vs langchain-mcp-adapters

If an integration already uses the older, separate package, here is the honest comparison, including what the new API does not do yet.

langchain-mcp-adapters (older, separate) langchain.mcp (built-in, beta)
Install pip install langchain-mcp-adapters pip install "langchain[mcp]>=1.4.0"
Entry point MultiServerMCPClient({...}).get_tools() async with MCPAdapter(target) as adapter: await adapter.list_tools()
Resources Supported Not exposed. Drop to the underlying fastmcp.Client
Prompts Supported Not exposed. Same workaround
Tool call interceptors Supported (logging, retry, Command updates) No interceptor hook in this beta. Wrap tools yourself after list_tools()
Progress callbacks Supported Not part of the public surface reviewed
Structured content Via ToolMessage content ToolMessage.artifact["structured_content"]
Error handling handle_tool_errors flag isError=True becomes status="error" automatically; transport errors raise
Tool metadata Ungrouped One tool.metadata["mcp"] namespace
Elicitation Not built in Automatic, via LangGraph interrupt()
Status Mature, stable Beta, "the API may change"
Key ideaThe honest takeaway for a client project

If you need resources, prompts or interceptor-style middleware around MCP calls today, langchain-mcp-adapters still does things langchain.mcp does not. If you are starting fresh and only need tools, the built-in path is where LangChain is clearly heading. This is not "old bad, new good". It is different surface area, and the new one is not a full superset yet.

Repo noteClass 22 describes the older package

The Class 22 write-up (Chapter 17) explains LangChain's MCP support in terms of MultiServerMCPClient and the adapters package. The newer notebooks use MCPAdapter from langchain.mcp. Both rest on FastMCP and the official SDK. They are two generations of the same idea.

10. The Weekend 13 starter

Weekend 13/langchain.py is the smallest version of all of this:

from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.mcp import MCPAdapter

async def run_agent(server) -> dict:
    # Discover the server's tools, then hand them to the agent like any other tools.
    async with MCPAdapter(server) as adapter:
        tools = await adapter.list_tools()
        agent = create_agent("claude-sonnet-5", tools)
        return await agent.ainvoke(
            {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the forecast for Oslo?"}]})

The agent stays usable for the life of the adapter context, because the tools hold the client. Use the agent inside the async with block. Using the tools after the block exits is a common bug.

From the docs: what the LangChain MCP page adds

Added from the LangChain "MCP tools" page (read 30 Oct 2026). langchain.mcp is beta and needs langchain[mcp]>=1.4.0.

  • Lifetime: MCPAdapter is used as an async context manager and the tools hold the client, so the agent works only while the adapter context is open.
  • Content: model-visible MCP content becomes standard content blocks (text, image, file).
  • Structured results are stored on the ToolMessage as an artifact, an MCPToolArtifact whose structured_content holds the data (or None), not in the text the model reads.
  • Errors: a server result with isError=True becomes a ToolMessage with status="error" so the model can recover; transport or session failures raise exceptions.
  • Metadata sits under metadata["mcp"]: tool (annotations such as read_only_hint and destructive_hint, plus _meta) and server (name, version). Everything is optional, so read it defensively with .get().
  • Gating by hint: read destructive_hint once when you discover tools and build the interrupt_on map from it, using an InterruptOnConfig with allowed_decisions and a when predicate that can inspect request.tool_call["args"]. This replaces hardcoded tool names.
  • Elicitation is on by default: when a server needs input mid-call, the adapter raises a LangGraph interrupt. Use a checkpointer and the same thread_id, and answer with Command(resume={"responses": {key: answer}}) where each answer is accept (with form content), decline or cancel.
Common trapResuming re-runs the tool from the start

After an elicitation answer the tool restarts, so work done before the question can repeat. Make that work idempotent.

Common trapSampling and roots raise errors

The sessionless protocol has no back-channel for sampling or roots requests, so they raise errors. Servers that push elicitation over a legacy handshake session cannot be answered this way. This matches the legacy versus modern split in Chapter 17.

From the Craft "LangChain MCP" Colab notebook

I opened the Colab linked on the Craft page's MCP section in the desktop browser (read 30 Oct 2026; its cell outputs were visible). It is a short notebook, and its most useful content is a real install trap.

The CineBot server in the notebook is a three-tool FastMCP server: check_showtimes (a lookup in a small dict), cancel_booking marked with ToolAnnotations(destructiveHint=True) ("Irreversible"), and get_seat_map, which returns structured data (a dict with available and sold-out rows) instead of text. The destructive hint is exactly what the MCP-tools page uses to decide which tools need human approval (see the docs section above).

The adapter in one line. The notebook's own comment: "one adapter, a universal translator: it figures out on its own whether it is talking to a local MCP or an HTTP MCP". Its last cell opens MCPAdapter("https://docs.langchain.com/mcp") and calls list_tools(), which connects to LangChain's own documentation MCP server over a URL.

Common trap`pip install langchain.mcp` installs the wrong package

The notebook runs pip install "langchain[mcp]" first, and pip warns langchain 1.3.18 does not provide the extra 'mcp' (the extra arrives with langchain>=1.4.0, matching the docs). It then runs pip install langchain.mcp, which resolves to an older, unrelated package, langchain-mcp 0.2.1. That package pins langchain-core~=0.3 and mcp~=1.0, so pip downgrades langchain-core to 0.3.86 and mcp to 1.30, and prints conflicts against langgraph, langchain and langgraph-sdk, which all need langchain-core 1.4 or newer. Running pip install fastmcp langchain afterwards restores langchain-core 1.6.5 and mcp 2.2.0 but leaves langchain-mcp complaining. Lesson: the namespace langchain.mcp is imported from the langchain package (via its mcp extra); it is not a separate PyPI package called langchain.mcp. Upgrade langchain to 1.4 or newer, or use the older langchain-mcp-adapters package, and check pip list after any install that prints a resolver error.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Using the agent after leaving async with MCPAdapter Tools fail, the client is closed Run the agent inside the block
Expecting resources or prompts from MCPAdapter Not available Use the underlying fastmcp.Client, or the older package
Assuming a transport failure gives the model an error message An exception is raised Wrap the call, and use retry middleware
Trusting a destructive-hint filter without testing it Dangerous tools run unprompted Print tool.metadata and the filter's result, and confirm the tool is selected
One MCPConfig for legacy and modern servers Everything drops to the oldest era Use ClientGroup
Putting auth on MCPAdapter Ignored Configure auth= on the Client
Expecting audio results NotImplementedError Not supported yet
Hard-coding absolute paths or keys in a notebook Breaks on another machine, leaks secrets Relative paths and environment variables

  3. Give the same tools to create_agent and ask about showtimes.
  4. Print ToolMessage.content and .artifact["structured_content"] for get_seat_map.
  5. Call a failing tool and read the status="error" message. Then kill the server mid-call and watch the exception.

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

LangChain treats MCP as a source of tools. I open an MCPAdapter over a transport, URL, config or client group, list the tools, and give them to create_agent. Tool errors the server reports reach the model as error messages it can correct, while transport failures raise. Destructive tools can be gated by human approval built from the server's annotations, and elicitation surfaces as an interrupt. For mixed-era fleets I use a client group, and auth is set on the underlying client.

Basics

How does a LangChain agent use an MCP server?

Through an adapter. It connects, discovers the server's tools and returns them as ordinary LangChain tools that you pass to create_agent. The agent is the host and LangChain builds the client.

Can LangChain build MCP servers?

No. Its MCP support consumes existing servers as tool sources. Building servers is for libraries such as FastMCP.

How do you test an MCP tool without a model?

Call it directly with await tool.ainvoke({...}) on a tool from list_tools(). That proves the server works before adding an agent.

Intermediate

What is the difference between a tool error and a transport error?

A tool that ran and failed (isError=True) becomes a ToolMessage with status="error", which the agent can read and correct. A transport or session failure raises an exception because nothing came back to convert.

How do you require approval for dangerous MCP tools?

Read the server's annotations (such as destructive_hint) from tool.metadata, build the interrupt_on dictionary for HumanInTheLoopMiddleware from those tools, and pass the middleware to create_agent. The server decides what is dangerous.

How does elicitation work with LangChain?

The adapter converts a server's request for more input into a LangGraph interrupt(). A human answers outside the graph, and you resume with Command(resume=...). The tool call is retried with the answer.

MCPConfig or ClientGroup?

MCPConfig makes one aggregate connection with prefixed tool names and a shared protocol era, so the fleet negotiates down to the oldest. ClientGroup keeps independent connections with {server}_{tool} names, each with its own era and auth. Use a group for mixed fleets.

Where do you configure authentication?

On the FastMCP Client (bearer token string, "oauth" or an OAuth object with storage), not on MCPAdapter. Use a client group to give each server its own auth.

Tricky

What does the built-in module not support that the older package does?

Resources, prompts and tool-call interceptors (and progress callbacks are not in the reviewed public surface). The new module adds automatic elicitation and metadata namespacing, and is still beta.

How would you advise a client choosing between them?

If they need resources, prompts or interceptors today, use langchain-mcp-adapters. If they only need tools and are starting fresh, use langchain.mcp, accepting beta churn. Do not frame it as old versus new, because the new one is not a superset yet.

Why must the agent run inside the async with block?

The tools hold the client. When the context exits, the connection closes and the tools stop working.

What happens with an audio result?

AudioContent is not yet supported and raises NotImplementedError.

A destructive filter selects nothing, so dangerous tools run without approval. How do you debug it?

Print tool.metadata for each tool and the helper's result, and compare. The notebook itself shows destructive_hint: True in the raw metadata next to a helper result of False, so never assume the filter works. Fix the lookup until the dangerous tool is selected, and add a test for it.

Quick revision

Practice project: the AI newsletter (MCP connectors)

The page has an AI newsletter project with two parts: a request, then the long prompt that came out of it.

The request (a prompt given to a Claude chat): build an AI newsletter and updater that searches recursively using Tavily, goes in depth on each story, and splits news by industry (tech, business and so on). Then create an HTML draft in Gmail, an 8 AM Google Calendar event to read it, and two Apple Notes (a LinkedIn post and a Markdown article for Substack), using apps already connected through connectors and MCP.

The workflow the prompt defines (the visible part of the page; the rest of the prompt is clipped on the page):

Step Action
0 Check Google Calendar for a recurring "Read Today's Update" event (8:00 to 8:15 AM, daily). Create it only if it does not exist, so no duplicates
1 Broad search with Tavily, one search per category (AI, Tech, Business, Finance and markets) for the last 24 hours, shortlisting 2 to 4 significant stories each
2 Recursive deep dive: a follow-up Tavily search on each shortlisted story for context, numbers, reactions and why it matters, done independently per story (the branching search)
3 Synthesise into four sections, 2 to 4 sentences per story (what happened, why it matters, source), dropping thin or unverified items
4 Create a Gmail draft (do not send): subject "Daily Update - date", clean HTML with one section per category and source links, no sign-off or contact details
5 Create two Apple Notes: a LinkedIn post about the single most interesting story, and a Markdown article
Common trapWhy this prompt is built this way

Two good habits are visible. It checks before creating (the calendar event), so a daily run never makes duplicates, and it drafts instead of sending (the Gmail step), so a human reviews it first. Both are the same safety ideas as human-in-the-loop in Chapter 10.

From the docs: MCPAdapter, connections and authentication

From three LangChain docs pages read in full on 31 Oct 2026: MCP, Connections and Authentication. This extends the section above that came from the MCP tools page.

Basics. MCPAdapter is built on FastMCP, which handles transport inference, protocol negotiation, connection management and auth; LangChain adds the layer that adapts a server's tools into LangChain tools for create_agent. The langchain.mcp namespace needs langchain[mcp]>=1.4.0, is in beta and warns once per process. If you used MCP before 1.4.0 there is a migration guide from langchain-mcp-adapters. The adapter infers the transport from its target:

Target Transport
An http(s) URL string Streamable HTTP
A Path to a script Launched as a subprocess over stdio
An in-process FastMCP server In memory, no subprocess or socket (ideal for tests)
A transport object, a prebuilt fastmcp.Client, or an MCPConfig dict As configured (the dict puts several servers behind one adapter)

A plain string must look like an http or https URL. FastMCP would otherwise treat a string that names an existing .py or .js file as a script to launch, and strings often arrive from config or from a model, so the adapter rejects non-URL strings. The LangChain docs themselves are available as a public MCP server at https://docs.langchain.com/mcp (no key; tools to search the docs, read them through a virtual filesystem, and submit feedback).

Lifecycle. MCPAdapter is an async context manager. Discover tools inside async with and build the agent there; the returned tools hold the client, so they stay callable after the context exits. They are also reentrant: each tool call opens the client, runs the call and releases it, so a run uses one session per tool call and a long-running agent does not pin an idle connection. To hold one session across several calls, keep the adapter's context open around the agent call.

Several servers.

Need Use Notes
Many servers behind one connection MCPConfig dict ({"mcpServers": {...}}) Tools are prefixed with the config key (weather_...); servers can mix transports, but the fleet shares one negotiated protocol era, so a legacy-only member drops the whole fleet to legacy
Separate auth, protocol eras or pools per server ClientGroup Each member keeps its own era, auth and handlers; tools are namespaced {server}_{tool}; calls route back to the client that advertised the tool

Scaling a deployment. Discover per run but reuse connections underneath: build the agent in a langgraph dev graph factory, use list_tools(cache_mode="use") to serve a cached tool list within the server's TTL (modes: use, refresh, bypass; caching is opt-in and only works with modern-era servers that advertise hints), and share one HTTP connection pool across clients through an httpx_client_factory. In a graph factory the annotated types must be importable at runtime, not only under TYPE_CHECKING, because langgraph-api reads them with get_type_hints().

Protocol eras. The legacy era starts every connection with an initialize handshake; the modern era (protocol version 2026-07-28 and later) discovers support by probing a server/discover endpoint. FastMCP negotiates per connection (mode="legacy" pins the handshake era; mode="auto", the default, picks the newest the server understands).

Authentication. Any credential a fastmcp.Client accepts works: a bearer token string (Client(url, auth=token)), the literal "oauth" for the full OAuth 2.1 flow (discovery, dynamic client registration, browser redirect, token exchange; tokens are in memory by default, so pass an OAuth(..., token_storage=...) provider to persist them), or any httpx.Auth. For several servers, give each client its own auth inside a ClientGroup. For a deployment, use per-user authentication: authenticate the caller at the LangGraph server with a custom auth handler, then in the graph factory read runtime.user.identity and build the client with a per-user token (for example an OAuth gateway exchanging the session). Isolate any cached responses per user so one user never sees another's cached tool list.

Part E Advanced · Chapter 19

Multi-agent patterns

The five official LangChain v1 multi-agent patterns (subagents, handoffs, skills, router and custom workflow), when to use each, what they cost in model calls, and the project built around each.

Weekend 14Notebook-based, no class summary50 min readCode: Weekend 14
Jump to a section
Repo noteThis chapter comes from notebooks, not a class write-up

There is no written summary for this weekend. The content is built from the repo's multi-agent notebooks: an overview, four project notebooks and one large combined notebook. The student-facing notebooks call a live OpenAI model, so they need an OPENAI_API_KEY.

Why it matters

"When would you use multi-agent?" is a senior-level question, and the honest answer is "less often than people think". This chapter gives you a decision guide, the cost of each pattern in model calls, and the ability to say which pattern fits a scenario and why. Because patterns combine, the skill is choosing per sub-problem, not once for the whole system.

Key ideaDefault to a single agent first

Reach for multi-agent only when tools, context, teams or latency genuinely demand it. A single agent with dozens of similar-looking tools and one long prompt works fine until it does not: the model must choose between look-alike tools, hold unrelated domains in one context window and follow one prompt that tries to cover every situation.

Practitioner discussions in 2025 and 2026 (cited in the course's interview question file) echo this: too many tools can degrade the model's tool choices, though the exact threshold varies by task and model. That is one real reason specialised agents with narrower toolsets exist.

The core idea stays Agent = Model + Harness (Chapter 1). A multi-agent system is several agent objects wired together in one of a small number of well-understood shapes.

NoteCode in this chapter is simplified

The snippets below are condensed sketches that show each pattern's shape. They follow the notebooks but are not copied line for line. For the full, runnable versions open the notebooks linked under Sources.

The five patterns at a glance

Pattern Core mechanism Best fit
Subagents A supervisor agent calls other agents as tools Distinct domains, each with its own tools and prompt, with centralised control
Handoffs One agent's prompt and tools change based on state (or agents trade off with Command) A sequential workflow where behaviour should change as it progresses
Skills One agent loads specialised prompt content on demand Many possible specialisations, loaded only when needed, keeping context small
Router A classification step fans out to specialised agents in parallel, then synthesises Distinct knowledge verticals queried independently and combined
Custom workflow A hand-built LangGraph graph, any shape Anything the others do not fit, or a mix

Core ideas

1. Subagents, handoffs and router: do not confuse them

  • Subagents: the supervisor is itself a full agent. It decides, turn by turn, which sub-agent-as-tool to call, sequentially or in parallel. The sub-agents do not talk to the user directly, and the supervisor sees only their final answers, not their internal reasoning or tool calls.
  • Handoffs: there is no supervisor doing live reasoning about where to route. State (such as current_step, or which agent is active) determines which prompt and tools are in effect right now.
  • Router: a classification step (often one structured-output LLM call, not a full agent) decides once which specialists are relevant, dispatches to all of them in parallel, and a synthesis step combines the answers. No multi-turn orchestration.
Key ideaSupervisor vs router

A supervisor is a full agent that maintains conversation state and decides across multiple turns. A router is a single classification step with no ongoing state. Use a router for explicit control over parallel execution with light classification. Use subagents when you want the model to decide dynamically, turn by turn.

2. Pattern 1: Subagents

@tool
def check_seat_availability(showtime: str) -> str:
    """Check how many seats are left for a showtime."""
    return f"{showtime}: 12 seats remaining in Screen 3."

booking_specialist = create_agent(model, tools=[check_seat_availability], ...)

@tool
def book_seats(request: str) -> str:
    """Delegate a booking request to the booking specialist."""
    result = booking_specialist.invoke({"messages": [("user", request)]})
    return result["messages"][-1].content

supervisor = create_agent(model, tools=[book_seats, ...])

The project: a personal assistant. A supervisor coordinates a calendar agent (scheduling, availability, events) and an email agent (drafting and sending), with human-in-the-loop review so a person can approve, edit or reject sensitive actions such as an outbound email. The low-level tools (create_calendar_event, get_available_time_slots, send_email) are stubs, so the whole notebook runs without any external service. The calendar agent never sees send_email. Each specialist is independently testable.

Tool design choices:

Pattern Best for Trade-off
Tool per agent Fine-grained control over each subagent's input and output More setup, more customisation. Pick it for a handful of subagents you tune individually
Single dispatch tool (task(agent_name, description)) Many agents, distributed teams, convention over configuration Simpler composition, less per-agent customisation

Sync or async? Synchronous when the main agent's next move depends on the result, or failures should block the response. Asynchronous when the work is independent and the user should not be frozen waiting.

3. Pattern 2: Handoffs (state machine)

A single agent whose system prompt and tools change depending on where the conversation is. The core is a state field such as current_step.

from langchain.agents import AgentState, create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import wrap_model_call, ModelRequest, ModelResponse
from typing_extensions import NotRequired
from typing import Literal

class SupportState(AgentState):
    current_step: NotRequired[Literal["warranty_collector", "issue_classifier", "resolution_specialist"]]

@wrap_model_call
def apply_step(request: ModelRequest, handler):
    step = request.state.get("current_step", "warranty_collector")
    # choose the prompt and the tool list for this step, then continue
    return handler(request.override(system_prompt=PROMPTS[step], tools=TOOLS[step]))

The project: customer support. The agent collects warranty information, classifies the issue as hardware or software, then gives a solution or escalates to a human, keeping state across turns.

Key ideaTools drive the state

The key idea: tools return Command objects that update both the data they collected and the workflow step. Each "step" is a different configuration of the same underlying agent, selected dynamically by state. It is not a separate agent instance. This reuses Chapter 6's custom state, Chapter 9's wrap_model_call and Chapter 10's Command.

4. Pattern 3: Skills (progressive disclosure)

The agent sees lightweight skill descriptions up front and loads the full content on demand through a tool call, instead of swapping the whole system prompt.

SKILLS = {
    "refund_policy": "Full refund if cancelled 2+ hours before showtime; 50% credit within 2 hours.",
}

@tool
def load_skill(skill_name: str) -> str:
    """Load a specialised skill's full content.

    Available skills:
    - refund_policy: refund and cancellation rules
    """
    return SKILLS.get(skill_name, f"Unknown skill: {skill_name}")

The project: a SQL assistant for an organisation with many business verticals. Loading every schema into the prompt would overwhelm the context window. The agent sees the descriptions of two skills (sales_analytics, inventory_management) and loads the full schema and business logic only when relevant.

Why progressive disclosure Trade-off
Only 2 to 3 relevant skills load per task, not all Loading adds one extra tool-call round trip the first time
Different teams maintain their own skills independently Basic versions rely on prompting, not hard constraints
Scales to dozens or hundreds of skills Enforcing "always load A before B" needs custom logic
One agent, one thread, no sub-agent orchestration to track

5. Pattern 4: Router

import operator
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import Send

class RouterState(TypedDict, total=False):
    query: str
    answers: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]     # results from parallel branches are merged
    final: str

A classify node picks the relevant specialists, Send dispatches to each in parallel, and a synthesize node combines the answers.

The project: a multi-source knowledge base. A router queries a GitHub agent (code, issues, pull requests), a Notion agent (documentation) and a Slack agent (threads) at the same time, then synthesises. For "How do I authenticate API requests?" the router decomposes the question into source-specific sub-questions. Three state shapes keep it clear: AgentInput (just a query), AgentOutput (source plus result) and RouterState (the workflow).

6. Pattern 5: Custom workflow

A hand-built LangGraph StateGraph, node by node, mixing deterministic steps and agent steps in any shape. There is no separate "custom workflow API": it is the same StateGraph, START and END building blocks used elsewhere. The router example is already one.

Choosing a pattern

Your situation Pattern
A central agent keeps conversational control and calls specialists Subagents
One task flows through clear stages, each needing different tools or instructions Handoffs
Many optional specialisations, most irrelevant to a given request Skills
Independent knowledge sources that can be queried at the same time Router
None of these describe your system Custom workflow

What each pattern optimises for (five stars is best):

Optimise for Subagents Handoffs Skills Router
Distributed development (separate teams) 5 none 5 3
Parallelisation 5 none 3 5
Multi-hop (chaining several subagents) 5 5 5 none
Direct user interaction 1 5 5 3

Cost in model calls (more calls means more latency and cost). The notebook summarises the official worked examples:

Scenario Subagents Handoffs Skills Router
One-shot request 4 calls 3 calls 3 calls 3 calls
Repeat request (same turn type) 8 calls (4 plus 4) 5 (3 plus 2) 5 (3 plus 2) 6 (3 plus 3)
Multi-domain (3 parallel topics) 5 calls, about 9K tokens 7+ calls, 14K+ tokens 3 calls, about 15K tokens 5 calls, about 9K tokens
Key ideaWhat the numbers mean

Subagents are stateless by design: strong context isolation, but they repeat the full flow every request, so there is no "already loaded" discount. They suit parallel, large-context domains. Handoffs and skills are stateful: once a step or skill is active, repeat requests skip re-routing or re-loading, saving 40 to 50% of calls on the second ask. They suit repeated requests needing direct user conversation. Router is stateless per request (a classification call every time) but supports true parallel fan-out, best for clear parallel verticals when the router itself need not remember anything.

Pro tipPatterns compose

A subagents system can have a sub-agent that is internally a router. A handoffs stage can use skills to manage its own context. A subagent architecture can call tools that run custom workflows. Pick per sub-problem.

How the notebooks verify themselves without a key

The combined notebook defines a small test double, ScriptedToolModel, which plays back a scripted list of AIMessages (some with tool_calls) in order. Everything downstream is real: create_agent runs its loop, tools execute, Command objects update real graph state, StateGraph.invoke() traverses real nodes, and InMemorySaver persists real checkpoints. Only which words the model chooses is scripted. A DeterministicFakeEmbedding stands in for real embeddings so a vector store can be built and queried with zero network calls. The point is that the interesting part (wiring, state transitions, tool dispatch, handoffs) does not depend on what a live model says. The student-facing notebooks, by contrast, need a real key.

From the docs: what the multi-agent pages add

Added from the LangChain Subagents, Skills and Router pages (read 30 Oct 2026). Handoffs follow in the next section.

Subagents (supervisor). Subagents are called as tools and are stateless by default, so the main agent holds all memory; each call runs in a clean context ("context isolation"). A supervisor is a full agent that keeps context across turns and can call several subagents in parallel; a router is usually one dispatch step.

Decision Options
Sync or async Sync blocks; async starts a background job, usually with three tools (start, check status, get result) and needs a way to notify the user
Tool pattern One tool per agent (fine control) or a single task dispatch tool taking an agent name (scales better, less per-agent control)
Specs for a dispatch tool List agents in the prompt (under about 10), constrain the name with an enum, or give a discovery tool for large registries
Inputs Isolated (only the task; clean but re-derives work) or forked (parent history; continues work but a bigger prompt)
Outputs Tell the subagent to put results in its final message, since the supervisor sees only that; extra state can come back via a Command

By default a subagent uses an inherited checkpointer (fresh each call, supports interrupts, safe in parallel); checkpointer=True gives it persistent history. Because subagents run inside tool functions, LangGraph cannot discover them statically, so get_state with subgraphs will not show their state; call the subagent from a node in a custom graph to inspect it. The langgraph-supervisor package is no longer maintained.

Skills. Skills are mainly specialised prompts loaded on demand: a load_skill(skill_name) tool whose docstring lists the available skills, plus a system prompt naming them. This is progressive disclosure, the same idea as Agent Skills and llms.txt. Use it when one agent needs many specialisations, you do not need constraints between skills, or several teams build capabilities independently. Extensions: loading a skill can also register new tools in state, skills can form a tree (a data_science skill with sub-skills), and a skill's prompt can point to files read only when needed.

Router. A routing step classifies input and sends it to specialised agents, zero or more in parallel, then results are synthesised. Use Command (with goto) for one target and Send for parallel fan-out (a list of Send objects each carrying a sub-query). Routers are stateless by default. For multi-turn, either wrap the router as a tool inside a conversational agent (simplest) or store history in the router yourself, which needs custom management and can feel disjointed if agents have different tones. When multi-turn conversation is central the docs recommend handoffs or subagents.

From the docs: handoffs in detail

Added from the LangChain Handoffs page (read in full 30 Oct 2026).

The term comes from OpenAI, who used tool calls such as transfer_to_sales_agent to move control. The state-variable idea (current_step or active_agent) is the same one you met above.

  • Use when steps must happen in a fixed order, capabilities unlock only after preconditions (collect a warranty id before a refund), or you build a multi-stage conversation.
  • The tool must return a ToolMessage. A handoff tool returns a Command updating state, and when it also updates messages it must include a ToolMessage with the matching tool_call_id, or the history is malformed.
  • Approach 1, single agent with middleware (recommended): a wrap_model_call reads current_step and overrides the system prompt and tools for that call. State extends AgentState; a checkpointer keeps it across turns.
  • Approach 2, agent subgraphs: each agent is a graph node; handoff tools return Command(goto=..., graph=Command.PARENT); an active_agent field records who is in control; router functions end the run or hand over depending on active_agent and whether the last message has tool calls. Use it only when a node needs its own complex internals.
  • Context for subgraph handoffs: pass only two messages, the AIMessage holding the handoff tool call and a ToolMessage acknowledging the transfer, not the whole sub-agent history. That keeps the receiver focused and tokens low; if it needs more, summarise inside the ToolMessage. When returning control to the user, the final message should be an AIMessage.
  • Decide: how much history each agent gets (full, filtered, summary), whether a handoff tool only routes or also has side effects (opening a ticket), and how you control token growth.

Try it: six patterns in a kitchen

Added from the instructor's "Multi-Agent Systems" guide, part of his seven-part interactive series (read 30 Oct 2026). The guide explains six patterns with a restaurant analogy; the widgets are rebuilt from its descriptions.

Interactive demo (needs JavaScript): chain, parallel, controller, feedback loop, hierarchical and planner-executor, each with a Run button.

Pattern What it is Where you meet it
Chain Agents run in a fixed order, each output feeding the next Draft a post, then fact-check, then format
Parallel Independent agents run at once and a merge step combines results Claude's Research feature: a lead agent starts several subagents on independent threads
Controller (router) One agent only decides who handles a request A support inbox that forwards billing, technical and general questions to different specialists
Reactive (feedback loop) A second agent checks the first's output and sends it back if it is not good enough Code checked by a test-running agent, an email checked by a tone reviewer
Hierarchical An orchestrator calls specialist agents as tools ("agent as a tool") A lead researcher that calls specialised subagents and synthesises the results
Planner-Executor One agent turns a vague goal into steps, another works through them "Plan and book my trip to Lisbon"

The guide also walks through a supervisor example: asked "what does our policy say about expense reimbursement, and is Priya free tomorrow afternoon to discuss an exception?", a supervisor splits the request, a knowledge agent searches the policy documents, an action agent checks the calendar, and the supervisor combines both answers. It quotes figures for Claude's own Research feature (from the guide, not checked against a primary source): 3 to 5 parallel subagents, 90.2 percent better than a single agent on broad research, at roughly 15 times the token cost.

Interactive demo: answer four yes or no questions to see which pattern to start with.

NoteHow this maps to LangChain's names

The guide's names differ from the LangChain docs. Roughly, its hierarchical pattern corresponds to what the docs call subagents (a supervisor calling agents as tools) and its controller to a router, while chain and planner-executor are closest to custom workflows (my mapping). Chapter 19 above uses the LangChain names.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Going multi-agent too early Extra latency and cost for no gain Start with one agent
Confusing a supervisor with a router Wrong design Supervisor: full agent, multi-turn. Router: one classification, parallel
Subagents for repeat user requests Repeats the whole flow every time (8 calls) Handoffs or skills are stateful and cheaper
Loading every schema into one prompt Overflowing context Skills with progressive disclosure
Skills where an order must be enforced Prompts only guide, not enforce Add custom logic or use handoffs
A router that needs memory It is stateless per request Use a stateful pattern
Forgetting results from parallel branches must merge Lost answers Use a reducer such as Annotated[list, operator.add]
Handoffs implemented as separate agents Lost state One agent, state field, wrap_model_call

Interview corner

Say it in 30 seconds

I start with one agent and go multi-agent only when tools, context or latency demand it. If a central agent should coordinate distinct domains I use subagents. If behaviour changes as a task progresses I use handoffs with a state field. If there are many optional specialisations I load skills on demand. If independent sources can be queried at once I use a router with parallel fan-out. Anything else is a custom LangGraph workflow, and patterns combine per sub-problem.

Basics

Why multi-agent at all?

A single agent with many tools and one long prompt struggles to choose between similar tools and hold unrelated domains in context. Splitting into focused specialists keeps each simple and independently testable.

Name the five patterns.

Subagents, handoffs, skills, router and custom workflow.

Subagents vs handoffs vs router?

Subagents: a supervisor agent calls other agents as tools, deciding turn by turn. Handoffs: one agent's prompt and tools change with state. Router: one classification step fans out to specialists in parallel and then synthesises.

Intermediate

When would you choose skills?

When one agent has many possible specialisations and most are irrelevant to any request. It loads descriptions up front and full content on demand, so context stays small and teams can maintain skills independently.

How does a handoff work in practice?

A custom state field (such as current_step) selects the system prompt and tool list in wrap_model_call, and tools return Command objects that update the data and the step. It is the same agent in a different configuration each step.

How are parallel router results combined?

Send dispatches to each specialist, and a reducer such as Annotated[list[str], operator.add] merges their outputs into shared state before a synthesis step.

Tool per agent or a single dispatch tool?

Tool per agent for a few subagents you tune individually, with fine control and more setup. A single task(agent_name, description) tool for many agents or distributed teams, with simpler composition and less per-agent customisation.

Sync or async subagents?

Sync when the next step depends on the result or failures should block. Async when the work is independent and the user should not be frozen.

Tricky

Which pattern is cheapest for a repeat request, and why?

Handoffs and skills (about 5 calls for a repeat against 8 for subagents), because they are stateful: once a step or skill is active, repeat requests skip re-routing or re-loading. Subagents repeat the whole flow each time.

Which pattern wins for three parallel topics?

Subagents and router (about 5 calls and 9K tokens each), because they parallelise. Handoffs would need 7 or more calls and 14K or more tokens, and skills load about 15K tokens.

Can you combine patterns?

Yes. A subagents system can have a router inside a sub-agent, a handoffs stage can use skills, and a subagent can wrap a custom workflow. Choose per sub-problem.

What is the weakness of skills?

They rely on prompting to guide usage, not hard constraints, and loading adds an extra round trip the first time. Enforcing order needs custom logic.

How can you test multi-agent wiring without calling a model?

Use a scripted fake chat model that plays back predetermined AIMessages with tool calls. The graph, tools, state updates and checkpoints still run for real. Only the model's wording is scripted.

It is useful for seeing how an agent loop or subagents actually behave, which is the same thing Chapters 6 and 19 explain in text.

Repo note: the multi-agent sketch in test.py

Weekend 14.../Multi Agents in Langchain/test.py is a short, non-runnable sketch of the subagents idea: three create_agent specialists built from one model (init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5.5")), each with its own tools and a one-line system prompt: a GitHub expert (search_code, search_issues, search_prs), a Notion expert (search_notion, get_page) and a Slack expert (search_slack, get_thread). The tool functions are never defined, so it will not run as committed, and the file ends by invoking only the Slack agent with a time-off question. Read it as the shape of the pattern, one narrowly scoped agent per knowledge source, which a supervisor would then route between.

From the docs: choosing a pattern, and the custom workflow

From two LangChain docs pages read in full on 31 Oct 2026: Multi-agent and Custom workflow.

Do you need multi-agent at all? Not every complex task does: a single agent with the right (sometimes dynamic) tools and prompt can often do the same. People usually mean one of three needs: context management (specialised knowledge without overflowing the window), distributed development (teams own capabilities independently) or parallelisation. Patterns pay off when one agent has too many tools and picks badly, when tasks need specialised knowledge with long prompts, or when you need sequential constraints that unlock capabilities. At the centre is context engineering: what each agent sees. For built-in support the page points to managed Deep Agents (subagents, skills, planning, a virtual filesystem and context management).

Pattern How it works
Subagents A main agent coordinates subagents as tools; all routing passes through it
Handoffs State changes (set by tool calls) switch the active agent or its tools and prompt
Skills One agent stays in control and loads specialised prompts and knowledge on demand
Router A routing step classifies input, sends it to one or more agents, and synthesises their results
Custom workflow A bespoke LangGraph flow mixing deterministic logic and agents; other patterns can be nodes

The page also rates each pattern with stars on four criteria: distributed development (can teams maintain parts independently), parallelisation, multi-hop (calling several subagents in series) and direct user interaction (can subagents talk to the user). Handoffs have no rating for distributed development or parallelisation, and routers have none for multi-hop; the per-column star counts did not come through in the page text I read, so use the table's own page for the exact ratings. Patterns can be mixed.

Performance, from the page's three scenarios (model calls, tokens):

Scenario Subagents Handoffs Skills Router
One-shot ("Buy coffee") 4 calls 3 3 3
Repeat request (two turns) 8 (4+4) 5 (3+2) 5 (3+2) 6 (3+3)
Multi-domain (compare three languages, about 2,000 tokens of docs each) 5 calls, about 9K tokens 7+ calls, 14K+ tokens 3 calls, about 15K tokens 5 calls, about 9K tokens

Why: subagents add a call because results flow back through the main agent, and they are stateless, so a repeat costs the full flow again (strong context isolation, repeated cost). Handoffs and skills are stateful, so a repeat skips the hand-off or the skill load and saves roughly 40 to 50 percent of calls. Routers are stateless, and each request needs a routing call (wrap one as a tool in a stateful agent to optimise). For multi-domain work, parallel patterns (subagents, router) win; skills have fewer calls but accumulate context (every later call re-reads all the loaded skill text, about 67 percent more tokens than subagents here); handoffs run sequentially and cannot parallelise. Handoffs and skills are best for repeat requests, subagents and router for parallel execution, subagents and skills for large-context domains.

Custom workflow. Define the graph yourself with LangGraph: sequential steps, conditional branches, loops and parallel execution. Each node can be a plain function, an LLM call or a whole agent, and you can call create_agent(...).invoke(...) directly inside a node. The page's example is a RAG pipeline for a WNBA assistant with three node types: a model node (rewrite the query with structured output), a deterministic node (vector retrieval, no LLM) and an agent node (answer from the retrieved context, with a news tool), passing a TypedDict state between them. The router pattern is itself a custom workflow; a tutorial builds a router over GitHub, Notion and Slack in parallel. In production, swap the in-memory vector store for a persistent one.

Part E Advanced · Chapter 20

Meridian AI: a full-stack project tour

A small web app that answers questions about your documents (RAG) and audits a purchase request with three specialist agents and a CFO memo. A tour of how the pieces fit, why the code is split, and how it deploys.

Weekend 14Project, no class summary40 min readCode: Weekend 14
Jump to a section
Repo noteThis chapter comes from the project's own README and code

No class write-up exists for this weekend. It is built from the meridian-ai-learner-main folder: its README, DEPLOY.md and the backend source. The Oct 10 to 11 weekend folder holds only two links: the repo mayank953/meridian-ai-learner and a course site, meridian-ai-course.netlify.app. The project is fictional: the company, Aldermoor Industries, and its sample documents contain made-up data.

Why it matters

This is a capstone-style "put it all together" project: RAG, multiple agents with tools, an API, a front end, logging, tests, containers and cloud deployment. In an interview, being able to walk through how a real system is laid out and why matters as much as any single concept. It also contains two honest teaching points: the audit runs agents one after another (not in parallel), and its "checks" are done by an AI from general knowledge, so it is a demo and not a compliance tool.

Key ideaWhat it does
  1. Document Q&A (RAG). Upload PDFs (policies, contracts, reports) and ask in plain English. Answers use only what is in the documents.
  2. Purchase audit (agents). Paste a purchase request. Three specialist agents review it (risk, tax, accounting), and a final "CFO" step writes one short memo with a decision: approved, conditional hold or rejected.

Core ideas

NoteSplit with the RAG book

This chapter is the capstone: how the whole app fits together, the audit agents, the middleware, and how it ships (Docker, Cloud Run, CI). The document Q&A half, including Vertex AI Vector Search costs, is taught in the RAG book.

1. The technologies, as a restaurant

Technology What it is Restaurant analogy
React (frontend) The page you click on The dining room, menu and buttons
FastAPI (Python) Receives requests and returns answers The waiter
Pydantic Checks requests are filled in correctly The order form
LangChain Connects AI steps together The recipe book and workflow
Gemini (Google's model) Reads text, writes answers The chef
Embeddings Turn text into numbers that capture meaning GPS coordinates for ideas: similar ideas sit close
Vertex AI Vector Search Finds stored text closest in meaning to a question A library catalogue organised by meaning
RAG Find the right pages first, then answer from them An open-book exam
Agents and tools AI that decides to run small programs to get facts A chef who uses a scale and a thermometer
Cloud Storage Keeps files in Google Cloud A filing cabinet
Docker Packs the app and its needs into one box A lunchbox that opens the same anywhere
Cloud Run Runs that box on the internet, only when someone visits A pop-up shop
Secret Manager Stores keys and passwords safely A safe
GitHub Actions Builds and delivers the app automatically A delivery robot
Logging (structlog) The app writes down what it does The kitchen diary

2. How it fits together

Asking a question. The page sends it to the backend, which turns it into an embedding. Vector Search returns the three stored pieces closest to it. The backend gives Gemini those pieces and the question ("answer using only this"), and the answer goes back to the page.

Running an audit. You submit a request. The risk, tax and control agents each read it, decide which tools to use (for example "check the exchange rate") and write a short report. A final step reads the three reports and writes one memo with a decision.

3. Why the code is split into many files

A ten-line experiment can live in one file. A real app cannot: it is a kitchen where everyone cooks on one table. The rule is one file, one job.

Problem with one big file How splitting helps
Hard to find things The name tells you where to look
Changing one thing breaks another A change stays inside its own file
Hard to test (needs the internet to start) Parts can be tested alone
Copy-pasted code drifts One function written once and reused
Many people editing one file clash People work in different files
Intimidating to read Read one small file at a time 
backend/
  api/        the "waiter": main.py (creates the app), endpoints.py (web addresses), schemas.py (request shapes)
  rag/        llm.py, embeddings.py, vector_store.py, data_ingestion.py, retrieval.py
  agent/      tools.py (five tools), prompts.py (instructions per agent), agents.py (creates and runs agents)
  config/     settings.py (keys and names from outside the code)
  logger/     custom_logger.py (JSON log lines)
  tests/      automatic checks that need no accounts
frontend/     React + TypeScript; src/lib/api.ts is the only file that talks to the backend
sample_docs/  four made-up PDFs
.github/workflows/deploy.yml   builds and deploys
Dockerfile, requirements.txt, .env.example, DEPLOY.md
Key ideaThe dependency rule

Each package depends only on the ones below it: api depends on rag and agent, which depend on config and logger. The web layer does not know how AI works. The AI code does not know what a web address is. This is a clean layered architecture you can name in an interview.

4. The RAG side

The document Q&A half of Meridian (ingestion into chunks of about 1,000 characters with 100 of overlap, embeddings, Vector Search, and three retrieval strategies) is taught in the RAG book: embeddings and ingestion, retrieval and the answer chain. The one fact to keep here: the answer prompt says to use the retrieved context and to say "I do not know" otherwise.

5. The audit side

class ProcurementSupervisor:
    def __init__(self):
        self.risk_agent = create_specialized_agent(
            [check_sanctions_list, get_vendor_credit_score], RISK_AGENT_PROMPT)
        self.tax_agent = create_specialized_agent(
            [calculate_cross_border_tax, validate_fx_hedge], TAX_AGENT_PROMPT)
        self.control_agent = create_specialized_agent(
            [categorize_expense], CONTROL_AGENT_PROMPT)

    def run_audit(self, request: str) -> dict:
        risk_result = self._invoke_agent(self.risk_agent, request)       # phase 1
        tax_result = self._invoke_agent(self.tax_agent, request)         # phase 2
        control_result = self._invoke_agent(self.control_agent, request) # phase 3
        cfo_memo = self.llm.invoke(SYNTHESIS_PROMPT_TEMPLATE.format(...)) # phase 4, no tools
        return {"risk_result": ..., "tax_result": ..., "control_result": ..., "cfo_memo": ...}
Agent Tools What it checks
Risk and compliance check_sanctions_list, get_vendor_credit_score Whether the vendor is on restricted lists; creditworthiness
Tax and treasury calculate_cross_border_tax, validate_fx_hedge VAT or GST and import duties; whether the FX rate is within a 5% variance of market
Financial control categorize_expense Capital (CapEx) or operational (OpEx) under accounting standards
CFO synthesis None (one plain LLM call) Reads the three reports and writes one memo with a decision
Common trapThis is not the subagents pattern, and not parallel

Chapter 19's patterns do not quite describe this. The supervisor is plain Python that runs three agents one after another and then makes one LLM call. Each specialist is a create_agent with its own prompt and tools. It is a fixed pipeline (closer to a custom workflow) rather than a supervisor agent deciding dynamically. Because the three checks are independent, a router with parallel fan-out would be faster, and that is a good improvement to propose in an interview.

NoteHonest limits, stated in the README

The audit's checks are done by the AI from general knowledge. Only the exchange-rate check uses a live data source. It is a demo of how such a system is built, not a real compliance tool. Answers change wording each run, but the layout stays the same. create_agent is built on LangGraph, but the project never writes graph code.

The audit endpoint is POST /api/agent/audit with a body such as {"request_text": "Purchase of 200 PLC controllers from Takumi Controls Europe B.V. (Netherlands). Total 480,000 EUR. Origin JP, destination DE. FX rate quoted: 1 EUR = 163.5 JPY."}. It returns four texts: the risk, tax and control reports and the CFO memo, and can take a minute or more because several AI calls happen.

6. Running it

git clone https://github.com/mayank953/meridian-ai-learner.git
cd meridian-ai-learner
python3.12 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
cp .env.example .env            # set GOOGLE_API_KEY to your Gemini key
uvicorn api.main:app --app-dir backend --reload --port 8080

Then open http://localhost:8080/docs (FastAPI's automatic page). Try GET /api/health (returns {"status": "ok"}), then POST /api/agent/audit. For the web page, run npm install and npm run dev in frontend/ and open http://localhost:3000. Run every command from the project's main folder, because the app looks for .env where you start it.

Document Q&A needs Google Cloud. Upload the sample_docs/ PDFs and ask: total revenue in FY2024 (about EUR 2.84 billion), payment terms for servo motor suppliers (Net-45), customs duty on PLC controllers from Japan (2.2%), depreciation of filling line equipment (10 years). Then ask something not in the documents to check it admits it does not know.

7. Deploying to Google Cloud

You do four things: make a Google Cloud project, make a robot (service) account GitHub can use, give GitHub the robot's key and your Gemini key, and press Run workflow. The workflow .github/workflows/deploy.yml creates everything with gcloud (database, storage, server) and publishes the app: no manual setup.

Service How you are charged
Vector Search Billed by the hour while deployed, even with no users; the main cost and the likeliest surprise bill. Details in RAG: costs
Cloud Run Only when used. Light use is usually inside the free allowance
Cloud Storage, Cloud Build, Secret Manager A few cents or free allowances
Gemini API A free tier exists, and free-tier content may be used to improve products, so use only the sample documents
Common trapVector Search bills while idle

The setup script does not choose a machine size or replica count. Google's documentation says replicas default to 2, so the hourly cost can be higher than one small machine. Do your cloud work in one sitting and switch the database off when you finish. Recreating it takes 30 to 45 minutes.

  • The $300 free credit: new customers get $300 for 90 days, need a card (a temporary hold, not a charge), and are not charged automatically at the end. The trial ends at whichever comes first: 90 days or $300. After a 30-day grace period, trial resources are deleted. Only new customers qualify, and some generative-AI services are restricted on trial accounts.
  • Set a budget alert first. It emails you as spending grows but does not stop it.
  • The chat model uses your Gemini key, so trial limits do not affect it; the embedding step can be rate-limited.

8. Tests, logging and settings

  • Tests need no accounts, so the project can be verified without cloud credentials (backend/tests, conftest.py).
  • Structured logging writes JSON log lines (structlog): "the kitchen's diary". The audit logs each phase start and result, which is how you trace a slow or wrong audit.
  • Settings are read from outside the code via a Settings class with environment variable aliases (for example VERTEX_LLM_MODEL_NAME and VERTEX_EMBEDDING_MODEL_NAME). Keys live in .env and Secret Manager, never in Git, as in Chapter 1.

Update from the current Meridian learner repo

Added from a fresh clone of github.com/mayank953/meridian-ai-learner (read 30 Oct 2026): its README, the 18-file docs/ learner guide, and the backend code. This repo is newer than the copy in the course folder that the sections above were built from.

Common trapWhat changed since the earlier copy

The current repo adds an APP_MODE switch (local or cloud), writes the RAG chain as a plain LCEL pipeline instead of create_retrieval_chain from langchain-classic, and puts a middleware stack around all three agents. Where the sections above describe create_retrieval_chain or have no middleware, the current repo differs.

The four scenarios to try

All work with the four sample PDFs in sample_docs/.

Scenario Do this Expect Why it matters
A. A policy question Ask for FY2024 revenue; also payment terms for servo-motor suppliers, duty on PLC controllers from Japan, depreciation of filling-line equipment About EUR 2.84 billion; Net-45 for suppliers with a credit score of 75 or more; 2.2 percent duty; 10 years straight line The answer comes from your documents, not the model's memory
B. Not in the documents Ask "Who won the 2018 World Cup?" The app says it does not know The prompt says to answer only from context; "I don't know" beats inventing
C. A normal audit 200 PLC controllers, 480,000 EUR, a Netherlands supplier, made in Japan, 1 EUR = 163.5 JPY Cautious risk report for an unknown supplier, import VAT near 19 percent plus duty, CapEx needing a Department Head's sign-off (over EUR 250,000; over EUR 1,000,000 needs the CFO and Management Board), and a CFO memo Three specialist reports feed one memo
D. A suspicious rate Same request with 1 EUR = 190 JPY The tax report flags FX ALERT (more than 5 percent from market) and the memo becomes CONDITIONAL HOLD The decision follows written rules, not mood

The CFO decision rules

The CFO step reads exact words in the three reports:

Word found Decision
RED ALERT REJECTED
FX ALERT or HOLD FOR TREASURY AUDIT CONDITIONAL HOLD
All APPROVED or SUCCESS APPROVED TO PAY
Key ideaFixed layouts are a contract

The CFO rules depend on those keywords, so each agent prompt ends with an exact output layout and a rename must be made in both places. Each agent prompt has the same four parts: a role, responsibilities, a decision framework and an output format.

What the app does not do

Limit Consequence
Four of the five tools ask the model from general knowledge; only the exchange-rate check uses live data (and falls back to the model if the site is unreachable) A real system needs sanctions, credit and tax services
Wording changes between runs A person reviews important decisions
No sign-in and open access Never upload private documents to a public demo
Upload history lives in memory A database would keep it
Only text-based PDFs work Scanned images need OCR first

A tool that fails returns a SYSTEM WARNING ... Manual review required text instead of crashing the audit, so errors can hide inside text: read the logs.

Local mode and cloud mode

One line in .env decides where data lives: APP_MODE=local (a Gemini API key only, Chroma on disk) or APP_MODE=cloud (Vertex AI Vector Search and Cloud Storage).

Concern Local Cloud
Embeddings gemini-embedding-001 (API key) text-embedding-005 (Vertex AI)
Vector database Chroma in .meridian/chroma Vertex AI Vector Search
Original PDFs .meridian/uploads/ A Cloud Storage bucket
Log upload Skipped Copied to the bucket on shutdown

Everything that needs storage asks one question (settings.is_cloud) and gets back a LangChain VectorStore, so ingestion and retrieval never know which database is behind them. This is the strategy pattern: same interface, swappable implementation. Both modes use 768-dimensional vectors, but the two databases are separate, so re-upload after switching. If APP_MODE=cloud but the index id is empty, the API answers 503 with the list of missing settings instead of a stack trace.

The RAG chain

The current repo writes the RAG chain as one plain LCEL pipeline instead of create_retrieval_chain from langchain-classic, with three strategies (similarity, multiquery, contextual). See the RAG book, retrieval and the answer chain.

The middleware stack around the agents

def build_agent_middleware() -> list[AgentMiddleware]:
    return [
        PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True),
        PIIMiddleware("credit_card", strategy="mask", apply_to_input=True),
        ModelCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=settings.agent_max_model_calls, exit_behavior="end"),
        ToolCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=settings.agent_max_tool_calls, exit_behavior="continue"),
        ModelRetryMiddleware(max_retries=settings.agent_max_retries, initial_delay=1.0),
        ToolRetryMiddleware(max_retries=settings.agent_max_retries, initial_delay=0.5),
        log_tool_calls,
    ]
Step Middleware Purpose here
1 PIIMiddleware for e-mail (redact) and card numbers (mask) Hide contact details before Gemini sees the request
2 ModelCallLimitMiddleware End a phase after N model calls, a cost guard against loops
3 ToolCallLimitMiddleware Cap tool calls per phase
4 ModelRetryMiddleware Retry Gemini on transient errors (429 and 503) with backoff
5 ToolRetryMiddleware Retry flaky tools such as the live exchange-rate API
6 log_tool_calls (custom) One JSON log line per tool call: name, arguments, duration, result preview

The custom one is about ten lines with @wrap_tool_call: log "started", call handler(request), log "finished" with the duration and a 200-character preview, or log the error and re-raise. It is the same shape as the middleware in Chapters 7 and 9, so it makes a good interview example.

Design decisions, and which are shortcuts

Choice Why Shortcut or trade-off
Three specialist agents, not one Short, focused prompts and only the tools each needs More model calls: slower and costlier
Plain-Python supervisor plus one summary call Control flow you can read and debug Less flexible than a self-organising graph
Agents run one after another Easy to follow in logs Could run in parallel
temperature = 0 Same question, nearly the same answer, easier to debug
Models and connections created on first use (lru_cache) The app starts, and /api/health and tests work, before any cloud setup
/api/status never calls the cloud It must work exactly when the cloud is misconfigured
Tests use fake settings Anyone can run them with no accounts They test wiring, not answer quality
Docker with a two-stage build and .dockerignore hiding .env Small image, secrets never packed
--max-instances 3 Limits cost and abuse Heavy traffic is limited
--allow-unauthenticated, a project-wide secret grant, a key file for the robot, and broad editor plus projectIamAdmin roles Simplest setup Shortcuts: production uses sign-in, narrow roles and keyless sign-in

A production version would add: real data sources for sanctions, credit and tax; sign-in and tighter permissions; a database for history; automatic tests in the workflow; answer-quality measurement; real streamed progress for the audit; keyless sign-in from GitHub to Google Cloud.

Layer Used here Alternatives the guide lists
Cloud Google Cloud AWS, Azure
Web framework FastAPI Flask, Django, Express
Vector database Vertex AI Vector Search Postgres with pgvector, Pinecone, Chroma
Agents LangChain create_agent LangGraph, Google ADK, CrewAI, AutoGen
Hosting Cloud Run App Engine, Kubernetes, a virtual machine
Cloud setup gcloud in GitHub Actions Terraform (not used)

Costs and accounts

Item Detail
Gemini API key Free tier with rate limits; free-tier content may be used by Google, so use only the sample documents
Google Cloud $300 credit for new customers, 90 days, card required (a hold, not a charge)
Vector Search Billed by the hour while deployed, even with no users; the main cost and the likeliest surprise bill. Details in RAG: costs

The most common errors

You see Do this
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'api' Run from the main folder: uvicorn api.main:app --app-dir backend --reload --port 8080
Browser says blocked by CORS The backend is not reachable; start it on port 8080
404 ... model ... not found The model was retired; set a current model name
