Context: immutable, set per invocation and passed fresh every call (a user's membership tier for this request). Store: survives across any number of sessions (a saved dietary preference recalled weeks later).

A tool declares a parameter named config. What happens?

config is reserved for RunnableConfig. The framework intercepts it before the function body runs, typically producing a TypeError about a missing argument. It is an easy accident because config is an ordinary variable name.

A plain string versus a Command return?

A string only answers. A Command can write to agent state. Example: a tool that upgrades a customer's loyalty tier after a large order must confirm the upgrade and store the new tier for later tools and turns, which a string cannot do.

Why is wrap_model_call gating stronger than telling the model in the prompt not to use a tool?

A prompt instruction depends on the model choosing to comply and a persuasive message may talk it round. Gating removes the tool from request.tools before the call, so no tool definition exists to reference: a structural guarantee, not a request.

What is a headless tool, and what could only be done that way?

Its schema is registered on the server so the model can call it, but it executes on the client (typically the browser) through an interrupt and resume handshake. Example: reading the user's live geolocation, which a Python server cannot access.

Chapter 6: Agents, memory and middleware

Does a tool result go to the user?

No. It goes back to the model, which produces the final reply. The user sees only that. (return_direct is the deliberate exception.)

What is the agentic loop?

Receive a message, the model decides whether a tool is needed, run it, append the result, and repeat until the model answers in plain text. It was called the ReAct pattern.

How does an agent remember a conversation?

A checkpointer (for example InMemorySaver) passed to create_agent, plus a thread_id in the config. The same id restores the history; a new id starts fresh.

Is thread_id a reserved keyword?

No. It is just the identifier the checkpointer looks for in the config. The application decides how ids are generated and assigned.

How would you give VIP users an extra tool?

Use middleware that reads trusted state or context and filters the tool list before the model call, so non-VIPs never see the tool. Do not ask the user, and do not rely on a system-prompt instruction.

Why not use an if/else outside the agent to choose a tool list?

Code outside the agent cannot read the agent's live state or store (for example a growing message count). Only code running inside the agent, such as middleware, can.

What is dynamic tool loading, and what are its two approaches?

Modifying the available tools at runtime instead of defining them all upfront. Either filter a pre-registered set based on state, permissions and flags, or register tools dynamically when they are not known ahead (for example from MCP).

Memory saver vs memory store vs cache vs database?

Saver: one conversation's history by thread id. Store: facts about a user across conversations. Cache: short-lived results of repeated expensive calls. Database: general persistent application data. Choose by use case and lifetime.

The middleware kept reading is_vip_member as False even when you passed True. Why?

The agent only tracks fields in its state schema. A custom field passed to invoke is dropped unless a custom state schema declares it. Declare it and the middleware sees it.

What is a headless tool?

A tool whose definition lives on the server with the agent, but whose implementation runs on the client (clipboard, location, payment), executed through an interrupt-and-resume handshake. The agent decides to use it; the user's device does the work.

Why is loading hundreds of tools bad even if the user cannot use them?

Their definitions are loaded into context and sent to the model on every call, costing tokens and possibly causing wrong tool choices. Load only what is relevant.

Where would you store "I prefer Python"?

In the store (long-term memory), so every future conversation can use it. A checkpointer is tied to one thread and would not carry it across chats.

Does a tool call cost money like a model call?

No. Only model calls consume tokens. A tool running on its own, with no model call, does not (though the tool's own API may have fees).

Chapter 7: Mastering middleware

What are the six built-in middlewares?

Summarisation, human-in-the-loop, model call limit, tool call limit, model fallback and PII detection.

Why is HITL only applied to tool calls?

Because reasoning before a tool call changes nothing in the world. The tool call is where the agent acts, so that is where a human decision matters.

Guardrail vs middleware?

A guardrail is the concept, protecting the agent from undesirable behaviour. Middleware is the mechanism used to implement it. Guardrails are applied as middleware.

Redact vs mask?

Redact removes the sensitive value before it reaches the model. Mask replaces part of it (for example the last digits stay visible) so the model knows something exists without seeing the real value.

How do you configure summarisation?

SummarizationMiddleware with a model (can be a cheaper one), a trigger (tokens, messages or a fraction of context) and keep (how much recent history stays untouched).

How does HITL actually work?

The middleware interrupts before a configured tool runs. The state is saved by the checkpointer. A human approves, edits or rejects, and the developer resumes with Command(resume=...) or through a custom UI. LangChain ships no UI.

Can I have two levels of sign-off?

Not out of the box. That needs custom middleware.

Why not just tell the model "do not call the tool more than twice"?

A model can ignore the instruction, and it breaks if the model is swapped. A call limit enforced in code is specific and dependable.

Is a transfer to a human agent human-in-the-loop?

No. A transfer hands off the whole conversation. HITL keeps the agent in the loop and pauses only for a decision.

What does model fallback not do?

It does not route by cost or speed or choose the best model for a task. It switches only when the primary model hard-fails (for example a 404 or an expired key), passing the full history to the backup.

Will middleware add latency?

Depends. If it calls a model (summarisation does), some. If it is pure code (a call limit check), minimal.

Does a summarising middleware share the agent's main context?

No. It runs against its own separate text rather than the agent's main running context.

In what order do multiple middlewares run?

Not randomly: by a defined priority or the order declared. They are designed not to collide.

How do you handle country-specific ids like Aadhaar?

Built-ins cannot cover every country. Define a custom detector with a regular expression and pass it to PIIMiddleware with a strategy such as mask.

When do you drop from LangChain middleware to LangGraph?

When you need precise, deterministic control of internals such as checkpointers, stores and interrupts. For most agents, including simple RAG chatbots, LangChain with built-in middleware is enough.

Chapter 8: Guardrails, todo lists, resilience

Run limit vs thread limit?

Run limit caps calls within one invoke. Thread limit caps calls across the whole conversation and needs a checkpointer. A meal versus a day.

What are the four PII strategies?

block (raise an exception), redact (replace with a placeholder), mask (partly hide) and hash (deterministic hash that keeps identity without the value).

What does the todo list middleware add?

A structured, maintained plan object the agent updates as it works. A prompt alone does not reliably create and track one.

Tool error vs tool retry?

Error handling converts one failure into a readable tool message without retrying. Retry actively re-runs the call with backoff. Use error handling for permanent failures and retry for transient ones.

Why does a tool call limit produce a tool message rather than an interrupt?

An interrupt asks a human for a decision. A limit rejection needs none, so it is returned to the model as information.

How does the LLM tool selector differ from dynamic tool loading?

Dynamic loading filters by known state (who the user is). The selector filters by the content of the current query, using a possibly cheaper model with structured output to choose relevant tools.

When should you not use the LLM tool selector?

When the answer is already known with certainty, such as a non-logged-in user who must never see a booking tool. Put that in code. Models are fuzzy; code is not.

What is the backoff formula and why use it?

delay = initial_delay × backoff_factor ^ retry_number. Waiting longer between attempts gives a briefly failing service time to recover, max_delay caps the wait and jitter avoids synchronised retries.

How does max_retries count?

Retries after the first call. max_retries=3 allows up to four calls in total.

Your flaky tool ran 8 times with max_retries=3. Why?

The middleware made 4 calls, returned a failure tool message, and the model decided on its own to call the tool again, starting another cycle of 4. The middleware controls only its own retries. Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model not to retry after a reported failure.

Why was the credit card not masked in the demo?

The card detector checks numbers with the Luhn checksum. An arbitrary digit string fails it, so it was not recognised as a card.

Even with a "do not misuse personal data" prompt, why use PII middleware?

Because sending the data to a third-party provider is itself a compliance issue. Middleware prevents it leaving your boundary at all. Compliance rules come from outside the framework: policy, regulation, certification.

If a tool needs the real value behind a hash, what happens?

A separate lookup outside the model's view resolves the hash when a tool genuinely needs it. The model never sees the real value.

What is the LLM tool emulator for?

Testing. A model fabricates a plausible tool result without running the tool, so you can validate agent logic without cost, risk or side effects. It is not for production.

How should card payments be handled in an agent?

Not through the model. Use a headless tool: a secure payment page the user interacts with directly, outside the model's view.

A production agent appears to hang. How do you debug it?

Check tracing first (LangSmith or equivalent) and look at the last completed step. The usual causes are a tool blocked on a slow external call with no timeout, or an agent that never reaches a stopping condition because no call cap was set. The hardened fix is a tool and model call ceiling in middleware plus real timeouts on external calls, set up before an incident rather than discovered during one.

Chapter 9: Shell tools and custom middleware

Multi-agent: LangChain or LangGraph?

The same agent from the end user's view. LangGraph gives deeper control of the underlying graph. LangChain already supports multi-agent setups. Use LangGraph when you must intervene inside the graph (custom state changes, fine control).

Is the execution graph a DAG?

No. The agentic loop can cycle: model, tool, model again. LangGraph exposes and lets you control that graph; LangChain builds and runs it for you.

Should I use an agent to validate login or session status?

No. That is plain coding. Reserve agents for points that need intelligence or tools. Putting an agent on routine auth is a design mistake.

Does every workflow step cost tokens?

No. Tokens are consumed only when the model is called. Your own Python logic costs nothing, and tool execution triggered by a model decision adds no extra holding cost. Prompt caching reduces cost.

Should one project mix LangChain, LangGraph and other frameworks?

Generally no. Pick one framework and build multiple agents inside it. For separate systems that must talk, connect them with A2A (agent-to-agent) or a plain API.

I edited a transfer amount in HITL and the agent asked for approval again. Why?

That came from the model's judgment, not the framework. After the partial transfer, it reasoned a remaining balance needed handling and asked again. It is not scripted behaviour of HumanInTheLoopMiddleware.

Can an agent reach a remote secured machine (for example Kubernetes) over SSH?

Yes: set the SSH connection as a startup command in the shell tool's configuration, and the agent inherits that access through your connected machine.

Can a browser web app get a terminal like Claude Code?

No. Browsers are sandboxed and cannot reach your file system or terminal, which would be a severe security flaw. You need an installed application (a VS Code extension) or a proper access layer like MCP, never raw browser automation.

Is it safe for an agent to read an OTP to automate a login?

Only through an explicit, legitimate integration (an MCP connection or messaging tool that accesses mail or messages with the user's knowledge). Never by simulating browser or screen automation to intercept an OTP. That is a serious security anti-pattern.

Name the six hooks and which run once.

before_agent, before_model, wrap_model_call, after_model, wrap_tool_call, after_agent. Only before_agent and after_agent run once per invocation; the others run on each pass through the loop.

How do coding assistants edit files?

They have terminal access. A shell tool lets the model request commands, your machine runs them and the output returns as a tool message. The model supplies the brain; execution happens where the agent runs.

Decorator or class middleware?

Decorators for a quick single hook. Classes for several hooks, internal state, sync and async versions and reuse across projects.

before_model vs wrap_model_call?

before_model receives state and runtime and is for observing or setting state. wrap_model_call receives the actual request so you can change the model, messages, tools and settings before calling the handler.

Where would you redact PII, before_agent or before_model?

At before_model, because tools may need the raw value but the model does not. Also check the model's output at after_model.

Where would you open and close a database connection?

Open in before_agent and close in after_agent: each runs exactly once per invocation.

How would you implement cost-aware model selection?

A wrap_model_call that counts messages and calls handler(request.override(model=...)), using a cheap model for short chats and a stronger one past a threshold.

In what order do hooks run with several middlewares?

before and wrap hooks in the declared order. after hooks in reverse, so whatever opened first closes last. The class says wrap_tool_call stays in declared order; I would confirm that with a quick print test.

Why is there no before_tool hook?

A LangChain design choice: wrap_tool_call covers it. ADK exposes separate before and after tool callbacks. Different frameworks make different trade-offs.

A subclass overrides before_model. What happens to the parent's behaviour?

It is replaced. Copy the parent's logic first and add to it, or you lose existing behaviour. You can also add a hook the parent never defined.

Should authentication use an agent?

No. It is routine code. Use agents where intelligence or tool access is needed, not for login or session checks.

When is HostExecutionPolicy acceptable?

For trusted environments such as a personal notebook or dev sandbox. For anything less trusted, use an isolated Docker or sandbox policy so nothing touches the host.

Chapter 10: Runtime and human-in-the-loop

My agent has a response_format and tools. Why does even "hi" come back structured?

Expected. Once structured output is configured the agent always tries to shape its final answer that way. That is separate from a tool's return_direct, which controls whether the tool's raw result skips the model.

Does the order of ToolErrorMiddleware and ToolRetryMiddleware matter?

Yes. Retry has to be resolved before an error is finally reported, so declare retry ahead of error handling. The other way can cause confusing looping rather than "retry a few times, then report".

Is MCP the same as defining tools in LangChain?

In a simple sense, yes: MCP is a collection of tools in a standard protocol. The "agent calls a tool" mechanic does not change. MCP changes how tools are packaged, discovered and shared across applications.

RAG or fine-tuning to keep a model current with changing company policy?

RAG. Fine-tuning is expensive and slow and will not reliably track fast-changing policy. RAG handles frequently updated reference material far better.

Is RAG always needed for agent memory?

No. If you simply persist and look up structured data, a plain database read through LangChain works as well. RAG fits when you retrieve documents by meaning.

How do you cut tokens in a long-running conversation?

Use long-term memory (the store via runtime). Retrieve only memories relevant to the current message instead of loading the whole history. Whether to load everything, load selectively or summarise is a design decision LangChain does not make for you.

Can decorated middleware functions have any name?

Decorator-based: yes, any name, because the decorator registers the hook. Class-based: no, the method name must match the hook it overrides (for example before_model).

What does an interviewer for agentic roles care about?

Software engineering fundamentals and problem solving over memorised syntax. You should explain why code does what it does, including basics such as what Pydantic is for. Someone strong in general development can integrate AI anywhere; the reverse leaves a real gap.

What is runtime, and what are its five components?

Information that is not part of the conversation but travels with the agent into every tool and hook: context, store, stream_writer, execution_info and server_info. Hospital wristband analogy.

What are the four HITL decisions?

approve (run unchanged), edit (change arguments then run), reject (skip, with a reason) and respond (answer without calling the tool, for clarifying questions).

Why does HITL need a checkpointer?

The agent pauses mid-run and resumes later. The checkpointer saves state and the thread_id finds it again. Without them there is nothing to resume.

What does Command(resume=...) do?

It is the answer to an interrupt. Invoke the same thread with it and the agent continues according to the decision.

State vs context?

State is mutable and persists across invocations in a conversation (for example a running count). Context is immutable per run (a user id or credentials). Only state changes carry across tool calls in one invocation.

How does a tool access runtime?

By declaring a runtime: ToolRuntime parameter. It bundles the runtime components with state, config and tool call id. It is hidden from the model's schema. A tool never receives the raw shared store directly.

What do hooks receive?

Node-style hooks (before_model, after_model) get state and runtime as two parameters. Wrap-style hooks (wrap_model_call) get one request object containing both. Names do not matter, position and count do.

How do you personalise the system prompt per user?

A @dynamic_prompt function that reads request.runtime.context and returns a prompt, rebuilt on every call.

How do you interrupt only for large refunds?

Add a when callable to interrupt_on that inspects request.tool_call["args"] and returns True when the amount exceeds the threshold. Small refunds run; large ones pause.

What is respond for, and how is it different from approve?

respond is for tools that are really asking the user something. It skips the tool and feeds the human's message back as if the tool returned it. approve runs the original tool call.

Can an agent change a context value mid-run?

No. Context is immutable per run. If a value must change, it belongs in state.

Why not give tools the raw runtime object?

LangChain deliberately controls what each component receives. Tools get ToolRuntime, so they see only what they are explicitly handed.

Why might an agent ask for approval twice after you edit an amount?

That is the model's own judgment: after a partial transfer it decided a remaining balance needed handling. It is not scripted behaviour of the middleware.

When do you stop using HITL's interrupt_on shortcuts and write custom middleware?

For needs the middleware does not offer, such as two levels of sign-off. Then write custom middleware (Chapter 9).

What is the difference between an agent's thread_id and its context?

thread_id scopes conversation history: it persists automatically across calls that share it, through the checkpointer. context carries per-run data (a user id, session details) that you must pass fresh on every invocation; it does not carry over like history. Mixing them up is a common real bug once an app has several users.

Chapter 10A: Streaming agent output (from the docs)

What are the three stream modes in the LangChain agents docs?

updates (state after each step), messages (token plus metadata from any LLM node) and custom (data your own code writes with the stream writer).

How do you stream tokens?

stream_mode="messages". Each item has the token and metadata, and metadata["langgraph_node"] says where it came from.

How does a tool report progress?

It calls get_stream_writer() and writes values, which arrive in custom mode. It only works inside a LangGraph run.

What does version="v2" change?

Every chunk becomes a dict with type, ns and data, so you branch on type instead of unpacking tuples. invoke(version="v2") returns a GraphOutput with .value and .interrupts. Needs LangGraph 1.1 or later.

How do you stream a sub-agent's output and know who is speaking?

Set name= on each agent, pass subgraphs=True to stream(), and read lc_agent_name from the metadata.

How do you get complete tool calls while streaming?

Use ["messages", "updates"], or add the tool_call_chunks together and finish when chunk_position == "last", then read tool_calls.

Why is event streaming "typed projections" better than stream modes?

Each projection (messages, tool calls, values, sub-agents) is its own iterator, so a component consumes only what it needs without branching on mode strings. You can also drain a projection to get the final value, or interleave several in arrival order.

A user's email appears in a live stream even though you redact in after_model. Why?

Redacting state does not touch tokens already sent to a live reader. Use PIIMiddleware with apply_to_output=True, which also registers a stream transformer so streamed text, tool arguments, outputs and snapshots are redacted before they are delivered.

When would you write a custom transformer?

When you need a projection the built-ins do not offer, for example retrieval progress or artifacts. Pass it in transformers=[...] or ship it from middleware, then read stream.extensions[...].

Chapter 11: Why MCP exists

How is MCP different from calling a REST API directly?

The end result can be the same, but with a raw API you maintain the wrapper, auth and error handling in every project. With MCP, the server owner maintains it once and every AI host just connects a client.

Is MCP an orchestrator?

No. It is a connection protocol between a host and external tools. It does not plan or sequence agent behaviour.

How is MCP different from RAG?

They are unrelated ways to give a model context. RAG retrieves text and injects it into a prompt. MCP lets a model call tools and actions on external systems.

Can one server extend another, like inheritance?

Not in a code sense, but a server can contain an MCP client internally and forward requests to another server. Possible, not common.

How is a server deployed?

Like any other server: a plain process, a Docker container or a cloud service such as Cloud Run or AKS. MCP mandates no deployment method.

Can tool access be limited per user role?

In principle yes. The client requests the tool list, so the server can check the caller's auth token or scope before deciding which tools to return. MCP does not prescribe it; you build the check.

A company already has 25 to 30 working APIs. Why build an MCP server on top?

AI hosts speak MCP natively. Without a server, every team wanting AI to use those APIs writes and maintains its own wrapper, the duplication MCP exists to remove.

Do I need MCP for a small project?

Maybe not yet. One app and a handful of tools with nobody else reusing them is fine with plain function calling. MCP starts paying off once more than one app or team needs the same tool.

Is MCP an Anthropic product I pay for?

No. It is a free, open specification, now governed by a multi-company foundation. OpenAI and Google support it even though Anthropic built it first. "Agreed" is the key word: a protocol is a shared agreement, a library only works if everyone adopts one company's code.

What problem does MCP solve?

Function calling made every company wrap, authenticate and maintain the same tools on its own. At scale that is duplicated work that breaks when APIs change. MCP standardises the connection so the provider maintains one server and every host speaks to it the same way.

Define host, client and server.

The host is the AI application a person uses. The client is created inside the host and holds a dedicated 1:1 connection to one server. The server exposes tools, resources and prompts.

What are the three primitives?

Tools (actions that do something), resources (read-only data to read) and prompts (reusable templates that shape a request).

Which transports does MCP use?

STDIO for local servers and Streamable HTTP for remote ones. Streamable HTTP replaced HTTP plus SSE, deprecated in the March 2025 spec. The messages are JSON-RPC 2.0.

Why does each server get its own client?

Decoupling, safety (a crash stays contained), scalability (load is local to the pair) and parallelism (talk to several servers at once).

Why not just keep using function calling?

For one app and a few tools, you can. Beyond that the maintenance, auth and breakage burden repeats per team. MCP moves it to whoever owns the server.

Why is MCP not "USB-C for AI"?

The instructor felt it oversimplifies. An MCP server is a collection of tools (mostly) wrapped around existing APIs, plus resources and prompts, behind a shared protocol that decides who maintains what.

What is MCP Inspector?

A browser tool that connects to any MCP server (acting as host and client) so you can list and call its tools without a full AI app. Start it with uv run fastmcp dev server.py.

Resource vs tool?

A resource is read-only reference data with no side effects, like a thermostat display. A tool runs an action and has an effect. Use a resource when many clients need the same reference data, so there is one source of truth.

MCP versus RAG?

Different mechanisms. RAG retrieves text and injects it into the prompt. MCP is a protocol for calling tools and actions on external systems. They are not usually compared directly.

What hidden cost comes with connecting many MCP servers?

The tool list from every server is sent on the first message, so tokens balloon (tens of thousands with two servers in the demo) and the agent can get confused. Reduce it with clear descriptions and by filtering tools with middleware.

How would you restrict a tool to some users?

Check the caller's auth token or scope in the server before returning the tool list or running the tool. MCP does not prescribe this; you build it.

Is MCP an orchestrator?

No. It is a communication protocol between host and external tools. It does not decide what happens next.

Why do OpenAI and Google support a protocol Anthropic created?

Because it is an open specification governed by a multi-company foundation. A protocol only works as an agreement everyone adopts, unlike a single company's library.

How does an agent discover MCP servers and their capabilities?

It does not "find" them. Servers come from configuration or an allow-listed registry. The initialize handshake has both sides declare capabilities, and tools/list returns each tool's name, description and schema, which is exactly what the model sees. Tool descriptions are prompt input, so pin and review them like code.

Chapter 12: MCP primitives, lifecycle, JSON-RPC

Can one MCP server call another?

Yes. A server can act as a client to another server internally, chaining them.

Is FastMCP the only way to build a server?

No. It is the most popular, alongside Anthropic's official MCP SDK. The relationship is like Keras on top of TensorFlow: the official SDK is the base and FastMCP makes building on it easier.

I already have REST APIs and a chatbot. Why build an MCP server?

The scalability maths. Connecting N applications to M tool sets means roughly N times M custom integrations. MCP standardises to about N plus M. It was candidly acknowledged that MCP can feel like needless abstraction over an API call; the value is making access usable by non-technical end users and cutting integration burden at scale.

How does a client know which server to connect to?

The address is given when the client is configured (like pasting a URL into "Add custom connector"). It is not discovered dynamically at connection time.

How does a server know which client a request came from?

That is resolved inside the transport layer: once connected, both sides keep session details internally, like any client-server connection, abstracted from the user.

How do I make my own email domain MCP compatible?

You cannot make an existing product inherently compatible. You build a normal MCP server for it exposing the tools, resources and prompts that make sense.

What are the three MCP lifecycle phases?

Initialization (handshake and capability exchange), operation (the real work) and shutdown (closing the connection, usually initiated by the client).

What are the three handshake steps?

The client sends initialize with an id, protocol version and capabilities. The server responds with the same id, its version, capabilities and name. The client sends an initialized notification with no id, which expects no reply.

What is the id field for?

It matches a response to its request. Responses can arrive asynchronously and out of order, so without an id you cannot tell which answers which.

Which primitive lets the AI act?

Tools. Resources are read by the application and prompts are chosen by the user or app, so the tool is the one the model decides to use.

Why JSON-RPC instead of REST?

Lightweight JSON, transport-agnostic (STDIO or HTTP), two-way so a server can initiate (for example progress on long tasks), notifications with no id, and standard error codes.

JSON-RPC two-way vs asynchronous vs WebSocket?

Async means the client fires and continues but the server never initiates. Two-way means either side can initiate. A WebSocket is a persistent open connection, which is heavier; two-way is a protocol property and does not require it.

How does version negotiation work?

The client sends the latest version it supports. If the server supports it, it echoes it. Otherwise it replies with its latest and the client decides if that is acceptable. With no overlap, they disconnect. Never send a list.

Is JSON-RPC an MCP invention?

No. It is an existing general-purpose spec that Anthropic adopted because it fit.

What does a client do first after connecting?

Calls the list functions (tools/list, resources/list, prompts/list) to learn what the server offers before using any of it.

Can a server serve more than one client?

Yes. A client has exactly one server, but a remote server typically serves many clients. Local STDIO servers typically serve one.

Why might a connector show a warning icon before you use it?

At startup the host initialises every configured server. If the handshake fails, it already knows and flags it.

Why must a serious custom client think about older protocol versions?

Versions can behave differently, like WhatsApp message deletion across versions. A production client must decide which versions it supports and handle each behavioural difference, not just connect to any URL.

What can be sent before the handshake completes?

Only pings: the client before the server responds to initialize, and the server before it receives initialized.

What is the business case for MCP in numbers?

N applications by M tool sets means about N times M custom integrations. A standard protocol reduces that to about N plus M, because any compliant host talks to any compliant server.

Chapter 13: Capability negotiation and operation

How do we restrict specific tools for specific users in an MCP setup?

That is not an MCP-architecture concern. It is ordinary software engineering, solved with middleware (the guardrail and dynamic tool loading patterns from earlier chapters), not a built-in MCP feature.

Can I create my own MCP server inside Claude?

No. You can connect your own server to Claude, but Claude is not where you build and host one.

Does calling an MCP tool cost LLM tokens?

No. A tool call is a plain client-server transaction. Tokens are spent only when the model is invoked to reason or generate.

Does MCP have built-in caching?

Not by default as far as could be confirmed live. If you want caching, build it separately.

Are Claude's "connectors" the same as MCP servers?

Yes. Claude uses friendlier words ("connectors", "tools") for a general audience to avoid confusing non-technical users.

Should I claim a "production-grade" AI project on my resume if it was not deployed at scale?

Describe it honestly and frame it around the real problem it solved, not the technology. Interviewers care about problem-solving depth, and shallow claims are exposed quickly under questioning.

What is capability negotiation?

Both sides declare what they are capable of so each knows what it may ask for later. Client capabilities include roots, sampling, elicitation, tasks and experimental. Server capabilities include tools, resources, prompts, logging, completions and experimental.

What is elicitation?

A server requesting additional information from the user, through the client, mid-interaction. In LangChain it appears as a LangGraph interrupt that a human answers before the run resumes.

What are the two steps of the operation phase?

Discovery (tools/list, automatic and free) and calling (tools/call, needing a tool name and arguments).

Does discovery cost tokens?

No. No LLM is involved. It is just the client asking the server what it offers.

Why call tools/list if negotiation already says there are tools?

Negotiation confirms tools exist as a category. Discovery retrieves which tools, their descriptions and argument schemas.

Elicitation vs HITL?

HITL is an approval layer over tool calls (approve, edit, reject, respond). Elicitation is a native MCP mechanism for the server to request missing information from the client and user.

Are we exposing data to the LLM with MCP?

Yes. Tool results flow client to host to model provider. That is why you restrict what a connection can see (for example locked notes), and use PII middleware and guardrails on custom clients.

What does a good tool definition contain?

A name, a description and an input schema. The description quality decides whether the model picks the right tool.

How should a client handle old and new servers?

Try the newer handshake, fall back to the older one on an error, and explicitly support both. Most servers take 8 months to a year to migrate.

Claude Desktop's logs used to show full JSON and now do not. Did the protocol change?

No. The client changed how much it writes to disk (from 26 June 2026 it logs only a terse summary). It is unrelated to the MCP version. The wiretap script recovers the full conversation.

How does the wiretap work?

It sits between Claude Desktop and the real server. Claude Desktop launches the wiretap, which launches the real server and relays every byte unchanged while printing each message. You put the real command after -- in the config.

How would you build a vulnerability agent when connectors are locked down?

A custom self-hosted MCP server, possibly containerised, so sensitive data never leaves the organisation through a third-party connector.

A multi-service no-code workflow dropped some stories. Why?

The model made its own undocumented assumption about how many items to include. Be explicit about the detail wanted in the prompt, and test.

Is "brain decides, tools act" still true across many services?

Yes. The model decides which tool, arguments and how to interpret results. Data movement only happens through tool calls.

How do you tell tool failures apart from empty results?

Three outcomes: success with data, success but explicitly empty ({"count": 0, "items": []}), and failure as a result with isError: true and an actionable message. Bad parameters are protocol-level JSON-RPC errors. Never return {"error": ...} as a success. Monitor with a per-tool ok, empty, error metric, because tool errors still arrive as HTTP 200.

Chapter 14: Shutdown, transports, first server

If an agent talks to a database-backed MCP server, is one tool needed per read operation?

Yes. One tool per meaningful operation (get profile, get transactions), with the model choosing at runtime which best matches the request.

Why does an LLM call list_recipes first instead of get_recipe?

It only learns that get_recipe exists through discovery (tools/list), and it does not know valid ids until it lists them. At real scale there could be thousands of records, not three.

How does an LLM know what kind of file a resource holds?

Through the resource's declared MIME type, the same web concept: plain text, PDF, audio, video and so on.

Should I name frameworks like FastMCP in an interview?

Concepts first. Knowing why MCP is structured as it is, and the legacy vs modern history, separates real understanding from the many who can define an MCP server but cannot explain what happens underneath.

Does the language (Python or Node) matter for a good MCP server?

No. The protocol does not care. The choice comes from your team's stack.

How does MCP shutdown work?

Through the transport layer, with no JSON-RPC messages. STDIO: the client stops sending input, sends a terminate signal and, as a last resort, kill. Streamable HTTP: close the HTTP connection.

STDIO vs Streamable HTTP?

STDIO runs a server as a sub-process on the same machine over stdin and stdout: fast, secure, simple, local only. Streamable HTTP is POST requests to /mcp over the internet: reachable anywhere, serves many clients, needs real auth.

What endpoint does Streamable HTTP use?

A single endpoint, almost always /mcp, with the JSON-RPC message in the POST body.

What does @mcp.tool do?

Registers the function as a tool and handles tools/list and tools/call from its signature and docstring. @mcp.resource and @mcp.prompt do the same for the other primitives.

Why does shutdown depend on the transport and not JSON-RPC?

JSON-RPC defines what is said. Closing the connection is about how the parties are connected. On a phone call you hang up; on WhatsApp you close the internet. Same language, different ending.

FastMCP vs the official SDK?

The official mcp SDK is correct but verbose (hand-written list_tools, nested if/elif). Jeremiah Lowin (Prefect) built FastMCP to make it easy, and a version was folded into the official SDK. Like Keras and TensorFlow.

Is FastMCP from the FastAPI team?

No. Unrelated projects with similar naming. They work well together.

Why add a resource listing valid tags?

A model cannot know valid values that only appear inside tool results. The resource lets it learn them upfront so a vague request maps to a real tag.

What if the HTTP server closes unexpectedly?

It signals something went wrong server-side. A good client attempts to reconnect gracefully rather than failing silently.

Why is shutdown "almost always" client-initiated in STDIO?

The client launched the server as a sub-process and owns its lifecycle. The server can close its own output stream and exit, but that is rare.

Can STDIO ever work across machines?

Not by default: it needs a parent and sub-process on one machine. Only if proxied through something else.

How do you get a local server in front of a remote agent?

Tunnel it (for example ngrok) to a real internet URL for testing, or deploy it properly to a cloud host (Chapter 16).

How do you register a custom server in Claude Desktop?

uv run fastmcp install claude-desktop server.py, which writes a config entry with "transport": "stdio" and a uv run --with fastmcp fastmcp run <file> command.

Why show the legacy approach at all?

So its pain is felt, and because that code still appears in real companies.

Chapter 15: The Time Tracker project

For deployed production APIs, auto-convert or build manually?

Auto-conversion is the faster, safer start because it does not touch trusted production code. Go manual once you need finer control: better descriptions, combined calls or prompts.

If I have 5 connectors, do they all go in one config file?

Yes. Each connector is its own server entry and the host starts each independently, like multiple servers running side by side.

Is GitHub to Horizon like a Java developer deploying to Kubernetes?

Conceptually yes: take working local code and make it a reachable running service, but through a platform built for MCP servers rather than a general container orchestrator.

Will authorisation be added?

Yes, as a next step once hosted. A publicly reachable time-tracking server for a real company needs real access control.

Is writing code without AI help expected in interviews?

Not in this course. AI-assisted coding is treated as a normal professional skill. What matters is understanding the architecture and decisions well enough to explain and defend them.

Connectors vs config file?

Connectors are the friendly UI. The config file is what actually holds the entries for both. Developers edit it to run a local server that has no public URL.

Who decides which tool to call?

The model, through the client. The server only executes the tools/call it receives.

How do you auto-convert an API to MCP?

FastMCP.from_fastapi(app) with the existing FastAPI app. Every endpoint becomes a tool.

Auto-convert or manual: how do you choose?

Auto-convert when the goal is quick access to trusted APIs. Manual when you need combined calls, richer AI-oriented descriptions or prompts. Teams often prefer manual so they do not edit deployed APIs.

What does auto-conversion not give you?

Prompts, resources, custom descriptions and tools that combine several calls.

How do you mount an MCP server inside FastAPI?

mcp_app = mcp.http_app(path="/"), create FastAPI(lifespan=mcp_app.lifespan), then app.mount("/mcp", mcp_app).

How do you deploy to Horizon?

Put only the server files (main.py, database.py, pyproject.toml, uv.lock) in a clean GitHub repo, sign in with GitHub, select it, set the entrypoint main.py:mcp, and deploy. The URL looks like your-project.fastmcp.app/mcp.

Why might Claude Desktop not show your local server?

Commonly a bare uv or python in the config. Claude does not know where it is installed, so use the full path from which uv.

Why path="/" and not "/mcp"?

app.mount("/mcp", ...) already adds the prefix, so using /mcp in both would double it into /mcp/mcp.

What does the Mcp-Session-Id header do?

The server returns it on initialize, and the client sends it on later requests so the server can tell sessions apart over HTTP.

Why is a hand-built MCP layer sometimes safer in a company?

It leaves already-deployed, trusted API code untouched, while still letting you write richer AI-facing descriptions and prompts.

What breaks if you host with a local SQLite file on a serverless platform?

Data can disappear when the function goes cold. A real hosted database is needed for durability.

Chapter 16: Deploying servers, building a client

Is a third-party Postgres MCP server on my laptop really "local"?

Yes. "Local" describes where the MCP server process runs, not where the data lives. A Postgres MCP server started with npx on a laptop is local even though it calls a remote database, like a browser being local while websites are not.

Where do the tools inside a Postgres MCP server come from?

From whoever built it. A vendor or community writes execute and list_tables once, packages them as an MCP server, and everyone who runs it gets them without understanding the driver.

Always MCP, or sometimes a plain tool?

A plain tool is often right for a narrow, fixed action such as sending an email through one channel. MCP earns its place for breadth: supporting a large surface without hand-building dozens of tools.

One setup for several databases (Postgres, Oracle, a mainframe)?

Two options: one custom MCP server with all of them wired in, or an MCP gateway that aggregates several existing servers behind a single entry point so the client connects to one place.

How do I stop an AI from modifying production data?

A common pattern is an environment variable read at startup (for example READ_ONLY=true) that controls which tools the server even registers. Write tools are never exposed, rather than blocked afterwards.

uv vs uvx?

uv works inside your project. uvx runs a tool in an isolated temporary environment without touching the project, like npx. Use uvx for one-off tools.

Does the host platform care whether my server calls an AI model?

No. A call to an LLM provider is just another API call. A generic platform does not distinguish.

How do I keep state per call, per thread and per application?

Application-wide state lives as long as the process. Session state ties to a client-provided session id. Thread-level state is the hardest and has no free built-in mechanism, so you must design how a thread or request owns its context.

Why do shared MCP servers run over HTTP?

A STDIO server is only usable by whatever launched it. HTTP is reachable by many clients from anywhere, at the cost of a network round trip.

fastmcp run vs uvicorn main:app?

fastmcp run starts only the MCP server over STDIO. uvicorn main:app starts the whole app (website, API and mounted MCP endpoint).

What does a hosting platform need from your repo?

main.py, database.py, pyproject.toml and uv.lock: the code plus the dependency list and exact pinned versions.

Does MCP need an API underneath?

No. A calculator with a plain add function is a valid MCP server.

Why is your local database unaffected by the deployed one?

They are separate files and separate data. A .gitignored local database never ships, and the server creates its own.

Why must the client, not the model, call the tool?

The model only emits which tool and arguments. The client holds the connection to the server, so it executes call_tool and feeds the result back. MCP standardises how that travels; it does not change who does it.

What is harness engineering?

Building the layer that connects a raw model to tools: the loop, tool formatting, execution and message handling. Every chat application is one.

How do you let several databases sit behind one MCP entry point?

Either one custom server wiring them all, or an MCP gateway that aggregates existing servers behind one endpoint.

How do you stop an agent from writing to a production database?

Register only read tools at startup when a flag such as READ_ONLY=true is set, so write tools are never offered.

Is a Postgres MCP server running on my laptop local or remote?

Local: the server process runs on your machine. The data it queries may be remote.

Why might a deployed server lose data?

SQLite on a serverless host can lose its file when the function goes cold, and it is a local file rather than a shared database. Use a hosted database.

What are the two honest gaps in this project?

A local SQLite file instead of a hosted production database, and synchronous database calls so two requests cannot run at the same time.

Plain tool or MCP?

A plain tool for a narrow fixed action. MCP for breadth where you would otherwise hand-build and maintain many tools.

How do you run an MCP server with several replicas when sessions are stateful?

Prefer running stateless (stateless_http=True) so any replica serves any request. Otherwise use sticky routing on Mcp-Session-Id at the ingress (not sessionAffinity: ClientIP), or a shared session store such as Redis. Test with two or more replicas and a multi-turn conversation.

How do you make a money-moving tool safe across retries and crashes?

An idempotency key as a tool argument, stored in the same database transaction as the transfer so a repeat returns the stored result, and balances re-checked at execution time rather than at approval.

How do you scope OAuth for sensitive tools?

One tool, one scope (payments:read differs from payments:transfer). Check the scope on every call, filter tools/list by scope, return 403 insufficient_scope and trigger step-up plus human approval. Tokens are short-lived and audience-bound to one server; downstream APIs get a token exchange, never passthrough.

A server changes a tool's parameters. How do you avoid breaking agents?

Only additive changes in place; breaking changes ship as a new tool name alongside the old. Restart agents or handle tools/list_changed, run the eval suite because descriptions change routing, and diff tools/list snapshots in CI.

Chapter 17: Legacy vs modern MCP

Should I worry about mastering every previous MCP version?

No. Modern adoption will take time, and understanding legacy deeply is what makes the modern one make sense.

Is sampling controlled by my code or called automatically?

By the tool's own code. If its logic needs a completion, it calls the provider (now directly). The framework does not trigger it automatically.

Are sampling and elicitation MCP concepts or framework features?

Both are part of the MCP specification. A framework like FastMCP provides the implementation.

Does LangChain's MCP support let me create servers?

No. It only consumes existing servers as a tool source for an agent. Creating servers is for libraries like FastMCP.

Does LangChain-as-host still do the handshake?

Yes. The adapter builds the harness and client for you, but the same handshake and discovery happen underneath.

Will an OpenRouter key work for the client exercises?

Yes, with a small change to point at the right endpoint and model string. The pattern does not change.

What is the central difference between legacy and modern MCP?

Legacy remembers the client with a session handshake and Mcp-Session-Id. Modern has no session: every message carries its own context, so any server can handle it.

Will my existing servers break?

No. Modern adoption is opt-in and legacy keeps working. Deprecated features have a twelve-month minimum before removal is even eligible.

What do Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name do?

They are HTTP headers on each request that let load balancers route by glancing at the method and name, instead of reading the body.

Why did elicitation, ping and sampling break?

They relied on the persistent two-way session. The modern revision is stateless with no back-channel, so a server cannot send an unsolicited request to the client.

How do you fix each?

Sampling was deleted: have the tool call the LLM provider directly. Elicitation and ping: create the client with mode="legacy", or for elicitation use the modern InputRequiredResult re-invocation pattern.

When can a server ask the user a question in modern MCP?

Only while handling a request the client already sent, and the reply must contain a real question. Think of the kitchen sending a waiter back, not asking an empty table.

How does a question get answered if a different server picks up the reply?

Like an OTP at checkout: the answer is submitted with a reference that carries everything needed, so any backend can complete the order.

What do ttlMs and cacheScope do?

ttlMs sets how long a server's answer stays fresh in milliseconds. cacheScope says whether it is safe to share across users or private to one.

Why is stateless better for scale?

A stateful system can only be handled by whoever met the client first. Stateless requests can go to any server, so you can add servers behind a load balancer without anyone needing to remember a client.

Deprecated vs removed?

Removed means gone (old handshake, ping, logging/setLevel, the old session header). Deprecated still works on a timeline (Roots, Sampling, Logging, HTTP plus SSE) with a minimum twelve months.

The spec says twelve months but my SDK dropped a feature. Contradiction?

No. Twelve months is the spec's promise. A specific library's maintainers can remove the code sooner, as FastMCP did with sampling.

What does async with client as client guarantee?

That the connection is closed (step 5) no matter what, including on an error. It is the same five steps as a manual try/finally, in one line.

Where does ANTHROPIC_API_KEY need to live after the sampling change?

In the server process, because the tool now calls the provider itself. For a stdio subprocess, pass it explicitly in the transport's env, because the subprocess environment is isolated.

How does LangChain relate to FastMCP and the SDK?

LangChain MCP Adapters build the client on FastMCP, which sits on the official MCP Python SDK. LangChain only consumes servers; it does not build them.

What changed in the latest MCP spec, and how does it affect running servers?

The 2026-07-28 spec is stateless: no initialize handshake (version and capabilities travel in _meta on every request), no Mcp-Session-Id, so any replica serves any request, and cross-call state becomes a handle returned by tools. Roots, sampling, logging, HTTP plus SSE and dynamic client registration are deprecated, replaced by tool parameters, direct provider calls, OpenTelemetry or stderr, Streamable HTTP and Client ID Metadata Documents. Most production servers still run 2025-11-25.

Chapter 18: MCP inside LangChain

How does a LangChain agent use an MCP server?

Through an adapter. It connects, discovers the server's tools and returns them as ordinary LangChain tools that you pass to create_agent. The agent is the host and LangChain builds the client.

Can LangChain build MCP servers?

No. Its MCP support consumes existing servers as tool sources. Building servers is for libraries such as FastMCP.

How do you test an MCP tool without a model?

Call it directly with await tool.ainvoke({...}) on a tool from list_tools(). That proves the server works before adding an agent.

What is the difference between a tool error and a transport error?

A tool that ran and failed (isError=True) becomes a ToolMessage with status="error", which the agent can read and correct. A transport or session failure raises an exception because nothing came back to convert.

How do you require approval for dangerous MCP tools?

Read the server's annotations (such as destructive_hint) from tool.metadata, build the interrupt_on dictionary for HumanInTheLoopMiddleware from those tools, and pass the middleware to create_agent. The server decides what is dangerous.

How does elicitation work with LangChain?

The adapter converts a server's request for more input into a LangGraph interrupt(). A human answers outside the graph, and you resume with Command(resume=...). The tool call is retried with the answer.

MCPConfig or ClientGroup?

MCPConfig makes one aggregate connection with prefixed tool names and a shared protocol era, so the fleet negotiates down to the oldest. ClientGroup keeps independent connections with {server}_{tool} names, each with its own era and auth. Use a group for mixed fleets.

Where do you configure authentication?

On the FastMCP Client (bearer token string, "oauth" or an OAuth object with storage), not on MCPAdapter. Use a client group to give each server its own auth.

What does the built-in module not support that the older package does?

Resources, prompts and tool-call interceptors (and progress callbacks are not in the reviewed public surface). The new module adds automatic elicitation and metadata namespacing, and is still beta.

How would you advise a client choosing between them?

If they need resources, prompts or interceptors today, use langchain-mcp-adapters. If they only need tools and are starting fresh, use langchain.mcp, accepting beta churn. Do not frame it as old versus new, because the new one is not a superset yet.

Why must the agent run inside the async with block?

The tools hold the client. When the context exits, the connection closes and the tools stop working.

What happens with an audio result?

AudioContent is not yet supported and raises NotImplementedError.

A destructive filter selects nothing, so dangerous tools run without approval. How do you debug it?

Print tool.metadata for each tool and the helper's result, and compare. The notebook itself shows destructive_hint: True in the raw metadata next to a helper result of False, so never assume the filter works. Fix the lookup until the dangerous tool is selected, and add a test for it.

Chapter 19: Multi-agent patterns

Why multi-agent at all?

A single agent with many tools and one long prompt struggles to choose between similar tools and hold unrelated domains in context. Splitting into focused specialists keeps each simple and independently testable.

Name the five patterns.

Subagents, handoffs, skills, router and custom workflow.

Subagents vs handoffs vs router?

Subagents: a supervisor agent calls other agents as tools, deciding turn by turn. Handoffs: one agent's prompt and tools change with state. Router: one classification step fans out to specialists in parallel and then synthesises.

When would you choose skills?

When one agent has many possible specialisations and most are irrelevant to any request. It loads descriptions up front and full content on demand, so context stays small and teams can maintain skills independently.

How does a handoff work in practice?

A custom state field (such as current_step) selects the system prompt and tool list in wrap_model_call, and tools return Command objects that update the data and the step. It is the same agent in a different configuration each step.

How are parallel router results combined?

Send dispatches to each specialist, and a reducer such as Annotated[list[str], operator.add] merges their outputs into shared state before a synthesis step.

Tool per agent or a single dispatch tool?

Tool per agent for a few subagents you tune individually, with fine control and more setup. A single task(agent_name, description) tool for many agents or distributed teams, with simpler composition and less per-agent customisation.

Sync or async subagents?

Sync when the next step depends on the result or failures should block. Async when the work is independent and the user should not be frozen.

Which pattern is cheapest for a repeat request, and why?

Handoffs and skills (about 5 calls for a repeat against 8 for subagents), because they are stateful: once a step or skill is active, repeat requests skip re-routing or re-loading. Subagents repeat the whole flow each time.

Which pattern wins for three parallel topics?

Subagents and router (about 5 calls and 9K tokens each), because they parallelise. Handoffs would need 7 or more calls and 14K or more tokens, and skills load about 15K tokens.

Can you combine patterns?

Yes. A subagents system can have a router inside a sub-agent, a handoffs stage can use skills, and a subagent can wrap a custom workflow. Choose per sub-problem.

What is the weakness of skills?

They rely on prompting to guide usage, not hard constraints, and loading adds an extra round trip the first time. Enforcing order needs custom logic.

How can you test multi-agent wiring without calling a model?

Use a scripted fake chat model that plays back predetermined AIMessages with tool calls. The graph, tools, state updates and checkpoints still run for real. Only the model's wording is scripted.

Chapter 20: Meridian AI project tour

What does Meridian do?

Two things: answer questions about uploaded documents using RAG, and audit a purchase request with risk, tax and control agents plus a CFO memo that decides approved, conditional hold or rejected.

Why split the code into many files?

So each file has one job: findable, testable in isolation, no duplication and no clashes between people. The web layer does not know about AI, and the AI code does not know about web addresses.

State the dependency rule.

api depends on rag and agent, which depend on config and logger. Dependencies go one way, downwards.

Which audit tools exist and what does each agent do?

Risk: check_sanctions_list and get_vendor_credit_score. Tax: calculate_cross_border_tax and validate_fx_hedge. Control: categorize_expense. A final CFO step (a plain LLM call) writes the memo.

Which multi-agent pattern is the audit, and how would you improve it?

It is a fixed sequential pipeline (closer to a custom workflow) with plain Python orchestration, not a subagents supervisor. The three checks are independent, so a router that fans out in parallel then synthesises would cut latency.

How trustworthy is the audit?

It is a demo. The checks come from the model's general knowledge, and only the FX check uses a live source. It must not be used as a real compliance tool.

How is this project tested without cloud accounts?

The tests in backend/tests are written to need no accounts, using test fixtures instead of live services.

The agent in one picture

from langchain.agents import create_agent

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",              # "provider:model", any model you can access
    tools=[get_weather],                 # functions or @tool functions
    system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant",
    checkpointer=InMemorySaver(),        # memory (needs a thread_id when invoking)
    middleware=[...],                    # control (call limits, HITL, PII, custom)
    response_format=MySchema,            # structured final answer
    context_schema=MyContext,            # immutable per-run data
    store=my_store,                      # long-term memory
)
agent.invoke({"messages": [("user", "Weather in Delhi?")]},
             config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "t1"}},
             context=MyContext(user_id="u1"))

Agent = Model + Harness. An agent is a model calling tools in a loop until the task is done. The model never runs a tool; the agent does. (Ch 1, Ch 2)

The raw loop

for _ in range(max_turns):
    msg = model.invoke(messages)                   # with tools bound
    if not msg.tool_calls: return msg.content      # plain text = final answer
    messages.append(msg)
    for call in msg.tool_calls:                    # the CODE runs the tool
        messages.append(ToolMessage(content=str(tools[call["name"]](**call["args"])),
                                    tool_call_id=call["id"]))

Models and messages (Ch 3)

Need Use
A model init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5.5", temperature=0.5, max_tokens=1000, timeout=30, max_retries=6)
Messages SystemMessage, HumanMessage, AIMessage, ToolMessage
One answer / progress / many .invoke() / .stream() / .batch() (batch_as_completed for results as they finish)
Exact cost response.usage_metadata
Show a tool, do not run it model.bind_tools([f]), then read response.tool_calls (empty content)
Teach by example Few-shot: prior Human and AI message pairs

Batching does not save tokens. It saves cost and time (provider batch APIs, fewer round trips).

Structured output (Ch 4)

class Booking(BaseModel):
    action: Literal["book", "cancel"]
    seats: int = Field(default=1, ge=1, le=10, description="Number of seats")

model.with_structured_output(Booking)                    # on a model
create_agent(..., response_format=ToolStrategy(schema=Union[A, B]))   # several intents
ProviderStrategy ToolStrategy
How The provider's native feature A synthetic tool call
Where Supported models only Almost any tool-calling model

Validation errors go back to the model, which retries. A raw model cannot do tools and a schema together; an agent can.

Tools (Ch 5)

@tool(args_schema=Input)             # docstring is the description the model reads
def book_seats(...): ...

@tool
def f(x: str, runtime: ToolRuntime) -> str:      # hidden from the model
    runtime.context.user_id; runtime.store.get(...); runtime.state
  • Never name an argument config or runtime (fails at runtime).
  • return_direct skips the model's final pass.
  • Server-side tools run on the provider; headless tools run on the user's device.

Memory (Ch 6, Ch 10)

Need Use
One conversation Checkpointer plus thread_id
Facts across conversations Store
Mutable data that persists in a thread State (custom AgentState fields)
Immutable per-run data Context
Repeated expensive calls Cache with a TTL by data volatility

Middleware (Ch 7 to Ch 9)

Hook Runs Use
before_agent / after_agent Once Setup / teardown
before_model / after_model Every loop pass Observe or change state; redact input, check output
wrap_model_call Every loop pass Rewrite the request: filter tools, swap model
wrap_tool_call Every loop pass Wrap a tool execution

Before and wrap hooks run in declared order. After hooks run in reverse.

Built-in Remember
SummarizationMiddleware model (can be cheaper), trigger, keep
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware Needs a checkpointer. approve, edit, reject, respond. Resume with Command(resume={"decisions": [...]})
ToolCallLimitMiddleware run_limit (one invoke), thread_limit (conversation)
ModelFallbackMiddleware Switches only on hard failure
PIIMiddleware block, redact, mask, hash; custom detector with a regex or function
TodoListMiddleware A maintained structured plan
LLMToolSelectorMiddleware Filters tools by the query; always_include
Tool retry delay = initial_delay × backoff_factor ^ retry_number; max_retries counts retries after the first call
LLMToolEmulator Fake tool results for testing

Guardrail is the goal. Middleware is the mechanism.

MCP (Ch 11 to Ch 17)

from fastmcp import FastMCP
mcp = FastMCP("Server")

@mcp.tool
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int: """Add two numbers."""; return a + b
@mcp.resource("file://notes")
def notes() -> str: ...
@mcp.prompt
def template(x: str) -> str: ...

mcp.run()                                   # STDIO (local)
mcp_app = mcp.http_app(path="/")            # HTTP: path "/" because mount adds the prefix
app = FastAPI(lifespan=mcp_app.lifespan)    # lifespan at construction
app.mount("/mcp", mcp_app)
Topic Remember
Architecture Host, then one client per server (1:1), then server
Primitives Tools (do), resources (read only), prompts (template). Each has list
Message format JSON-RPC 2.0. id matches response to request. No id means notification
Lifecycle Initialization, operation, shutdown
Handshake initialize (id), response (same id), initialized (no id)
Negotiation Each side declares capabilities. Latest version only, never a list
Operation Discovery tools/list (automatic, free), calling tools/call (name plus arguments)
Shutdown No JSON-RPC. STDIO: stop input, terminate, kill. HTTP: close the connection
Transports STDIO (local, fast, secure) and Streamable HTTP (POST /mcp, remote)
Auto-convert an API FastMCP.from_fastapi(app). No prompts, resources or custom descriptions
Deploy Clean repo (main.py, database.py, pyproject.toml, uv.lock), entry point main.py:mcp
Install in Claude Desktop uv run fastmcp install claude-desktop server.py (use which uv for the full path)

Legacy vs modern (2026-07-28): legacy remembers you with a session; modern is stateless and every message carries its context. Sampling is deleted (call the provider directly). Elicitation and ping need mode="legacy". Deprecated means at least 12 months before removal is eligible. (Ch 17)

In LangChain (Ch 18):

async with MCPAdapter(transport_or_url_or_client_or_group) as adapter:
    tools = await adapter.list_tools()
    agent = create_agent(model, tools)          # use the agent INSIDE the block

Tool errors (isError) become status="error" messages. Transport failures raise. Elicitation becomes an interrupt(). Auth goes on the Client.

Multi-agent (Ch 19)

Situation Pattern
A central agent coordinates distinct domains Subagents
Behaviour changes as a task progresses Handoffs (state field plus wrap_model_call, tools return Command)
Many optional specialisations Skills (load_skill)
Independent sources, query at once Router (Send, reducer, synthesise)
None of these Custom workflow (StateGraph)

Default to one agent. Handoffs and skills are cheaper on repeats (about 5 vs 8 calls). Subagents and router win on parallel topics.

Interview one-liners

  • Why LangChain? A harness: tool schemas, messages, the loop and provider switching, so I focus on behaviour.
  • bind_tools? Makes the model aware. Does not execute.
  • Why a schema? Free text is not a contract.
  • Why filter tools in middleware, not the prompt? A prompt can be talked around. A missing tool is not an option.
  • State vs context? State is mutable and persists. Context is immutable per run.
  • Why MCP? One server maintained by the provider instead of every team rewriting the same wrapper.
  • Why JSON-RPC? Lightweight, transport-agnostic, two-way, notifications built in.
  • Does shutdown use JSON-RPC? No. It is the transport's job.
  • Who calls the tool? The client or agent. Never the model.
  • When multi-agent? Only when tools, context, teams or latency demand it.

  4. Name two retriever search_type options and how they differ. (Ch 20)
  5. What is the difference between short-term and long-term memory in an agent? (Ch 6)
  6. Why would you choose TypedDict over a Pydantic BaseModel for structured output? (Ch 4)
  7. What does a checkpointer do, and what breaks if you forget it? (Ch 6)

Project idea: guideline Q&A with RAG

Goal: upload a handful of public guideline PDFs and answer questions using only their content.

  • Chunk with overlap, embed, store, retrieve the top three, answer from them.
  • The prompt must say "I do not know" when the answer is not in the documents. Test it with a question that is not covered.
  • Stretch: compare similarity, multiquery and contextual retrieval on the same ten questions and record which wins.

NoteReal data

What was run, and what was not

On 31 Oct 2026 I ran what can run without keys or a cloud account (Python 3.13, langchain-core 1.7, chromadb 1.5, langchain-chroma).

  • build/rag_foundations_test.py has 9 checks, all passing: the splitter settings (1,000 characters, 100 overlap), sha1 chunk ids replacing rather than duplicating and surviving a restart, the LCEL chain shape, similarity versus MMR on near-duplicates, multi-query de-duplication and reciprocal rank fusion arithmetic. These use fake embeddings and a stand-in model, so they check the logic, not answer quality.
