RAG · Chapter 1

RAG explained: why, and what the parts are

A model cannot know your documents. RAG looks the right pages up first and answers from them. This chapter shows the two stages, the ways basic RAG fails, and the eight parts you choose between.

RAGMeridian slides, module 415 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Companies keep rules in PDFs. A general chatbot has never seen them, so it either refuses or guesses. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) is the open-book exam: fetch the relevant documents first, then answer from them. The answer is only as good as what is retrieved.

Key ideaPrerequisites

Read Python and Agent Foundations chapter 2 first (embeddings, context window, hallucination). The examples come from Meridian, a fictional procurement app; its full tour is the last chapter of Agentic AI with LangChain.

Core ideas

The two stages

the model cannot know your documents; RAG is look up, then answer. Two stages: index once (read, chunk, embed, store), then per question (embed the question, find the closest chunks, prompt, answer). Keyword search misses what meaning search finds (for "who has to approve a very expensive order" they share no useful word). A "meaning map" shows 22 sentences as dots. Eight things go wrong, and a confident wrong answer usually means the right chunk was not retrieved.

Types of RAG, and when basic RAG hurts

basic RAG hurts when the words differ, the answer is split across chunks, or the right chunk is not first. Improve it before the search (change the question), during (change what is searched or how), after (clean the results) or beyond it. The site compares thirteen variants (I saw these among them: multi-query, contextual compression, HyDE, query decomposition, follow-up rewrite, hybrid search and reranking) and names four bigger ideas, of which I saw three: corrective RAG grades the retrieved chunks and tries again if they are poor, agentic RAG lets an agent decide whether, what and how often to search, and graph RAG works from a graph of the documents. Which first: right chunk found but not first, try reranking; users phrase things differently, try multi-query or HyDE; several-part questions, decomposition. Meridian uses three: similarity, multiquery and contextual (first-run times 7.1, 12.0 and 9.7 seconds).

The eight parts, and choosing tools

a RAG system has eight parts (parse, chunk, embed, store, retrieve, rerank, generate, evaluate), each a decision. For embeddings check dimensions (768 here), languages, input length, hosted or open, and the rule that one model must index and search. Choosing a vector database: how many vectors, do you already run Postgres or Elasticsearch, filtering, managed or self-run, cost.

The instructor's plain-language RAG guide

From "RAG, Properly Explained", part 4 of the instructor's series (read in full). Its figures about Anthropic's research are as the guide states them.

  • The problem. Your company's refund policy, contracts and wiki were never in any model's training data, and retraining on them is slow, expensive and would absorb private text into the model. What you need is to hand the model the right document at the moment it is asked.
  • Closed book versus open book. A plain LLM sits a closed-book exam from memory, so its answer can be stale or invented. RAG makes it open-book: the relevant pages are handed over first and it answers from them.
  • The library analogy, one to one. Books are your documents; right-sized chunks are the sections; the librarian is the embedding model; the card catalog is the vector database; the research assistant is the generation model (Claude). The librarian appears twice: once cataloguing, once looking up your question.
  • Setting up (once). Cut documents into chunks (too small loses meaning, too large blurs topics), embed each chunk, and store the vectors. Chunks about the same topic land near each other even if they share few words.
  • Using it (every question). Embed the question with the same model, find the nearest chunks, assemble a prompt (system instruction to answer only from the context, the chunks, the question) and send it to the model. Switching embedding providers without re-embedding everything breaks retrieval silently.
  • The whole pipeline. Raw data, information extraction (OCR, PDF parsing, crawlers), chunking, embedding, vector database; then query, embedding (same model), vector database, relevant chunks, model, response.
  • Do you even need RAG? If the whole knowledge base fits in the context window (the guide, following Anthropic's guidance, says under roughly 200,000 tokens, about 500 pages), you can paste it in and use prompt caching. Use RAG when the knowledge base is larger, changes constantly, or must be scoped per user or permission. Many systems use both.
  • Vector databases. Their job is storing vectors and answering "what is nearest" in milliseconds. The guide names Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector and Milvus, and says nearly all support hybrid search now, so the choice is mostly managed versus self-run and whether it fits a database you already run.

From the Meridian slides in full: chapters 13 to 15

Module 4 of the Meridian course slides (125 slides) was read in full on 31 Oct 2026. This section adds what the earlier digest left out.

Chapter 13, the idea, with real recorded answers. Asked "what payment terms do servo motor suppliers get at Aldermoor?" with no documents, the model (gemini-3.8-flash, temperature 0, 10 Oct 2026) gave generic advice that such terms are private and negotiated. With the procurement policy page in the prompt, it answered exactly: Net-45 for low-risk vendors with a credit score of 75 or more. The slides then test the prompt's honest exit across combinations of pages. With the instruction "answer only from the context, otherwise say you don't know" switched on, the tariff page alone gave "I don't know", and the policy page alone gave Net-45 even with the tariff page as a distraction. With the instruction off, the model answered from the policy page when it had it, and without it gave generic advice. One sentence in the prompt is what makes an honest refusal reliable.

The two stages in the project's settings: index once (PyPDFLoader reads each page and remembers the file name; RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter cuts chunks of about 1,000 characters with 100 overlap; an embedding model returns 768 numbers per chunk; Chroma saves numbers and text, with stable ids so re-indexing replaces) and then per question (embed the question with the same model, take the nearest three chunks, build the prompt, let Gemini answer). Real closeness scores sit in a narrow band (0.85 for the right sentence against 0.55 and 0.57 for the others), so compare scores with each other, never with zero.

On 22 sentences from the four sample documents and eight questions, keyword search found a correct sentence in its top three for 2 questions and meaning search for 8 (the instructor's own judgement of "correct"). For "who has to approve a very expensive order?" the sentences share no useful word, yet meaning search finds the EUR 250,000 and EUR 1,000,000 approval lines. For "when do we pay servo motor suppliers?" the nearest by meaning were the right sentence (0.67), the servo-motor tariff line (0.67) and a wrong-risk-class line (0.66), which is why ranking matters.

The eight things that go wrong, with the symptom, cause and fix.

Symptom Likely cause What to do
Confident but wrong The right chunk was not retrieved, or a near miss came first Look at the retrieved chunks before blaming the model; try another mode, a larger k, or a reranker
"I don't know" though the file has the answer The chunk was never found: wrong chunk size, a scanned PDF with no text, very different words Check the PDF has real text, try smaller chunks, try multi-query
Mixes two documents Chunks from different topics came back together Smaller k, rerank, filter by source, or contextual compression
Ignores the files The prompt does not force the context Keep "if you don't know based on the context, say you don't know"
Worse after changing the embedding model Index and search use different models Re-index everything with the new model; never mix
The same sentence twice A file was indexed twice with random ids Stable ids from file, page and position
Slow Each model-based step (rewrite, trim, rerank) adds a call Use plain similarity unless the question needs more
Key sentence cut in half A chunk boundary fell mid-sentence Overlap, recursive splitter, chunks large enough for a whole idea

Chapter 14, thirteen variants, each with a pipeline, a best use and a cost. Basic RAG hurts three ways: different words ("expensive order" versus "purchases above EUR 250,000"), wrong order (the right chunk is third), and noise or gaps. The variants improve it in four places.

Where Variant Idea Cost
Before the search Multi-query The model writes 3 rewrites; search all 4; merge 1 extra model call and 4 searches (12 s against 7 s in the run)
HyDE Search with an imagined answer (never shown or trusted) 1 extra call
Query decomposition Split a many-part question; search each; merge 1 call plus several searches
Follow-up rewrite "And for moderate risk?" becomes a standalone question 1 call per turn
During Hybrid Keyword and meaning rankings fused (often reciprocal rank fusion) A second index to keep
MMR Relevant but unlike each other A little computation
Parent pages Search small pieces, return the whole page Bigger prompts
After Reranking Fetch many, a stronger judge reorders (for example 20 down to 3) Latency and a reranker call
Contextual compression Fetch 10, the model copies only the relevant sentences (one call per chunk); one 844-character chunk shrank to 193 Many small calls
Corrective RAG Grade the results; if poor, rewrite and search again Extra calls
Beyond Agentic RAG An agent decides whether, what and how often to search Most expensive, least predictable
Graph RAG Entities and relations; follow links Building and maintaining the graph
Multimodal RAG Index images and tables too Heavier parsing

Which to try first: right chunk found but not first, rerank; users phrase things differently, multi-query or HyDE; questions with several parts, decomposition; chat follow-ups, rewrite; exact names or codes missed, hybrid; long noisy chunks, compression; near-duplicate results, MMR; the answer needs surrounding text, parent pages; the model answers when the documents don't cover it, corrective RAG. Meridian implements three (similarity, multiquery, contextual), timed at 7.1, 12.0 and 9.7 seconds in one run and 5.0, 9.8 and 5.8 in another: the numbers varied, the order held.

Chapter 15, the tools. The eight parts (parse, chunk, embed, store, retrieve, rerank, generate, evaluate), with the slide's example tools:

Part Examples In Meridian
Parse pypdf, PyMuPDF, Docling, Unstructured, LlamaParse, Google Document AI PyPDFLoader (pypdf)
Chunk Recursive, semantic or layout-based splitters Recursive, 1,000 and 100
Embed Gemini, OpenAI, Cohere, Voyage, BGE-M3, Qwen3-Embedding, Nomic gemini-embedding-001, 768 numbers
Store Chroma, FAISS, pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Pinecone, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch Chroma locally, Vertex AI Vector Search in the cloud
Rerank Cohere Rerank, BGE reranker, cross-encoders, a model as judge Not in the project (shown in the lab)
Evaluate RAGAS, DeepEval, TruLens, LangSmith, your own question list A five-question lab

Embedding models: check how many numbers, languages, how much text it accepts, hosted versus open, and use one model for both indexing and search; leaderboards such as MTEB change every few months, so test on your own documents. Vector databases store vectors with text and metadata, find neighbours, filter and update; exact search compares every vector, approximate search (often an HNSW index) looks at a clever subset, faster at millions with a small chance of missing the best match. Five questions to choose one: how many vectors (thousands: Chroma or FAISS; millions: Qdrant, Weaviate, pgvector or managed; billions: Milvus or managed); do you already run Postgres (pgvector) or Elasticsearch or OpenSearch; do you want to run servers; do you need filters or keyword search; where must the data live. Region, privacy and contracts can decide before performance does. Frameworks save plumbing, not thinking: LangChain here, LlamaIndex for indexing and querying, Haystack for typed pipelines, DSPy for tuning, or none.

Interview corner

What is RAG?

Find the right pages first, then answer from them: an open-book exam. Chunks of your documents are embedded, stored in a vector database and retrieved by meaning, then given to the model with the question.

How does it stop the model making things up?

The prompt says to answer from the retrieved context and to say "I do not know" otherwise.

RAG · Chapter 2

Embeddings, storing meaning and ingestion

How text becomes numbers, where those numbers are kept, and how a PDF is cut into chunks so the same file can be re-indexed without duplicates.

RAGMeridian slides and code15 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Ingestion decisions (chunk size, overlap, which embedding model) decide what retrieval can ever find. If they are wrong, no clever retriever can repair it.

Core ideas

Talking to Gemini and turning text into numbers

one shared model connection, created on first use with lru_cache. extract_text joins Gemini's content blocks because a reply may be a list of blocks. Real closeness scores sit in a narrow band (0.85 for the right sentence against 0.55 and 0.57 for the others), so unrelated is not zero. Numbers from two embedding models are like temperatures in two unknown units: they cannot be compared.

Storing meaning, and keeping the originals

a vector store keeps numbers, text and source, and survives a restart because Chroma writes to a folder. Keep the originals: a new embedding model, chunk size or bug fix means re-indexing everything. basename keeps only the file name so an uploaded name cannot write outside the folder.

Ingestion

three reasons to cut (a document is too big, one vector for a page describes everything and nothing, and a sentence can be lost). Chunk ids are a sha1 of source, page and position, so indexing the same file twice replaces rather than duplicates (the count stays at one).

Ingestion in the Meridian code

Ingestion: PDF, then pages, then chunks of about 1,000 characters, then embeddings, then Vector Search. Neighbouring chunks share 100 characters (CHUNK_OVERLAP = 100) so sentences are not cut off. Each chunk keeps its source in metadata so an answer can be traced to a file.

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=CHUNK_SIZE, chunk_overlap=CHUNK_OVERLAP)

Embedding settings come from configuration: the embedding model must output 768 dimensions to match the Vector Search index. A mismatch is a classic deployment bug.

Local and cloud stores

The app has one switch, APP_MODE, that decides which vector database sits behind ingestion and retrieval.

Concern Local Cloud
Embeddings gemini-embedding-001 (API key) text-embedding-005 (Vertex AI)
Vector database Chroma in .meridian/chroma Vertex AI Vector Search
Original PDFs .meridian/uploads/ A Cloud Storage bucket

Everything that needs storage asks one question (settings.is_cloud) and receives a LangChain VectorStore, so ingestion and retrieval never know which database is behind them. This is the strategy pattern: same interface, swappable implementation. Both modes use 768-dimensional vectors, but the two databases are separate, so re-upload after switching. The deployment side of APP_MODE is in the last chapter of the LangChain book.

From the Meridian slides in full: chapters 16 to 18

Chapter 16, the model and the embeddings (rag/llm.py 35 lines, rag/embeddings.py 41). Two jobs need the model (answering and later the audit agents), so one shared connection avoids two configurations. get_llm() is created on first use, not on import, so the API can start and answer health checks before any key exists, and lru_cache keeps one object. An empty key raises ConfigurationError with the address to get a key (HTTP 503 in the API). Gemini may reply with a list of content blocks, so extract_text keeps every text block and joins them; a plain string passes through. A gotcha found while writing the variants lab: reply.text is a special string type that the Google embedding client rejected (a 500 INTERNAL), while extract_text(reply.content) returns a plain string and works. embeddings.py follows APP_MODE: local uses gemini-embedding-001 through the Gemini API with a key; cloud uses text-embedding-005 through Vertex AI with Google Cloud credentials; both give 768 numbers, through one class (GoogleGenerativeAIEmbeddings, with vertexai=True for the cloud). embed_query turns one question into numbers; embed_documents does several at once, which is what indexing uses. Numbers from two models are like temperatures in two unknown units, and a store built for 768 numbers refuses 3,072. Change the model and you must re-index everything and keep one index per model; local and cloud both give 768 numbers but are different models, so never point cloud queries at a local index.

Chapter 17, storing meaning (vector_store.py 54 lines, document_store.py 80). The vector store keeps each chunk's numbers, text and source, finds nearest chunks, and survives a restart because Chroma writes to a folder (.meridian/chroma). The rest of the code uses only add_documents, similarity_search and as_retriever. The Chroma import sits inside the function so cloud images do not load it; the cloud path checks the settings with the Module 3 helper, raises an error naming any empty ones, imports Google Cloud packages only then, and builds the store from project, region, index and endpoint (stream_update makes new chunks searchable quickly). get_vector_store() connects on first use and one expression chooses the store from APP_MODE. The vector database holds chunks, not PDFs, so a new embedding model, chunk size or bug fix means re-indexing from the originals; document_store has save (a folder locally, a bucket in the cloud) and pdfs, a context manager that downloads to a temporary folder in the cloud and yields a path and a source name (local://file.pdf or gs://bucket/file.pdf) that is saved in every chunk. basename keeps only the file name so an uploaded name cannot point outside the folder.

Chapter 18, ingestion (data_ingestion.py, 73 lines). Three reasons to cut: a whole document is too big and costs more the longer it is, one set of numbers for a whole page describes everything and nothing, and a sentence is often the answer. The four sample PDFs are 645, 664, 845 and 950 characters, so each is exactly one chunk; the chunking matters for your own longer documents. PyPDFLoader reads page by page; the splitter uses 1,000 and 100; split_documents keeps each page's metadata. Chunk ids are a sha1 of source, page and position, so the same chunk always gets the same id and indexing again replaces instead of duplicating (the lab shows the count staying at one; random ids would give two and duplicate answers). ingest_pdf reads, turns a bad PDF into an IngestionError (HTTP 422), stamps the source on every page, cuts, assigns ids, embeds and stores. ingest_stored_pdfs logs where it is indexing, opens every stored PDF, calls ingest_pdf for each and counts files, pages and chunks (four, four, four); an empty store is a warning, not an error. The upload endpoint uses ingest_pdf and the "index everything" button uses ingest_stored_pdfs. Only text PDFs work: a scan has no text until OCR is applied.

From the docs: a semantic search engine in LangChain primitives

From the LangChain tutorial Build a semantic search engine, read in full on 31 Oct 2026. It is the generic version of what Meridian does.

  1. Document. LangChain's unit of text: page_content, a metadata dict (source, relations) and an optional id. A document is often one chunk of a bigger file.
  2. Embeddings. Vector search stores numeric vectors and compares a query vector of the same dimension by cosine or similar. The page lists many providers (OpenAI, Azure, Google Gemini, Vertex, Bedrock, HuggingFace, Ollama, Cohere, Mistral and others) behind one interface, and a deterministic fake for tests.
  3. Vector store. Add and query Documents with similarity metrics. Choices span in-memory (InMemoryVectorStore), hosted and self-run stores (Chroma, Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus, PGVector, MongoDB and others), all behind the same methods.
  4. Load and split a PDF. A page is often too coarse, so split it. RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter splits recursively on common separators until chunks reach the target size and is the recommended splitter for generic text; the page uses chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200, add_start_index=True (which keeps each chunk's character offset in start_index). A 107-page filing became 516 chunks.
  5. Index and query. add_documents indexes the chunks. Query by string (similarity_search), async (asimilarity_search), with scores (similarity_search_with_score; here the score is a distance, so lower means closer, and meaning varies by provider) or by vector (similarity_search_by_vector). Search by similarity or by maximal marginal relevance.
  6. Retrievers. A vector store is not a Runnable; a retriever is, so it supports invoke and batch sync and async. Wrap a function with @chain, or use vector_store.as_retriever(search_type=..., search_kwargs={"k": 1}). Search types: "similarity" (default), "mmr" and "similarity_score_threshold" (filter by score). Retrievers can also wrap non-vector sources. The next step is a RAG app that combines question and retrieved context in a prompt.

The Meridian code compares with this directly: it uses the same splitter with 1,000-character chunks and 100 overlap, and its three retrieval strategies are functions built on the same retriever idea.

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Embedding dimensions not matching the index Indexing or search errors Use a 768-dimension embedding model
Re-embedding with a different model but keeping old vectors Meaningless scores One model must index and search; re-index everything
Throwing away the original files Cannot re-index after a change Keep the originals

Interview corner

Why do chunks overlap?

So a sentence cut at a chunk boundary still appears whole in the neighbouring chunk. Meridian uses chunks of about 1,000 characters with 100 characters of overlap.

What breaks if the embedding model's output size differs from the index?

Indexing or search fails: the index expects 768 dimensions, so the embedding model must output 768.

RAG · Chapter 3

Retrieval and the answer chain

Three retrieval strategies with one signature, wrapped into a sixteen-line chain that answers only from the retrieved text.

RAGMeridian slides and code15 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

Retrieval is where answers are won or lost. Seeing retrieval as "question in, documents out" makes every variant in the next chapter easy to add.

Core ideas

Retrieval: three strategies, chosen by a parameter:

Strategy What it does
similarity (default) The 3 chunks closest in meaning to the question. Fast
multiquery Gemini rewrites the question several ways and merges the results
contextual Fetch 10 chunks, then Gemini trims each to the relevant part 
rag_chain = create_retrieval_chain(build_retriever(retriever_type), question_answer_chain)

The system prompt says: use the retrieved context, and if you do not know based on the context, say so. That is the guard against making things up. Try it: ask something not in the documents and the answer should say it does not know.

def build_rag_chain(retriever_type: str = "similarity"):
    """question (str) -> answer (str), written as one LCEL pipeline."""
    return (
        {"context": build_retriever(retriever_type) | format_docs, "input": RunnablePassthrough()}
        | ANSWER_PROMPT
        | get_llm()
        | StrOutputParser()
    )

Each strategy is a plain function from a question to a list of documents:

Choice in the screen retriever_type What it does Trade-off
Normal similarity The 3 closest chunks (k=3) Fastest
Multi-Query multiquery The model writes 3 alternative phrasings with structured output, searches with all 4, and merges while dropping duplicates Finds more, slower
Contextual Compression contextual Fetches 10 chunks, then the model copies only the relevant sentences from each (or replies NO_OUTPUT, which drops the chunk) Cleanest, slowest

The legacy helpers moved to langchain-classic in LangChain v1, so the two advanced strategies are written out in a few lines each, which is also easier to explain in an interview.

Beyond the classRetriever search types in LangChain

Any vector store becomes a retriever with .as_retriever(), which accepts a search_type: "similarity" (closest by meaning), "mmr" (maximal marginal relevance: relevant and diverse, so you do not get three near-duplicate chunks) or "similarity_score_threshold" (only chunks above a relevance score), plus search_kwargs such as k. Because every vector store implements the same interface, swapping the database is a one-line change. Source: the course's LangChain interview question PDF.

Repo noteThe retrieval code imports from `langchain_classic`

retrieval.py imports chains and retrievers from langchain_classic (the legacy package from Chapter 2) while the agents use the current create_agent. The project mixes old and new, which is realistic. Know which parts are Classic when you read it.

The chain, step by step

three strategies with one signature (question in, documents out) chosen from a dictionary, wrapped in RunnableLambda, then the whole chain in sixteen lines. Contextual compression runs batch over the chunks in parallel. Similarity is one model call, multi-query two, contextual one plus one per chunk.

The lab: ask the four documents

write the expected answers first, because a test without an expected answer is just a demo (EUR 2.84 billion, Net-45, 2.2 percent, 10 years, an honest refusal). All five matched in about 24 seconds. Ask the log, not memory: each question leaves a RAG query received line.

From the Meridian slides in full: chapters 19 and 20

Chapter 19, retrieval.py (115 lines). Retrieval has four jobs: find the closest chunks (three strategies with one signature, question in and documents out), format them as one block with source names, instruct the model to answer only from that text, and answer. The system prompt is a job description whose second sentence is the honest exit. A second prompt, used only by contextual compression, returns the marker NO_OUTPUT for "nothing relevant". The plain search is one line: ask the store for the k=3 closest chunks. Multi-query uses with_structured_output so Gemini returns an AlternativeQuestions shape (one model call, three rewrites), searches the original plus the three, and merges while skipping duplicates (up to four chunks). Contextual compression fetches ten chunks, builds a tiny chain (extraction prompt, model, text), runs batch over the chunks in parallel and drops empty answers and NO_OUTPUT; in the run one 193-character chunk survived. A dictionary of functions picks the strategy from the API's retriever_type, falling back to similarity with a warning; RunnableLambda wraps a plain function so it can join the pipe; format_docs joins the chunks with their source names. The chain, in sixteen lines: question in, context retrieved and formatted while the question passes through, both fill the answer prompt, the shared Gemini model, a string parser; read the pipe as "and then". This is LCEL.

Mode Model calls In the prompt One run
Similarity 1 (the answer) 3 chunks 7.1 s
Multi-query 2 (rewrite, answer) up to 4 chunks, merged 12.0 s
Contextual 1 plus one per chunk fetched only the relevant sentences 9.7 s

All three answered Net-45 correctly; the differences are cost and prompt size. Start with similarity, move to multi-query for vague questions or documents that use other words, and to contextual when chunks are long and noisy.

Chapter 20, the lab. A test without an expected answer is just a demo, so the answers are written first: revenue FY2024 about EUR 2.84 billion; servo-motor payment terms Net-45; customs duty on programmable controllers from Japan 2.2 percent; filling-line equipment depreciated over 10 years straight line; and a deliberate fifth question, "who won the football World Cup in 2022?", whose right answer is an honest refusal. All five matched in about 24 seconds (the refusal's wording varies, the refusal does not). Every question leaves two log lines, RAG query received (question and mode) and RAG answer generated (the text), which is how you answer "what did the system say at 2 a.m.?". If something goes wrong: a wrong fact (check the log, then the chunks found, then try multi-query); "I don't know" for a covered question (the index may be empty: ingest again and expect four, four, four); a 503 or API error (the key or a retired model name, set VERTEX_LLM_MODEL_NAME); a real answer to the football question (the instruction line is missing from the prompt); slow answers (network, or a mode with extra calls).

Interview corner

What are the three retrieval strategies?

Similarity (top 3 by meaning), multi-query (the model rewrites the question several ways and merges results) and contextual (fetch 10, then compress each to the relevant part).

RAG · Chapter 4

Advanced RAG: seven ways to change retrieval

MMR, HyDE, hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion, reranking, parent pages, decomposition and follow-up rewrite, run on the same question so you can see what each one changes.

RAGMeridian slides, chapter 2115 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

When basic RAG returns the wrong chunk, you change the question, the search, or the results. This chapter is a small lab of the options, with the costs of each.

From Chapter 21 of the slides, read in full. It runs seven retrieval variants on the same 22 sentences from the four sample PDFs (ids P procurement, A accounting, R annual report, T tariff) and one question: when do we pay servo motor suppliers? The right answer is P1 (Net-45); T2 ("Servo motors: 2.7 percent" duty) is a tempting distraction; P2 and P3 are the same page but the wrong risk class.

def mmr(question, k=3):
    return store.max_marginal_relevance_search(question, k=k, fetch_k=10)

def hyde(question, k=3):
    reply = get_llm().invoke(f"Write one sentence that could answer this question: {question}")
    imagined = extract_text(reply.content)      # a plain string; reply.text breaks the embedding client
    return store.similarity_search(imagined, k=k)

def hybrid(question, k=3):
    by_meaning = [d.metadata["id"] for d in store.similarity_search(question, k=len(DOCS))]
    fused = {}
    for ranking in (keyword_rank(question), by_meaning):
        for position, id_ in enumerate(ranking):
            fused[id_] = fused.get(id_, 0) + 1 / (60 + position)   # reciprocal rank fusion
    return [BY_ID[i] for i in sorted(fused, key=fused.get, reverse=True)[:k]]

def rerank(question, k=3):
    candidates = store.similarity_search(question, k=8)            # over-fetch
    # ask the model to score each candidate 0-10 (structured output), keep the best k
Variant Idea Cost What came back (one run)
Basic Plain similarity None P1, T2, P3: answer first, distractor and wrong class come along
MMR Fetch 10, pick 3 that are relevant and different None P1, T2, T4: more variety, but here that meant another unrelated sentence
HyDE Search with an imagined answer instead of the question One model call P1, P4, T2 (other runs: P1, P2, P3): varies between runs
Hybrid Keyword ranking plus meaning ranking, merged with reciprocal rank fusion (60 is the usual damping constant; needs no weights) None extra T2, P1, P2: the word "servo" pushed the tariff line to first. Worst here
Rerank Over-fetch 8, the model scores each 0 to 10, keep the best 3 One model call P1, P3, P2: removed T2 from the top three. Best here
Parent pages Search small pieces, hand over the whole page None Whole procurement and tariff pages: answer with context, bigger prompt
Decomposition Split a many-part question into simple ones, search each, merge by id One model call Found both parts: T2 (duty), P1 (terms), T1
Follow-up rewrite Turn "And for moderate risk?" into a question that stands alone One model call "What terms do moderate risk vendors get?"

The keyword side is a home-made ranking (shared words weighted by rarity, i.e. inverse document frequency); real systems use BM25 or a search engine. Run on 10 Oct 2026 with gemini-3.8-flash and gemini-embedding-001; the page itself calls it an illustration, not a benchmark.

Key ideaWhat to take away

No variant wins everywhere (hybrid made this question worse, reranking made it better, and on another question it could flip), and each has a price: extra model calls, a second index, bigger prompts. Start with basic RAG, add one variant at a time, and measure on your own list of real questions with known answers. MMR and parent pages change what is returned (variety and context, no model cost); HyDE, decomposition and the follow-up rewrite fix the question (one extra call each); hybrid helps with exact terms; reranking removed the distraction in this test.

Other numbers the slides record (verified by the instructor on 10 Oct 2026): the four sample PDFs are 645, 664, 845 and 950 characters and each becomes one chunk; on eight questions over the 22 sentences keyword search found a correct sentence in its top three for 2 and meaning search for 8 (the instructor's own judgement of "correct"); the chunk explorer is a JavaScript port of RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter that matched the library on 120 size and overlap combinations; the 2D meaning map keeps only about 26 percent of the variance, so the ranked list is the truth; library versions were langchain 1.2.11, langchain-core 1.2.18, langchain-chroma 1.1.0 and langchain-google-genai 4.2.1. Not tested: Windows PowerShell variants and cloud mode for any file.

Contextual retrieval, and a typical Claude stack

From the instructor's RAG guide, which cites Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval research.

Chunking has a quiet cost: a chunk that reads fine inside its document can become meaningless once cut loose ("the plan costs $12 a month": which plan, whose pricing, what year?). Contextual retrieval has Claude write a short note onto every chunk before it is embedded (for example "from Acme's 2026 pricing page, describing the Pro tier"). The guide reports Anthropic's benchmark figures: about 49 percent fewer failed retrievals from context alone, about 67 percent with reranking added, at roughly $1.02 per million document tokens thanks to prompt caching.

Production systems also add hybrid search (blend meaning search with keyword search, for exact terms) and reranking (a slower second pass over the top results), which this chapter's lab compares.

A typical stack in the guide: chunk with a splitter, embed with an embedding provider (Claude has no embedding model of its own; Anthropic's recommended partner is Voyage AI), store in a vector database, embed the question with the same model, retrieve with hybrid search and rerank, send question plus chunks to the model. Claude can cite which retrieved passage backs each part of its answer, and prompt caching makes repeated context cheaper.

Interview corner

Basic RAG returns the right chunk third, not first. What do you try?

Reranking: over-fetch (for example 8), have a model score each candidate, keep the best few. It costs one model call. Measure it on your own list of questions with known answers.

What does reciprocal rank fusion do?

It merges a keyword ranking and a meaning ranking by adding 1 / (60 + position) for each list, so no weights are needed. Hybrid helps with exact terms but can hurt on other questions.

RAG · Chapter 5

Costs, errors and tests for a RAG app

The money trap of a managed vector database, the errors you will meet, and how to test a RAG app without cloud accounts.

RAGMeridian repo8 min read
Jump to a section

Why it matters

A RAG demo is cheap until a vector index is left running. The failure modes are also repetitive, so a short checklist saves hours.

Core ideas

Costs

Common trapVector Search bills by the hour

Vector Search is billed by the hour while deployed, even with no users; it is the main cost of the whole project and the likeliest surprise bill. Delete the index when you stop, and set a budget alert (an alert does not stop spending).

The Gemini API free tier has rate limits, and free-tier content may be used by Google, so upload only the sample documents. Cloud Run, Storage, Cloud Build and Secret Manager usually stay inside free allowances (the deployment chapter has the full table).

Errors you will see

You see Do this
Searches return nothing right after upload New data takes about a minute to become searchable
DefaultCredentialsError gcloud auth application-default login
HTTP 503 listing missing settings APP_MODE=cloud with an empty index id; fill the settings
Indexing or search errors after switching models Embedding dimensions must match the index (768)

Testing

Tests in backend/tests need no cloud accounts: the model is replaced by a stand-in, so the suite runs in seconds with no key. A test that has no expected answer is only a demo, so write the expected answer first.

Cloud costs and the Vector Search bill, from Meridian module 7 (read in full)

NoteSource

Meridian slides, module 7 (chapters 36 and 40 and the reference slides), read in full on 31 Oct 2026. The slides quote no prices on purpose, because prices change; check Google's pricing pages.

What can exist in the project, and what each costs.

If this exists What it means for the bill
An index deployed to a Vector Search endpoint Billed by the hour, right now, even when nobody asks; machines stay reserved. Undeploy the index, then delete the endpoint and the index.
A Cloud Run service Billed only while requests are handled (request-based billing); scaled to zero it costs nothing for compute.
Buckets, images in the registry, secret versions Small storage charges; delete them when finished.
Only the project, with billing linked Nothing until you create something. Deleting the project removes all of it (recoverable for 30 days).
  • Index sizing. Google recommends at least 2 replicas for its availability guarantee; the Meridian workflow sets no replica count, so check what yours got. The first deployment typically takes 20 to 30 minutes (the workflow waits up to 45 tries of 60 seconds). 768 dimensions must match the embedding model.
  • Per request. Cloud Run: one request-length of compute. Gemini: per token. An ask makes 1 model call (about 2 s); an audit makes 11 to 12 calls (about 9,000 tokens on a lite model, 18,000 on gemini-3.8-flash, 13 s to about 98 s). Logs hold full questions and answers, so they cost money and are sensitive.
  • A budget alert only emails. What stops the bill is switching things off, above all the deployed index. Also remember the Cloud Build bucket PROJECT_ID_cloudbuild and the images when you clean up.
  • A real failure worth knowing. Google can refuse an index deployment ("Not enough resources available") after several minutes. If the workflow carries on, the app starts without a search index and errors with "Index ... is not deployed to endpoint ...". Check deployedIndexes on the endpoint before uploading.
  • Cheaper for small data. The slides note that Postgres with pgvector is simpler and cheaper than a deployed index for a small amount of text; Chroma on your laptop uses the same LangChain interface and costs nothing.
  • Free trial: $300 for 90 days, a card that is only checked, no automatic charge; resources are deleted after a 30-day grace period (Google's Free Trial page as read on 25 Oct 2026, so check it).

Common mistakes

Mistake Symptom Fix
Leaving Vector Search running Surprise bill Switch it off when done; set a budget alert
Uploading private documents with a free Gemini key Content may be used by Google Use only the sample documents

Interview corner

What is the biggest cost risk of deploying it?

Vector Search, billed by the hour even when idle, and possibly with two replicas by default. Do the work in one sitting, switch it off and set a budget alert (which does not stop spending).

Cheat sheet

The RAG pipeline, the retrieval choices and the cost traps on one page. Every item links back to its chapter.

Quick referenceCode is condensed. See the chapters for the full versions
Jump to a section

The pipeline (Ch 1, Ch 2, Ch 3)

Once:      PDF -> pages -> chunks (~1000 chars, 100 overlap) -> embeddings -> vector store
Each ask:  question -> SAME embedding model -> nearest chunks -> prompt -> LLM -> answer

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=100)

chain = (
    {"context": retriever | format_docs, "input": RunnablePassthrough()}
    | ANSWER_PROMPT | llm | StrOutputParser()
)
answer = chain.invoke("When do we pay servo motor suppliers?")

The prompt must say: use the context, and if you do not know based on the context, say so.

Which retrieval? (Ch 3, Ch 4)

Choice Extra cost Typical reason
Similarity (k=3) none start here
Multi-query 1 model call the user's words differ from the document's
Contextual compression 1 call + 1 per chunk prompts are too long or noisy
MMR none results are near-duplicates
HyDE 1 call the question looks nothing like the answer
Hybrid (RRF) none extra exact terms matter (names, codes)
Rerank 1 call the right chunk is found but not first
Parent pages bigger prompt a chunk needs its surrounding page
Decomposition 1 call the question has several parts
Follow-up rewrite 1 call chat questions like "and for moderate risk?"

The last column is my short summary of each idea, not a rule from the slides. Reciprocal rank fusion: score = sum over rankings of 1 / (60 + position). No variant wins everywhere; add one at a time and measure on your own questions with known answers.

Rules that save hours

  • One embedding model must index and search; dimensions must match the index (768 here). Switching models means re-indexing, so keep the originals.
  • Chunk ids from a hash of source, page and position make re-indexing replace, not duplicate.
  • Local mode uses Chroma (a folder); cloud mode uses Vertex AI Vector Search. One setting, APP_MODE, switches them; the two stores are separate, so re-upload after switching.
  • New data takes about a minute to become searchable.
  • Write the expected answer first; a test without one is a demo.
  • Tests replace the model with a stand-in, so they need no key.

Costs (Ch 5)

If this exists It costs
An index deployed to an endpoint By the hour, even with no users: the main bill
A Cloud Run service Only while it handles requests
Buckets, images, secrets Small storage charges
Only a project with billing linked Nothing

A budget alert only emails. Switch things off: undeploy the index, then delete the endpoint and the index. For small data, Postgres with pgvector or local Chroma is cheaper.

Errors (Ch 5)

You see Do this
Nothing found right after upload Wait about a minute
DefaultCredentialsError gcloud auth application-default login
503 listing missing settings APP_MODE=cloud with an empty index id: fill the settings
Errors after switching models Dimensions must match the index (768)
"Index ... is not deployed to endpoint" Check deployedIndexes on the endpoint before uploading
